The Course of the Coal Strike in the Zagłębie and Kraków Districts

[Zagłębie — miners' strike.]
Bloody demonstrations — killed and wounded. — Workers' wives attack the strike-breakers.
As is known, last Thursday a strike broke out in the coal mines of the Zagłębie and Kraków districts. The first days of the strike passed quietly, but already on Sunday it came to
bloody events at Ksawera,
which claimed human victims.
The details of the bloody events are as follows.
On Sunday morning a crowd of workers gathered at Ksawera. Since those assembled behaved quietly, the police patrol of 3[?] men did not intervene. When the size of the crowd grew greatly, the patrol ordered them to disperse, but the crowd not only did not obey the order, but began throwing stones at the police, and from one spot revolver shots were also heard.
Because of the threatening situation the police fired into the air, to which the crowd responded with a stormy attack.
A larger police detachment arrived on the spot and drove the crowd apart with rubber truncheons and rifle butts.
On the spot the 20-year-old Kajda fell dead; Grampszyk[?] and Czajka were seriously wounded. On the way to hospital Grampszyk[?] died.
In the course of that day there were also clashes at Piaski, Klimontów and Czeladź, where the police prevented the planned meetings.
On Monday morning at the "Mars" mines and in Klimontów it came to
unrest of workers' wives.
Several dozen women with their children gathered on the grounds of the "Mars" mine and prevented the workers from going down into the pit. The police who were called in put an end to the incidents.
The same scene was also played out at the coal mine in Klimontów.
In connection with the strike, which has now lasted a whole week, there took place
mass arrests in Zagłębie.
After the bloody events at Ksawera were put down, many communists were arrested, among them well-known communist activists.
On Monday the workers at the smaller mines and the workers of the "Strem"[?] factory in Strzemieszyce also went on strike.
On the same day in the afternoon there took place the second
bloody clash, in Czeladź.
At 4.30 in the afternoon a meeting was held at the "Saturn" mine, attended by about 1.000[?] people.
After the meeting ended, the crowd moved off through the town. Among the crowd there was a large number of women who had been incited to go after the shops. This caused a panic among the Jewish population, and all the shops were closed. Thanks to the police, who dispersed those assembled, nothing serious happened.
A little later a crowd of about 600 people gathered in the market square and held a mass meeting. The communist activist Mrs. Dusziekan[?] appeared as speaker.
The arriving police were met with a hail of stones, and from the direction of the cemetery (cmentarz) revolver shots were fired at the police several times.
At first the police fired into the air, but when the attacks from the crowd intensified, the police fired a volley into the crowd. One man fell dead at once and a second died later.
Besides this, several persons were also wounded.
After the events the crowd took revenge on the Jewish merchant Gelbard, because the police had used Gelbard's telephone to call for help.
The crowd tried to force its way into Gelbard's shop. The police did not allow it. In revenge, all the window-panes of Mr. Gelbard's flat and of his shop were smashed.
On Tuesday a certain calm set in among the workers' circles. It may be that this was brought about by the bloody events of Sunday and Monday, and also by the authorities' permission to hold meetings in closed halls.
In the course of Tuesday all the mines were on strike, with the exception of the smaller mines, where work did go on.
In Grodziec the strikers did not allow work at the local cement factory, but the police dispersed the demonstrators.
Window-panes smashed in Sielec.
In Sielec groups of workers demonstrated and smashed the panes of shop windows and of passing taxis[?]. The demonstrators overturned sleighs with passengers. The wives of the coal miners took an active part in the outbreaks.
On Selecka[?] Street a sick girl was riding in a sleigh. A group of workers dragged the sick girl out of the sleigh. One of the group tried to take from the sick girl the few złoty she had on her.
On Tuesday
Dr. Moraczewski came to Zagłębie,
where he held a series of conferences with the Kielce voivode and the Będzin starosta on the present situation in Zagłębie.
Moraczewski is to remain in Zagłębie until next Sunday. During this time he will give lectures on the economic situation in Poland.
On Tuesday at 6.30 in the evening there took place
a communist demonstration in Sosnowiec.
On Dekerta Street a small group of young people gathered and forced a demonstration on Modrzejowska Street. This caused a panic, and all the shops were closed. Mounted and foot police soon appeared and dispersed the demonstrators. Several dozen persons were arrested.
What Must Be Realized.

[Sosnowiec — Jewish community; a new cemetery; opinion piece.]
(Jewish Sosnowiec has no other choice; it must fulfil its duty.)
Our abnormality [?], our crippledness, our helplessness can be felt at every step and in everything we touch here. Everywhere one can see that we are not what a people with composure and with normal living conditions ought to be. Against whom is this said? Against Sosnowiec. Here we hear that the Jewish kehilla no longer has a cemetery. And it has come to such a pass that — may everyone live and be well — as soon as it turns out that a plot of ground is needed, there will be nowhere [?] to find one in the existing cemetery, so that a committee has been formed which is to take up the creation of a cemetery.
It goes without saying that to carry out the undertaking one needs first of all money, and more money. If at all times it was not so easy to obtain from the Jews of Sosnowiec, now, in the prevailing difficult situation, it is certainly, most certainly hard. It is surely neither pleasant nor aesthetic nor effective to set out through the streets rattling the charity boxes and proclaiming that people should have pity and help buy and build the cemetery the town needs.
Decent people do not behave like this. Among the nations of the world such matters are settled quietly and modestly; the street knows nothing about it and one need not turn to anyone, let alone proclaim things and rattle the charity boxes.
But why go so far? Let us take a look not far from here, at our neighbours the German Jews. They too do it quietly, nicely, modestly, so that one need not turn to anyone, and the order is after all so exemplary, so solid and so awe-inspiring.
Does it not grate on the ears when the newspaper has to raise a racket and give its readers to understand that they must remember where they stand in the world and must not wait until it is too late? Is this a pleasant mission? Should the press have to deal with it? Is it at all a matter for the public? For the broad strata of the population — is it permissible for such questions to be touched on in the middle of the street? Could one not have brought a little order here, certain reforms? After all, we were given our own autonomous self-governing bodies, where we have the right to decide on our kehilla questions in general and on the clergy [klei kodesh] in particular. Why, then, has this very question never been settled as it should be? Why was there not, for this purpose, a kind of iron fund at our disposal? Did our kehilla leaders not know where they stood in the world? Did they really never give thought to this serious question? Possibly not. Well, is that in order? Did it have to be so? That is how it is with us: for everything there is enough patience, time and money. For quarrels and squabbles and feuds and all kinds of behind-the-scenes politics, and for insults and humiliations — we stop at nothing; but as soon as it comes to practical economic questions, to matters that must be solved without any excuse, nobody will touch them. As if it were a superfluous thing. As if one could manage without it, as if others would take care of it.
True, there is a Chevra Kadisha [burial society], which actually ought to have dealt with this. But what do I know — the Chevra Kadisha surely says: give us something to do and we will carry out our part; more than that we do not know, more than that we do not want to know or hear about anything.
Yes, unfortunately it must be stated that we lack understanding, cultural maturity, which would have awareness, attention and reverence for such sensitive problems, which one must understand how and in what manner to settle.
And had that existed among us, people would have known how to deal [?] with these delicate matters; the street would not have needed to know, and we would not have had to talk about a cemetery. And so — since we are poor and abnormal outwardly and inwardly, since there is so little understanding for the said question — it comes to turning to the newspaper, which must take upon itself the mission, sometimes of shouting and sometimes of advertising and agitating. It is woe and alas, and nice it certainly, most certainly is not; but what is one to do when interested people come, those who do not want the town to remain like sheep without a shepherd, and plead that there is no other way, only the newspaper must help to realize the necessary plan? It goes without saying that then one must come to the aid of the will of the communal activists, and we must treat the question in the columns of our newspaper.
The gmina [community] is poor, public life is dead and there is no one to sit down at the table with, so the respectable householders of Sosnowiec must not take the matter lightly. Thanks to the critical situation in which the country finds itself, the question can be solved on very favourable terms; therefore it is only right not to stand aside, but to set to work energetically to realize and fully carry out the procedure. As said, thanks to the crisis there is now an opportune moment to settle everything on good terms, so it must be exploited for the good of the town, for the good of the Jewish kehilla of Sosnowiec.
After all, we have in town, no evil eye, rich Jews, who ought to have [taken it as] a duty. A sacred obligation to carry out, or at least help carry out, what Jewish Sosnowiec needs.
Unfortunately, for various reasons our kehilla representatives find themselves in such circumstances that we can hardly get anything from them, and at best a minimum, so that we must help ourselves; we must ourselves take care both of our welfare and of the rest that awaits each of us after a hundred and twenty years.
So let us take stock of the conditions we are in and of the situation in which the Jewish people lives.
After all, this is not now about some luxury one can do without: even the smallest and poorest Jewish townlets have cemeteries, and if poor, helpless, tiny "tal-umatar" townlets [i.e. tiny, out-of-the-way places; tentative] can attain this, then at least it should not be hard for such a kehilla as Sosnowiec, no evil eye, to attain it.
Let Jewish Sosnowiec prove that we will no longer have to write advertisements and pitiful begging articles on this question; let our householders now show understanding and will in order to realize what is most necessary.
For this purpose it is first of all desirable that the committee that has been formed begin intensive activity and create a practical modus for how the question can be definitively solved for the good of the town.
It does not matter — Sosnowiec will give money, especially when it concerns such a necessity, when there is no other way; what is necessary is that the committee should know how to organise itself, how and in what manner to raise the money.
— That is what is necessary, that is what the leaders of the newly formed committee must be made aware of.
Dr. Papuri.
Suicide of a Warsaw woman in the Sosnowiec bathhouse

[Sosnowiec — suicide.] In the municipal bathhouse in Sosnowiec a young woman took a bath-room. The staff, seeing that the woman did not come out after the set time and that altogether there was silence inside, opened the door of the room. Only then did they see the woman lying without any sign of life.
The doctor who was called established that she had poisoned herself with opium, and ordered her to be taken to the hospital.
The suicide is from Warsaw. A few days ago she came to Sosnowiec and took lodgings in the hotel "Wiktoria".
Distraint by the Health Insurance Fund on the Będzin Talmud Torah
[Będzin — community and education; health insurance fund.] An official of the Health Insurance Fund (Kasa Chorych) placed a distraint (sequester) on the tables and benches of the Będzin Talmud Torah.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — weekly feuilleton.] By B. Amotz [Ben Amotz].

Children of today..
By nature I am a lover of little ones; I have sentimental feelings for them, for small children, and therefore, when I meet the little crowd, I listen with great curiosity to their way of conversing, their way of talking. With them, after all, the truth is still present; in a single word of a child there are more truths than in a speech by the greatest diplomat who sits at the round table in Geneva and delivers sermons on the disarmament of nations..
The conversation we mention here I overheard from a group of young girls, pupils of a gymnasium. At the beginning of their talk I had the impression that they were repeating the difficult words of their lessons, but later it became clear to me that I had made a big mistake, and that these inexperienced girls were in fact talking about "important" matters.. Often [?] they repeated the "on" [?], "randka" [a date], "morowy chłopiec" [a great guy] and other "pearly" expressions, which produced a tangle in my brain.
And on what occasion [?] did this come up?
Last Sunday I happened to meet many mothers who were coming back from Fürstenberg's gymnasium; their faces were covered with black clouds; they had been shaken by the result of the "cenzurki" [school reports]; the "dwójki" [failing marks], together with poverty — are multiplying...
And let me be permitted to say that a large share in these poor "results" [?] belongs to the parents themselves. On the pretext of being "modern" they give the children full freedom, they allow the children to look at [?] all kinds of pictures of erotic content, they do not check where they spend their free hours and do not listen to their conversations, whose content is "on kocha" [he loves], "morowy" [great], "ten całował" [that one kissed] etc..
.. children of today..

The "culture" season..
"The sun also rises and the sun goes down" — the sun comes up and goes down again. The crisis grows worse from day to day, the number of those without a livelihood keeps growing. But in this time new shining "stars" have appeared on the Będzin horizon, who "gladden" our spirits and "drive away" the gloom that has squeezed itself so freely onto our shoulders...
— If [?] you are curious to know who these new "spreaders of culture" are? Then [?] don't be so dazed [?] and sunk in the vanities of this world, but go and stand by any fence and read:
— "Under the direction of the well-known dramaturge and stage director Itsek Lapserdak the well-known play 'The Lost Goat' will be performed — after the 3rd bell the doors are closed"...
That is only a miniature of everything to be found on the countless posters that appear almost every day in the streets; for the "artists" have no great trouble putting on "theayter": in the course of a few days the rehearsals are finished, off they run to the president of some little society or other (in this field, thank God, we are rich...), and the honourable president is, after all, also a "cultured" man — it would not become him to refuse such an important goal
— putting on theatre...
Yes, as it were, the remedy is sent before the blow: there is a crisis, bitter and sour on the soul, and (thanks to our little societies...) great talents are discovered, who revive us with their "intellectual leaps" and drive the melancholy mood away from us..
— More power to you...

"Culture" is growing.
The Central Committee of "Aguda" [Agudat Israel] in Warsaw deserves a "yasher koach" for the good tidings which its organ announced this week to Polish Orthodoxy.
It is only a pity that the Dicksteins and the "Gamanzons" [?; perhaps a misprint for Natansons] did not live to see with their own eyes how far culture has already penetrated the Orthodox ranks. They, Polish Orthodoxy (read: "Aguda"), are no longer satisfied with their own Jewish organ, weekly journals and culture booklets, but are beginning to publish booklets of Torah novellae. Oh! A mistake was made [?] — I mean a weekly in the Polish language which (according to the prospectus) will acquaint "the Polish-reading public from among Jewish Orthodoxy with the great creations of the Jewish spirit"...
The new Agudist organ in the Polish language will probably be, among Hasidic daughters, the representative of the "Shulchan Aruch", and at the same time articles will be found there on how one must wage a struggle against those "who want to modernise Jewish life"...!
— But be that as it may, the news gave me great satisfaction, because
— Jewish culture is growing...

A gift to Esau...
There is an insurance society for employees. A well-known society; Jewish employees pay enormous sums into it. When the society built huge buildings in Sosnowiec and in Będzin — Jews were the first to rent flats there. But when the society has something to say to its Jewish members and tenants, then the society takes on "a different face" and addresses the Jews in a foreign language...
And when the society decided to reduce the rent for its tenants, it was published in the local Polish press, because the management of the local administration is "convinced that all Jews who are its members and tenants read and speak only Polish"...
Incidentally, we are not surprised that precisely this society avoids the Jewish press. As a moral one can, after all, point to the Jewish merchants who speak with enthusiasm about Jewish nationalism and are the first to place advertisements in the lowest antisemitic rags...
And just as "as the Jews do, so do the Christians", when Jewish cinema owners take no account of their Jewish patrons, when Jewish merchants avoid the Jewish press — it is no wonder that a Polish society does the same...
— A gift to Esau...
Landslayt, Respond!

(An open letter to the people of Będzin and Sosnowiec across the ocean).
The extraordinary situation that now prevails everywhere has greatly intensified the want and poverty among the Jewish population. As everywhere, the situation here in Zagłębie is very depressed. From day to day the sources of Jewish income grow ever smaller.
Poverty is penetrating places that were once well established on good and secure earnings.
From the outside it is hard to recognise the want and poverty in such homes. The rooms are adorned with various handicrafts, house plants. Everything is clean, pure — only the pockets are cleaner still. Days and weeks go by in which one gets through the day on a dry crust.
By every means the families in such homes try to cover up the prevailing want. Representatives of various institutions very often turn to such families for support, and one carries out the złoty to them with a cheerful face in order to mask the poverty.
The złoty that was meant for a pound of sugar, or for a midday meal, is given away for a ticket to a performance for the benefit of some unimportant[?] institution. But hunger and cold cannot be hidden for long.
In such cases the institutions must come to the families' aid with whatever and as much as they can. Owing to the growing poverty, the situation in the many existing institutions of our town has greatly worsened.
Families who half a year ago were still giving the institutions „the finest donation“ with an open hand now turn for support, themselves or through others.
The persons who run the institutions are burdened with great debts. And they ask the population for help, but in vain: people want to help, but there is nothing to help with.
The various events bring in negligible income. Until recently the institutions functioned more or less normally, because the population supported them by every possible means.
Today all the hungry and those without a livelihood stretch out their hands for help to their sisters and brothers who are in a better situation, to the landslayt in America and in other countries. It is known that the situation there is also hard, that the world crisis has ruined many people there too, yet for a large part of our landslayt the situation is bearable.
We turn to those landslayt who could still help their relatives and friends in the old home with something, and do not want to.
Our call is addressed to those who have entirely severed the threads with the old home, and when the representatives of the Będzin and Sosnowiec society turn to them for support, or with a „ticket“ (bilet) for an event for the benefit of the institutions of their native town, meet them with a cold refusal and indifference.
Let the landslayt remember that at the time when they possess large and comfortable apartments, when their children have the best conditions and are well fed, their parents or friends find themselves in the direst straits and want.
Support therefore the Zagłębie philanthropic institutions such as the Jewish hospital, „Beit Lechem“, Linat Cholim, Moshav Zkenim, Gemilut Chasadim and Malbish Arumim — support them with whatever you can, for the situation is catastrophic.
Perhaps now, when want and poverty are penetrating the great gates[?] of rich America and you are already forced to set up cheap kitchens for the hungry, your heart will tremble and you will give a thought to your „own“, who have been wrestling with want not since yesterday, but for a couple of years.
Not tens of dollars do our institutions ask of you; let everyone without exception save just one cent a day. Let everyone donate from his clothes what is no longer of use to him, and then the hungry will be fed and the naked clothed.
Do not throw the whole burden onto single persons; let all of you take part with a little something, and then you will bring great help and rescue many of your sisters and brothers in your old home from want and hunger.
Film, Then and Now

(Poland at the Prague Fair).
From our correspondent P. Lagsztajn[?].
Of all the fairs of the whole world, only Prague will have the privilege that Poland should officially take part with an exhibition of its own at the coming fair; at the present Prague Fair, which opens on the 13th of March of this year, a separate exhibition of films and of the film trade will be opened for the first time.
Starting from the film industry's first attempt up to today's sound film, one will for the first time be able to see the whole process the film industry has gone through until it reached its present state.
It will also be interesting to see how the great film companies were founded and what path of troubles and suffering they had to go through until they developed to their present state. To this is added the great, hard struggle that the big companies wage, competing with one another.
The very greatest film stars now in Europe, such as for instance Emil Jannings and others, will appear at special events in their various roles, which have made them famous throughout the whole world.
With the introduction of sound film it became clear to every nation that now is[?] the right time for its own national actors, greater and lesser, to show what they can do and so to take a position that will make them and the whole country known to the four corners of the world.
At the Prague Fair every nation, starting from America, Germany, Sweden down to Latvia, will exhibit its film production in its own pavilions and exhibitions, in order to promote its national film industry and its own artists.
Poland will exhibit several thousand pictures from its own films and of artists such as Kiepura and others, some of whom already have a name in the international film world, while some are known only in their own country.
The entire international film world will be able to see at the present Prague Fair how far the individual countries have developed in the film field and what their artists are able to achieve.
It will be an interesting exhibition, about which the whole world is very curious.
A Little Feuilleton. My Life. (A bit of autobiography of the English Pound)

I was born in a very lucky hour.
Unlike other currency-children, I never had to be nursed[?]. From my birth on I stood firmly on my feet. Experts foretold me a rich future, and so indeed it happened.
All the time I was growing up, God and men, one may say, envied me; I spread my rule over the whole world. All nations delighted in me, pampered me as one pampers an only son.
After the war my strength grew especially; I became sole ruler of the currency world. Merchants bought and sold and generally conducted their business by my standard.
But.. evidently it is not always uphill.
The latest world epidemic, called "crisis", touched me too and almost ruined my health.
Suddenly I got the "falling sickness", God save us, and it began to throw me about and toss me to all sides; I fall and rise, just like a little boat on the sea.
The French little franc, that feeble soul, who until not long ago was a poor wretch, suddenly got the strength of a giant and started to speak up. First of all his might took itself out on my health. He literally knocked me off my feet. From all sides they look into my eyes as at a dangerously ill patient, take my pulse — am I still alive, is there still a little life left in me.
May it all be on good years — what I have been through, ah!
On the whole, one may say, I am very weak. Yet I have still not lost my hopes. I feel inside me that in a short while I shall again be able to stand on my feet and teach the world some manners...
Yes, that will be right, but where does one get a little strength until salvation arrives?
Phew, for now there is no more strength to go on talking...
When better times come — I will tell you the rest.
Rebus.
From the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael Committee in Strzemieszyce.

Under the chairmanship of Shmuel Fajtman a meeting of the national youth taking part in the work for the K.K.L. [Jewish National Fund] in Strzemieszyce was held in the premises of "Maccabi".
When the chairman delivered the report on the activity to date, the resignation of the trustee David Horowicz[?] was considered; the meeting did not accept the resignation, but expressed to Mr. Horowicz[?] confidence in his further work.
Pini Baal Lashon. So It Was and So It Will Be...

Have you ever heard the story of how Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdyczów once came late to Kol Nidre?
Yom Kippur eve, at dusk. The synagogue is packed, not a pin could drop through. The wax memorial candles burn brightly and make the heat unbearable. Jews sit dressed in kittels and prayer shawls and sweat. The sun is setting. It is already long past Tefillah Zakkah. All eyes look to the tzaddik's little door; they wait for the tzaddik to open it and come in to Kol Nidre. But the door is closed. The congregation is impatient; meanwhile they say a chapter of Psalms — the tzaddik does not come in. It is getting very late. The unrest grows; they go up to the tzaddik's door and knock carefully — no answer. The congregation is already boiling, already guessing who knows what; they pluck up courage and open the little door — and lo, the room is empty, the rebbe is not there!
And the congregation set out to search for the tzaddik. No small matter — perhaps, God forbid, something had happened to him. They searched every little corner of the shtetl and... found him standing in a small poor little room, rocking a little nursing baby!
And it turned out that while the tzaddik was walking from the mikveh he heard a child crying very bitterly. He went into the little room to see what had happened. He found no one there, except the child in the cradle with a little bottle of sweet water at its side. He understood that the mother had run off to the synagogue to hear Kol Nidre and had no one to leave the child with. So he stayed there to watch[?] over it...
— Rebbe, how can it be — it's Kol Nidre! — the Hasidim ask.
— Oh, my dear ones, wiping away a child's tears is a far greater mitzvah!... — the tzaddik answered.
And if that tzaddik was permitted to be late for Kol Nidre over a little child's tears, then we may surely devote a feuilleton to a couple of weeping grown-up Jews.
For what is the whole merit of us feuilletonists in this sad world, if not to wipe away a tear now and then, and to lessen the gloom, and to lighten the worries, and to laugh away the laments?
What would we not do to make the world merry and call forth a sweet smile on its lips?
And just as if out of spite, this is the hardest piece of work nowadays. People weep and want us feuilletonists to weep too.
One man, a Jew, a teacher, writes me this sort of little sermon:
— "You play the wise guy and mock the world, when the world is going under and Judaism is going under. Are you not one who 'sings songs to a heavy heart' [Proverbs 25:20], singing ditties to a grieving heart?"...
And a second Jew writes me this sort of lament:
— "Let me have a good cry before you! And not, God forbid, because the times are not good — no! Thank God I have a livelihood; but simply because our Judaism is going under!"...
And the Jew tells that at home he has full bookcases of Jewish holy books of old, and he also buys new books every time. But when he sits and looks at his bookcases of books and reflects that after a hundred and twenty years all these books will[?] remain complete orphans, poor things, and there will be no one to take them in, because his children, the doctors, the dentists, no longer want to bring any Jewish book into their homes — then he sits and bewails Judaism and the Torah, which are going to ruin...
At once, as I read through these letters of my weeping Jews, I "girded the loins of my pen", as they used to say, and ordered it to wipe away those Jews' tears.
For how can one have such a robber's heart as to watch tears and stay calm? Let alone us, the professional "tear-wipers"!
And so I take heart and say:
— Do not weep, do not lament, dear Jews, wherever you are, and whatever your names[?] are!
It is not the world that is going under, nor Judaism that is going under. Everything turns in a wheel, down and up, up and down. And we, the people, help turn the wheel as always, sometimes higher and sometimes lower.
Both the world and Judaism have already had worse times — and nevertheless the world is a world, and the Jews are Jews.
And if we only want to, the world today is more beautiful and wiser than in the past; and Jews today are stronger and more respected than in the past.
Torah and luck, my friends, can never be passed on by inheritance. There are fathers who are great scholars and connoisseurs, and their children are great ignoramuses. So it has been from time immemorial, since Moses our Teacher gave the Torah. He himself did not leave behind him children like himself, and afterwards others came and learned his Torah.
Why this is so, nobody knows. A secret. Even[?] money, which parents amass and hand over into the hands of their heirs, does not always stay with them for long. Mostly the heirs get rid of it very easily and quickly; let alone Torah, for which one needs a head and something more... will and something more.. understanding and something more... Few things one needs to be a man of learning! A trifle!
Take our authors and writers themselves: would that we all had as many good years as the number of children who cannot read a word in their fathers' writings.
Well, should all these authors and writers sit and weep over it? It isn't even worth it!
They know that they are not the first and not the last; many great fathers had very simple children; and many simple fathers had very great children.
So it was, and so it will be.
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 13)

He finished his speech, and the face of the gradonachalnik [Russian city governor], which had earlier looked angry and frowning, was now much milder; his eyes, which had earlier looked so sharp and piercing, were now softer. He even smiled slightly with satisfaction. One could see in him that the baron's speech had made a very good impression on him. Because of that, hearts felt easier. The baron felt that a good report would be submitted to the high places (literally "the high windows"), and it was possible that this would help prevent the decree that the enemies of Israel were planning to carry out...

For a while there was silence. Then the rabbi's voice was heard:
— And now let us pray for the health of our heir to the throne, Alexander Nikolayevich!

The rabbi began to recite verses from Psalms, and the assembled repeated each verse after him. The rabbi recited with enthusiasm; from the depth of his heart he prayed for the health of the heir to the throne. He knew very well that the enemies of Israel would exploit the illness of the naslednik [heir] for their purposes, and that if the heir to the throne recovered, their plans would be thwarted as a matter of course. With his recitation he inspired all those assembled. All the faces were serious and devout; all repeated the verses with heartfelt warmth. The gradonachalnik now looked at the Jews with great respect and with deference.

The reciting of the Psalm verses took a while. Afterwards the cantor with his choristers, who stood lined up at the reader's stand, sang "Ha-noten teshua la-melakhim" ["He who grants salvation to kings" — the prayer for the ruler]. They sang very beautifully and with feeling. The gradonachalnik and his adjutants stood by at attention, holding their right hands at the peaks of their caps.

And with that the service came to an end.

The gradonachalnik was very moved and highly satisfied. He warmly shook the hands of the baron, the rabbi and Mr. Dimentshtein, thanked them heartily for the service, took a very friendly leave, and he and his adjutants left the synagogue.

The crowd began to disperse; everyone felt lighter in spirit. Mr. Dimenshtein said to the baron:

— And I will drive home. I reckon that my daughter must already be back from the Vyrubova; perhaps she has some news to tell.
The baron said:
— I will drive with you. I too want to hear what she has to tell.

— If you will permit me — the rabbi spoke up, turning to the banker — I too will come along with you.
— By all means! — exclaimed Mr. Diment-shtein.

All three left the synagogue together. Mr. Dimentshtein called a carriage, they got into it, and the driver was told to go to the banker's house.
Outside it was a dry, mild day at the beginning of winter. From beneath the pale clouds drifting over the capital the sun could be felt. All three now breathed easily, and their hearts too felt lighter.

The baron spoke up:
— It seems to me the service made a proper impression on the gradonachalnik.
— The gradonachalnik was very moved — Mr. Dimentshtein replied — after all, he openly expressed his satisfaction and thanked us so warmly.
— It is to be hoped that he will submit a report that will be favourable to the Jews — the baron said again.
— I believe so too — Mr. Dimentshtein agreed.

— And I think — said the rabbi — that our prayers have been heard and God will help...
— Let us hope! — said the baron.

They said no more among themselves. They sat in silence, and the carriage ran through the rich Petersburg streets. Mr. Dimens-shtein was impatient. It seemed to him that they were driving too leisurely, so every little while he called out to the driver:
— Izvozchik [cabman], drive a bit faster!

He was sure that Sonia had already returned from the Vyrubova, was at home and waiting for him. And he was very curious to hear what she had to tell. Perhaps she had learned some news!
When they arrived at the banker's house and went inside, they did not find Sonia. The servant announced that she had not yet returned. So all three went into Mr. Dimentshtein's study and decided to wait until Sonia came.
They did not have to wait long. Half an hour later Sonia arrived.

With great impetuosity Sonia burst into her father's study. Her face was aflame; her eyes wide open and brightly shining; her lips parted, and she was breathing as hastily as if she had run hard a stretch of the way until she got here.
The three men who had been waiting for her at once jumped up from their places; their faces became slightly flustered. Their eyes too grew larger and shone. Questions were heard:
— Well, what's the news?
— How do things stand?
— Is there any news?

Sonia nodded her head yes. There is news... but she was out of breath and could not bring out a single word.
Mr. Dimentshtein exclaimed:
— So there really is news?
Again Sonia nodded her head yes and tried to catch her breath.
— Then why are you silent? Speak! — her father stepped up to her.

The rabbi spoke up:
— Mr. Dimentshtein! Let her catch her breath first! Don't you see how out of breath she is?
Her father took her by both hands and led her to an armchair. Sonia sat down heavily. At last she caught her breath and said:
— Archimandrite Feofan... is about to fall...
— What are you saying?! — exclaimed Mr. Dimentshtein.

Sonia nodded her head:
— Yes, father!... The Vyrubova told me this in secret... She herself is his enemy and intrigues against him... This very evening he will fall and lose his influence at court... Someone else will take his place... She assured me that tomorrow the archimandrite will be removed from court; of his agitation one need no longer be afraid...

All three men received the news as truly great tidings. Feofan's fall was a great comfort to them... although they did not yet know who the other one was who would take his place, and how he would relate to the Jews. For the time being they would be rid of Feofan, who had been conducting a bitter agitation against the Jews at court.
The rabbi exclaimed:
— Thank God! Our prayers have indeed helped!...

It was already dusk. Sonia was in her own room. She lay tired on the sofa, resting after the exertions of the day. She lay quiet, quite quiet. Motionless, she held an open book in her hands, but she was not reading. Her eyes were now very dreamy, and with ardent longing she was now thinking of the young Baron Zinberg, for whom she had for a long time nursed a great love in her heart... Now, in the stillness of dusk, she saw him as clearly as if he were standing here before her eyes; he is young and handsome, tall and slender. His soft, dark-shaded hair lies tousled in locks on his head; his forehead is smooth, clear and high; his somewhat sunken face with its sharp features expresses tenderness and energy. His black, cheerful eyes look at her with great respect and love.

(To be continued.)
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tisa)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ki Tisa
The Portion
—o—
a) "That there be no plague among them when thou numberest them" (30:12)
The Jewish tax was a half-shekel, equal for poor and rich. For levying a tax according to people's material circumstances causes a plague. One pushes the other, each intrigues against his fellow: he is richer, he owns more, he should be assessed a bigger tax...
Mechok mi-Dvash [sic, = Matok mi-Dvash?].
—o—
b) The half-shekel (ibid., 13)
The half-shekel is the symbol of the Jewish collective. Each one by himself is a half. Mostly [?], those who keep the commandments between man and his fellow do not keep the commandments between man and God. One is pious towards God and another is honest towards people. Again: the rich do sometimes perform a commandment in deed, but not with the heart. The poor, on the other hand, "perform" commandments [—] [?] with the heart, with good will... Thus each one by himself is only a half, half of a truly complete Jew.
Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
c) "Ye shall keep the Sabbath" (31:14)
The Maggid of Dubno once came upon a band of heretics who were smoking cigarettes on the Sabbath. He rebukes them for desecrating the Sabbath in public. But the wild youths ask him:
— Where is it written in the Torah that one may not smoke on the Sabbath?
— With you I will hold no debates, — replies the Maggid, — because you are greater experts ("those who can") than I.
And at once he adds:
— When I want to smoke on the Sabbath — I cannot. You, however — can. I, when I want to eat before praying, cannot. You, however, can. And so with all the sins. So you are, after all, greater "can-ers"...
—o—
d) "And all the people broke off the golden rings which were in their ears" (32:3)
a.
"That thou hast brought a great sin upon them." —
Moses argued to Aaron:
One could have pleaded in the Jews' defence that with the calf they had erred, and they thought [sic, the print repeats "they thought that they"] that they were doing a commandment, merely wanting [?] an intermediary between God and man. But when Aaron ordered: "Break off the golden rings" — bring money — and the Jews hurried so and quickly brought the money, that is the best proof that it is no commandment. For if not for a bad thing, Jews are not so hasty with money...
Karnei Re'em (Additions of the Rosh).
b.
Aaron wanted to drag the matter out, so he told the Jews to take off the earrings "which are in the ears of your wives and of your daughters". For he knew that it would not go so fast, that the women would not give up their earrings so fast... The Jews knew it too, and — "they broke off the golden rings which were in their ears": they took them off their own ears. With the women they knew they would not achieve it so quickly...
Torat Moshe (Alshich).
—o—
e) "Go, get thee down, for [Thy] people have corrupted themselves" [printed "ha-Shem" for "thy people"] (ibid., 10 [sic; the verse is 32:7])
If the people have become corrupt, if the people have fallen low — "go down": you, Moses, must go along with them, must lower yourself into their abyss... That is the way of a leader.
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
f) "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people" (32:9)
a.
"I have seen" — it pleases me ("I see"); I want — says God — that "it is a stiff-necked people", that Jews should be a stiff-necked people; otherwise they will not endure the exile...
Mei ha-Shiloach.
b.
An old parable:
The face and the nape of the neck held a polemic between them. The face argues: I am more important. I hear, I see, I speak. But the nape laughs at it: you speak, see, hear — but I am turned away; all the slaps you get, and not I...
That is the badness [?] of stiff-neckedness: to be ready to give up hearing, seeing and speaking, as long as one gets no slaps, as long as one can wriggle out...
Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
g) "And rose up to play" (ibid., 6)
When the famous Empress Maria Theresa came to Prague after the Seven Years' War with Frederick the Second, the Jews arranged a celebration for her. Jewish girls arranged dances and entertainments.
Later the "Noda bi-Yehuda" [R. Yechezkel Landau] presented himself before her to greet her. Present too was an antisemitic general, of whom it was told that at a decisive moment of a battle he had been carousing somewhere in a house of pleasure, and therefore the battle ended in defeat.
The Empress admires before the "Noda bi-Yehuda" the Jewish girls who can dance so beautifully. The general cannot bear it and remarks:
— Well, yes, Jewish daughters can dance ever since the affair of the calf, when they danced around the calf..
The "Noda bi-Yehuda" answers him sarcastically:
— Certainly. The misfortune then was that "Moses delayed", that the general abandoned the army...
—o—
h) "Lord, why doth Thy wrath wax hot against Thy people, which Thou hast brought forth out of the land of Egypt" (ibid., 11)
What vexes You so — said Moses to God — these bad traits that You reproach them with, they brought them along from Egypt, from the land to which You drove them... It is the exile that made them so bad.
Kometz ha-Mincha.
—o—
i) "The noise of them that sing do I hear" (ibid., 18)
Had it been "the voice of them that shout for mastery", "the voice of them that cry for being overcome" — had the tribes merely quarrelled and wrangled — there would still have been hope for peace. But listen to all the partisan voices of might [?] — you will hear the echo of "kol anot anokhi" (the voice of "I"). The "I" cries out. Each one means only himself, only his own interest... and [?] then there is no help any more, then the Tablets are already broken...
Knesset Yisrael.
—o—
j) "And Moses called unto them... and all the rulers of the congregation" (34:31)
It does not say "the rulers of the congregation" but "rulers in the congregation", that is, those who were raised up by the congregation.
For only such leaders — whom the people raised up, and not those who raised themselves above the people — did Moses call to himself — — —
Imrei Shefer.
Three Years of the Dąbrowa City Council and the Merits of President Dr. Madejski

[Article — Dąbrowa Górnicza, city council and municipal economy.] 2.

In my previous article (see “Zaglembier Tsaytung” No. 8) I promised to shed light on the plans of the Dąbrowa magistrate [municipality] for the future in the [field][?] of the municipal economy. [Incidentally][?], one must bear in mind that in [—] all budgets, even government budgets, which envisage a certain programme for the future, the extraordinary budget too rests on external loans and on revenues: from the municipal enterprises such as the water supply, the power station and the tramways; from the servitudes [land-use rights] that have been abolished, thanks to which the industrialists will have to pay considerable sums in tax; from the slaughterhouse, which is shortly passing into the hands of the magistrate, etc. — which may perhaps bring about a reduction of the municipal taxes.

Before we turn to the plans for the future, what has already been achieved must also be recorded. Thus, with a loan amounting to 1.430 000 zł., a housing quarter was built in which 3643 tenants, i.e. 10 per cent of the local population, received model dwellings; and incidentally, this housing construction has eased the housing shortage in the town of Dąbrowa.

Among the industrialists who now pay for water is also the Sosnowiec Company [Towarzystwo Sosnowieckie], which, in return for the water right, gave the town a plot of 35 morgs. A garden will be planted on this plot. There is no need to point out the importance of such a park for the local inhabitants, who breathe in the coal gases and other “fresh smells”. May this garden not remain the only one; may the magistrate have the means to plant several gardens, so that the poorer part of the population, which cannot afford to go away to a dacha [summer cottage], may enjoy healthy air on the spot...

A second plan of first-rank importance is the new post-office building, which is to stand on Kościuszki Street.

When the project arose to build the post office on this site, it was foreseen that the wooden booths now[?] standing [around][?] Kościuszki Square would be cleared away for aesthetic reasons. There may perhaps be grounds to believe that something else was intended here — that with this project the aim was to bring no benefit to the existing booth-holders. But thanks to President Madejski, whom the Jewish councillors’ club made aware that the new post office would ruin a number of Jewish traders, the plan for clearing the booths has been settled in such a way that the owners of the present booths remain the proprietors, except that they will have to build modern booths which are at the same time[?] to suit the new post-office building.

There are many more projects, but as we have already stressed, all plans depend on time and, even more, on the revenues that flow into the municipal treasury...

Now about the person of President Dr. Madejski and his attitude to the Jewish population. This is perhaps not the place and time to dwell on the individuality of this person, but we hold that if, speaking of the municipal economy, we did not mention Dr. Madejski’s democratic conduct, we would[?] be acting quite wrongly.

It was a year ago. A kindergarten was opened in Dąbrowa, where incidents occurred in which Jewish children were driven[?] out of the kindergarten.

When the president learned of this, he immediately addressed a letter to the kindergarten management, informing it that if such anti-Jewish acts were repeated he would withdraw the subsidy of 5000 zł. Nor was the president content with this alone: at the next plenary session he repeated the decision and added that as long as he is city president he will not permit such deeds.

With the same energy the president came out during the recent antisemitic incidents, [when][?] a group of students of the “Mining School” [Szkoła Górnicza] in Dąbrowa wished to show solidarity with their Endek [National Democrat] comrades and performed the “good deed” of carrying out attacks on several Jewish residents.

The Jewish club, taking[?] upon itself the responsibility to react against hooligan acts by students who are subsidised from municipal — better said, from Jewish — money, informed the president, as well as the chairman of the B.B. [BBWR] club, Mr. Kaczkowski[?], that at the plenary session of the city council a declaration would be read in the name of the Jewish club.

The above-mentioned gentlemen replied: “You are perfectly right. On the contrary — not only read such a declaration, but express the sharpest protest against the hooligans [łobuzy].”

The declaration was indeed read, and we Jews received full satisfaction.

In general, the attitude of the president as an outspoken friend of humanity cannot be valued highly enough. The members of the Jewish club cannot to this day record a single case in which an intervention with the president — even on the hardest question — failed to bring the desired result. In a word[?]: Dr. Madejski is the man[?] in whom the slightest trace of antisemitism has been erased. The best proof is that in such times as we are now living through, Dr. Madejski, the European, has won the greatest sympathy among the Jewish population. So much so that as soon as the conversation turns to him one can hear the wish:

— If only the whole Polish nation consisted of nothing but such Madejskis...

Councillor B.[?] Rechnic.
Legal Matters

[Law — legal matters.]
The poor man's right in civil proceedings.
In today's crisis and shortage of money, even well-off people refrain from going to court, reckoning with the court costs, which in civil proceedings are fairly high. It is therefore self-evident that people who are not well-off neglect their debt claims, and quite often in complicated proceedings, such as inheritance or mortgage matters, they are not able to bear[?] the great costs of court hearings.
It happens that poor people let their legal claims go, although these are juridically and legally well founded. It is therefore worth knowing that every plaintiff has the full right to enjoy the poor man's right (prawo ubogich) and to be exempted from paying court costs. The privilege is valid in all instances, not excluding the highest tribunal.
For recognition of the poor man's right, not only paupers may apply, but also those who are not able to pay the costs.
The request for recognition of the privilege must be filed with the court before or during the proceedings, and a certificate of poverty from the magistrate [municipality] must be attached.
The court has the full right to investigate the correctness of the stated financial condition, and may refuse or recognise the enjoyment of the poor man's right. The decision on this cannot be appealed.
Anyone who is proved in court to have enjoyed the poor man's right falsely, in a fraudulent manner, faces a fine of up to 500 zł. and compulsory payment of all court costs.
Jakob Rozner.
—o—
The law of bills of exchange.
The law of bills of exchange in force in Poland is built on the basis of the international bill-of-exchange order. This order, which was established in the year 1912 in The Hague after long deliberations that had stretched back as far as 1878, was adopted by almost all states of continental Europe, [and by] the Central- and South-American legal order, and gives this legal order — with changes corresponding to conditions in the individual countries — lasting validity.
For this reason, in all countries that have adopted the international bill-of-exchange order, the decisions of the German courts are theoretically applied. On this point[?] Poland too is no exception.
Section 1 of Article 1 of the Bills of Exchange Law of 14 November 1924 ("Dziennik Ustaw" 100.) stipulates that the name "bill of exchange" must be stated in the text of the bill in the language in which the bill is issued; the mere heading is not enough. If the bill is, for example, written in German, one cannot write instead of the word "Wechsel" "Urkunde", "Schuldschein", etc.
The Polish Codification Commission justified this by saying that the legislator was concerned to give the bill of exchange a solemn form.
By mentioning the name "bill of exchange" in the text of the bill itself, the drawer's attention is drawn to the special significance of the bill.
For this reason, the unification of the language in the bill, by stating the name "bill of exchange", plays a great role.
A bill that is, for example, issued in French is declared invalid if, instead of the word "bill of exchange", the French name "Billet a ordre" or "Letre de change" is given in the text. Despite this, here in Poland little attention is paid to it when bills are issued in foreign languages, although, as said, this causes the invalidity of such bills.
It is, however, a question whether this is the right provision for preserving the character of the bill of exchange. The law of bills of exchange in Poland has in general been adapted to the order of other modern European states; the Codification Commission, however, did not take into account that with us commerce lags far behind in comparison with other Western European states; it would have been much better if a solemn promise to pay the debt punctually on the day it falls due were written into the bill.
Dr. A. Akerberg.
I Am Not Paying...

[Satirical feuilleton — Brüning and the debts; Zagłębie, kehilla.] Conveyed by Gref Kali

Ma ka mashma lan [what does it teach us], Mr. Brüning?
What is it that he lets me hear?
That he no longer pays any debts,
and the world may turn upside down.
What do I care for the "Young Plan", what do I care for Versailles —
I,
who think nothing of the treaty...
Bravo, bravo, Chancellor Brüning!
You are a "modim" [?], you are a daring fellow...
That is exactly how one should speak,
in a pure, clear language:
Behold, "zayt khikhn" [?], gentlemen,
that I no longer pay a single
grosz...

That's the way, good brother, one must talk to today's creditors... Short words! I "don't pay, and sue me as far as 'Unetaneh Tokef'". Bravo, bravo, Mr. Brüning! You have an iron head on your shoulders!... Even Bismarck would not have [come up with] [?] such an idea...

What good, then, are all the twists and tricks and behind-the-scenes politics? Why play around with moratoriums and conferences, and other such childish games? That is for idlers and kibitzers, when it can be done short and sharp:
I'm not paying!.. and call me a "knak-nisl" [?]!...

Moratorium here,
moratorium there!
It is only a game
that has no sense.
Moratorium there,
moratorium here —
the game is over,
we are not paying any more...

That is from whom the merchants of Zagłębie should learn to run their business... And how is it with us? Some petty [?] little merchant from the "Old Market" or from the "Mandzhever" [?] [probably Modrzejowska street] spends thousands of złoty, gets well fleeced by all sorts of petty lawyers, suffers troubles upon troubles, does not sleep at night, and runs and chases around all kinds of offices, until he lives to obtain that bit of "nadzór" [court supervision]...
Isn't it simpler to do as Brüning does and issue a proclamation: gentlemen, I am not paying! — and the matter is done with...
Once again bravo, Chancellor Brüning! Not for nothing are you a son of that land which produced such great men as Goethe and Schiller... and Adolf Hitler. Your winged word, "I am not paying", will become a catchword and will enter the history of all nations...
All nations and states, and even parties, will snatch up your "slogan" like a precious stone, and at every favourable opportunity people will make use of it.

A voter, for example, will come with a demand to a minister, or to a Sejm deputy, and remind him that before the elections he promised his voters pie in the sky [lit. "the little plate from heaven"], such as tax reductions, cheap flats, subsidies for schools and the like — and the former candidate and present minister, the poseł, will twirl the left side of his moustache with his fingers and answer with the words: "I am not paying"...

A Zionist president will come to the English Colonial Secretary with a complaint: Gevald, robber, why are the requested certificates not being given? Thousands of halutzim stand at the gates of Eretz Israel; they want to till the fields of Eretz Israel with sweat and blood and give their lives for the building of the land; where are the golden promises that England gave the people of Israel? Why are the principles of the Balfour Declaration not being fulfilled? — and he, the English gentleman, will not want to talk much in order to justify himself with diplomatic twists and "oyber" [?] contrivances; he will even spare himself sending commissions to investigate the country and issuing White Papers; but short and stiff — in the English manner — he will say: I am not paying!..

The paupers of Podzamcze will come to the Jewish kehilla and start demanding: How so, Panie Prezesie [Mr. President]! You promised to assign a sum of money for coal for the poor, and now we are already, thank God, in the month of Adar — so what are you waiting for?... We are freezing in the damp, cramped cellar-dwellings with our tiny little children. Gevald, Panie Prezesie, why are you silent?...

Then our pan prezes will open his holy lips and, taking [printed "gemendig"] his little beard in his hand, answer thus:
Shh. Gentlemen, don't raise an outcry and a tumult; true indeed, I believe that you are cold, that you are freezing with your wives and little children. You are truly to be bitterly pitied; true for you, a sum really ought to be assigned for coal, only... what can one do?
"I am not paying"...

And even my wife will come to me with grievances: Gevald, murderer, what did you have against me? You took me young, fresh, blooming. Simply blood and milk, and:

Do you remember the night
when we went walking?
The moon was hanging
high in the sky,
and you swore
to me with fire
that you would forever remain
my one and only faithful one...
And now... in the course
of a few years
I have already become boring [?] to you
and ugly...
I even know
that you have a mistress [kochanka],
a girl, a blonde,
her name is Janka...
So where are your
sweet promises?
I sit a whole evening
at home, as in a prison...
Instead of the pleasures
that you were to share with me,
I am always just
peeling potatoes...
Instead of giving me
chocolate to nibble,
I have to just
wash the children's little heads...

Then I will stroke my poetic forelock [czupryna] and answer her thus:
Yes indeed, my little wife, it is all true, I did once promise you all the happiness in the world, but what comes of it is that:
I am not paying...

And so, gentlemen, of all the inventions — such as Zeppelins, poison gases, submarines, the "Forty-Two" [the German 42-cm gun] — the one I like best is Brüning's newest invention:
"I am not paying"...
What Is Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin — “The Sinners Want to Snatch Away the Torah”..

[Będzin — education, Talmud Torah.]
What is happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 19 Adar 5692 — piątek 26 lutego 1932 [Friday, 26 February 1932].)
Będzin
“The sinners (posh'im) want to snatch away the Torah”..
Last Sabbath the rabbi prayed[?] in the minyan of the Talmud Torah, where he delivered a sermon about the sad situation of the institution. In the sermon the rabbi appealed to the worshippers that they should not allow the sinners to snatch away the Torah...
After the sermon Mr. Eliezer Bożykowski took the floor and pointed out that, if only the “sinners” had indeed taken over the management of the Talmud Torah, it would not have come to such a sad state: the melamdim (teachers) would not strike every Monday and Thursday, and the poor children would not therefore become neglected and abandoned (hefker).
Intervention of the Merchants' Association Concerning the Telephone Charge

[Będzin — commerce, economic crisis.]
The “Merchants' Association” (Sochrim Ferajn) has turned with a memorandum to the telephone directorate, asking that, because of the crisis, the monthly charge for telephones be reduced.
The Rabbinate Turns for Help to the Kehilla Board

[Będzin — rabbinate, kashrut.]
The butcher Pozmantir (Wideras' house) does not want to give back the “kosher sign” (kosher tevele) which is issued by the rabbinate. Because of this the rabbinate has turned to the kehilla board, asking that with the help of the police the “kosher sign” be taken back from the above-mentioned butcher.
Meeting of “Ezrat Menachem Avelim”

[Będzin — societies, charity.]
Last Saturday night the annual meeting of the society “Ezrat Menachem Avelim” (Help for Comforting Mourners) was held in its own premises, with the participation of a large number of members. The chairman Abraham Icchak Sztark opens the meeting and hands over the chair to A.[Mr.] Wajcenberg.
The reports on the activity so far and on the treasury are given by the honorary secretary Mr. Weksselman. From the reports it emerges that the society conducts broad activity in the field of helping helpless poor families. After hearing the reports, those assembled expressed confidence in the old board. Because of this no election of a board took place.
Suicide of a Barber

[Będzin — suicide.]
In his own barber shop on Małachowska Street the owner Kwiczyński[?] committed suicide by hanging himself on the electric socket!
—o—
Second Appearance of Miriam Orleska
[Będzin — culture.]
This Saturday night the famous artist Miriam Orleska will appear in the premises of “WIZO” with a second recitation (word) concert. The programme contains a series of new works by Peretz, Sholem Asch, Leivick and others.
Concert of the “Hakoach” Orchestra

[Będzin — music, sport club.]
Next Monday the second concert will take place at the “Światowid”, performed by the orchestra of “Hakoach”. On the programme — the finest musical works. Since the orchestra does not decline any event (impreza) organised by whatever society — the concert ought to be properly supported.
Because of a Piece of Coal — They Met Their Death

[Będzin — crime, accident, crisis.]
On Monday evening several persons wanted to carry out a coal theft at the new station. When the policeman on duty noticed it, the thieves ran away. At that moment a passenger train passed by, which cut off the head of one of the thieves.
Suicide attempt in the field.

In the field behind the town a young woman was found unconscious; beside her lay an empty little bottle of vinegar essence. The woman was taken to hospital, where, after receiving first aid, she regained consciousness.
A few days ago the woman had been laid off („reduced“) from her job.
Tragic death of a Jew on the road from Zawiercie to Pilica.

On Sunday the 54-year-old Mendel[?] Elazar Strausberg was travelling from Zawiercie to Pilica. Halfway, because of the deep snow, the sleigh overturned, and Strausberg, falling out of the sleigh, received a heavy blow to the head, from which he lost consciousness; before he could be brought into Pilica he died.
Now it is dark in the synagogue too..

This week the electric light in the synagogue was also cut off.
—o—
Drawing and painting courses.
The well-known artist-painter Mr. Cygler has opened a studio, where courses in drawing and painting work are held.
—o—
A lecture by Dr. A. Gottesdiener.
Tonight, at the close of the Sabbath, Dr. Gottesdiener will lecture at the „Mizrachi“ — the continuation of the cycle of lectures on the movement of Shabbetai Tzvi.
—o—
Meeting of furrier workers.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Wygodzki[?] a general meeting of the furriers' trade was held. After the reports, a board, an audit commission and a comrades' court were elected.
Sosnowiec — General meeting of the „Kasa Udziałowa“. The bank has received a new name.

For several weeks, on the initiative of a group of merchants, a project has been worked out to unite all the small banking institutions into one solid bank. The group has gained supporters, so that up to today their number already reaches 80 members. The group's work first of all met with success with the management of the „Kasa Udziałowa“. The board and council, notwithstanding that the bank's condition is relatively better than in other „little banks“, agreed to this proposal for the good of the cause, for the realisation of the union — which strengthened the bank with a considerable sum of shares.
In connection with this a general meeting of the „Kasa Udziałowa“ was held. At the meeting the plan of union was approved and the name of the bank was changed to „Kupiecki Związek Kredytowy“ [Merchants' Credit Union].
The meeting was chaired by Mr. J. Krumer; as assessors Messrs. A. Jakubowicz and R. M. Raster, and as secretary Becalel Ferens[?].
After the reports on activity and the balance sheet, the following resolutions were adopted: 1) that a member may receive credit up to 6.000 zł. 2) the bank may take on obligations up to 300,000 zł. 3) the share-members shall cover 50 per cent of the anticipated losses. 4) for all transactions made up to the 22nd of this month the previous management is responsible, and 5) the „Kasa Udziałowa“ is renamed „Kupiecki Związek Kredytowy“.

To the council: D. Dziukiewicz[?] (president), J. Krumer (vice), M. Kornfeld, D. Marjanka, W. Berri[?], B. Zelinger and W. Grajcer.

The people of Modrzejów want a permanent rabbi

As is known, Rabbi Englard holds the title of Rabbi of Modrzejów. But the Modrzejów community is not satisfied that Rabbi Englard spends no more than a few hours a week there, and this week they took on the well-known prodigy (ilui) R' Yisrael Yitzchak Piekarski as moreh-tzedek (rabbinic judge) of Modrzejów.
It goes without saying that Rabbi Englard is not pleased with this „occupation“, and he has issued a public notice in which he forbids the new moreh-tzedek to rule on questions of religious law. In the notice the well-known „cursed be…“ formulas are mentioned several times... above all strong emphasis is laid on „Cursed be he who encroaches on his neighbour's boundary“...
The commissioner has approved the new budget.

At Monday's session of the commissioners' council the new budget for 1932/33 was approved. This year's budget has been reduced by 178 thousand zł., both in expenditure and in revenue.
At the session the commissioner, Mr. Kuszniak, presenting the budget, said: „It is true that the town finds itself[?] in a difficult[?], critical situation, but in other towns it is much worse than in Sosnowiec“.
Regional conference of merchants.

On the agenda are a number of questions of broad interest to the merchant community.
3 Brothers Sentenced to 22 Years in Prison.

[Zagłębie — court.]
Before the local district court stood the 3 Wajda [Wojda?] brothers, who were accused of circulating counterfeit 10-złoty banknotes.
The trial lasted several days. The verdict, delivered on Saturday during the day, reads: the brothers Alfred and Adolf Wajda — 7 years in prison each; Leon Wajda, who took part in the money forgery while he was a police przodownik [senior constable] — 8 years in prison.

Changes in the Judiciary

[Sosnowiec — court.]
Mr. Dr. Stanisław Czaputowicz, judge and chairman of the section for administrative penalties of the Sosnowiec District Court, has stepped down from his post and gone over to the bar, opening an office at Modrzejowska [Street] 20 in Sosnowiec.

From Artisans' Life.
[Sosnowiec — artisans.]
This week there stayed in Sosnowiec the director of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts Mal [?], Mr. Aksentowicz, and the instructor of the Kielce voivodeship Dr. Wojtowicz. The board of the Artisans' Association took the opportunity and sent a delegation of Messrs. President [printed “Pruzes”] Langer, Opatowski, Stern and Jaskirowicz, who held a conference. At the said conference the question of diplomas and of the annulled [?] examinations was discussed, to which the representatives from Kielce replied that the diplomas will already be distributed through the guilds on 1 April 1932.

In conclusion the representatives declared that the voivode has already signed a rescript giving the guilds the power to close down illegal workshops.
On Sunday, under the chairmanship of starszy [guild master] Cymberknopf [?], a members' meeting of the painters' guild took place, which dealt with the question of illegal workshops and of founding a painters' cooperative. An Offering of the Heart

Prof. Dr. Moshe Schorr.
An Offering of the Heart.
A few words on the current fund-raising campaign for the „Keren Hayesod“.
(Sent by the „Keren Hayesod“ head office)
A tax, when it is given voluntarily, enriches the giver. Already concerning the tax for building the Tabernacle it is said: „ויקחו לי תרומה מאת כל איש אשר ידבנו לבו“ („that they bring Me an offering, of every man whose heart moves him“) — they shall take for Me from everyone whose heart is willing. If someone gives from a willing heart, he takes more than he gives.
Whoever gives for a holy, exalted purpose takes, through his one-time gift, a lasting spiritual share in the magic radiance that shines out of the holy work and illuminates everyone connected with it. But only those givers are able to receive these bright rays who give without compulsion[?], without external pressure, but moved[?] by their own willing[?] heart. The heart is the medium that creates the magic bond between the donor and the goal for which he spends. And through this offering of the heart the donor becomes a co-creator and a co-participant together with millions of others who helped to build the work.
Now too we are building a Tabernacle, an exalted holy home for the people, a material and spiritual home where the Jewish nation can live its life freely and undisturbed. And there is no more exalted and holy gift than the gift to the fund that is building this home — to the „Keren Hayesod“. Those who bring an offering for this holy goal do not give; rather they take, for they enrich themselves with the blissful feeling that they share in spirit in the wondrous work of rebuilding our ancient fatherland and of reviving there our ancient people.
What substance has any other transient wealth against this eternal wealth of joy and pride, which grows and rises with every day, the more the work for which this offering of the heart is given grows and gains strength? And the gifts to the „Keren Hayesod“ are indeed an offering of the heart, of the Jewish heart that glows with love for its people.
I have had the great privilege of being elected chairman of the „Keren Hayesod“ board of directors in Poland. On taking up my office I have one wish: that the „trumah“ (contribution) for the „Keren Hayesod“ be a true „trumah she-b״b“, that it gladden and enrich the contributors with the greatest wealth, of which[?] generations have dreamed: that they and their children may be privileged to see with their own eyes the finished work they helped to build: the rebuilt Land of Israel and the revived Jewish people in the Land of Israel!
—o—
Some Explanations on the Turnover Ryczałt
We receive many inquiries about the ryczałt (lump-sum tax) that is now being introduced. We wish to answer all the inquiries here:
1) Thanks to the intervention of the Chamber of Commerce the government has raised the turnover limit for the ryczałt, which was previously set for merchants in Warsaw with* a turnover of up to 35[?] thousand zł. and in the provinces up to 25 thousand zł. The ryczałt is introduced for merchants in Warsaw whose turnover in Warsaw was up to 45 thousand zł., and for the provinces up to 35 thousand zł.
2) The average turnover will be calculated over 2 or 3 years, 1928, 1929 and 1930. For firms that did not exist in 1928 the average will be calculated from the turnover of the years 1929 and 1930.
3) Firms founded only in 193[—] will not be charged any ryczałt; they will be assessed at 2 percent of turnover.
4) Firms founded later will also be charged 2 percent.
5) On 15 April all merchants without exception will receive payment orders (nakazy) for the turnover of 1931, which will be assessed by the assessment commissions as hitherto. Only the turnover of 1932 will be subject to the ryczałt.
6) All merchants whose average turnover was higher than stated above will continue to have their turnover assessed and will be charged 2 percent.
7) The ryczałt will be the same for all branches. It will amount to 1 percent. Food merchants and retailers, who previously also paid 1 percent, will continue to pay 1 percent under the ryczałt; on the other hand, merchants of all other branches, who paid 2 percent, will benefit more.
8) [printed: 3] The ryczałt for artisans will also amount to 1 percent of the average turnover of the previous three years.
9) „Skup“ (buying-up) merchants of the 5th category will have a tax rate lower than 1 percent, namely half a percent.
10) Each instalment of the ryczałt obrotowy (turnover lump-sum) will be collected separately, and if it is not paid on time, distraint (execution) will be carried out.

Insurance Payments Reduced from 1 March
The [—] [probably the Powszechny Zakład Ubezpieczeń Wzajemnych] fire-insurance company will from 1 March this year reduce insurance payments by 10 to 40 percent, depending on local conditions in the individual districts.
This decision is a result of the very bad economic situation in the country and of the fall in the value of houses.
In this connection the preliminary sum of the payments for this year has been reduced from 60 to 50 million złoty.
It is worth adding that this is already the third reduction of the rates, apart from several local reductions made for individual powiaty (counties).
Compared with 1931, the overall rate-total of the insurance company has been reduced by 35 percent.

The Coal Strike in Zagłębie Continues

[Zagłębie — the coal strike.]
The decision of the majority[?] of the Upper Silesian mines, which came out against the coal strike, has had a certain influence on the strike situation in Zagłębie.
At the meetings held during the week, voices were already raised to go back to work for the time being[?]. The majority, however, is in favour[?] of continuing the strike until victory.
The course of the strike was calm throughout the whole week. Smaller clashes occurred at the „Saturn“ mine, where some workers who wanted to return to work were [attacked?] by the wives of the striking workers.
The workers' union of „Polska Praca“ held several meetings at which it was decided to break the strike.
The central union of the mine workers received telegrams from port workers in Gdynia, from transport workers[?] of Łódź, from the class union in Częstochowa, etc., expressing solidarity and wishing the strikers success.
On Wednesday a 5[?]-minute strike took place in Warsaw on account of the fallen[?] in Zagłębie.
Yesterday, Thursday, the [vice?-]minister Maraszewski[?] visited Zagłębie and held a conference at the starostwo [district office].
According to conjecture, the strike will be liquidated in the coming days.
