Zagłębie and the „Foundation“

[Zagłębie — economy and credit.]
Precisely in the year when Jewish credit cooperation in Poland suffered such a „fine“[?] blow — both for reasons of the general economic crisis and, to no small extent, for „specifically Jewish“ reasons — precisely in this year the „rich uncle“ — the „Foundation“ [the American Joint Reconstruction Foundation] — decided to draw the final balance with the central financial corporation of this movement — with the „Bank of Cooperatives“.
It is said that this reckoning has been dragging on for a long time, and just as the „behind-the-scenes“ led more than one credit cooperative astray, so too the Bank for Cooperatives had, to its own detriment, a „behind-the-scenes“ of its own, and so we now learn part of what the „Foundation“ has known for a long time.
Is the year 1932 the right time for such a reckoning?
Is the „Foundation“ — in its tactics — as innocent as a white dove?
Can one really demand of Jewish credit cooperation in Poland that at such a time it be financially stronger than the largest banks in England and Germany?
Would the people of the „Foundation“ have run the movement better and more successfully if, instead of the Bank for Cooperatives, they had decided everything themselves?
We have great doubts whether we may answer all these questions in the affirmative.
But —
Let us take the matter as it is.
Let us reckon with a fact.
The operation is being carried out. In place of the present Bank for Cooperatives there will arise — so we are assured — a new central financial institution, on sounder foundations and with a realistic economic policy.
And although we do not yet know what the new body will look like concretely, we wish to believe in advance that the new will be better and sounder, and consequently — more productive.
Lessons will be learned from the past, from practice, and since we have paid dearly enough in tuition, the lessons will probably bring good benefit.
A new chapter will begin in the Jewish cooperative credit movement in Poland.
This movement, in its first period, gave birth from the outset to children, and — if this is not mere sentiment — it is much[?] healthier for everyone that an end is being put to these illnesses. The movement as such will not become poorer and will not suffer at all. On the contrary, it will become even stronger. Now that what never should have been born has passed away — banks out of the ambition of individuals, banks out of the interests of individuals — better that they are gone. The process of crystallisation is over; the movement is now getting flesh and blood and — a healthy face. Falsehood and bad luck had to fall away from the movement.
And if the „Foundation“ really has this in view — blessed be the hands of its people.
And here we come to the main point that interests us in particular — us, the people of Zagłębie.
The cooperative credit movement here contained too large a percentage of what we described above as the element of falsehood and bad luck. This must be admitted. The wounds are still too fresh, and therefore we will be brief for now and not speak about it more concretely.
We have indeed paid for it, paid very dearly, paid with sacrifices, with blood. But our sacrifices must not be lost. „In thy blood live“ [Ezekiel 16:6]. Our sacrifices must and will be a lesson for us, a stern warning about what is permitted and what is by no means allowed.
But the movement, which is almost the only point of support for the poor and economically hard life of the Jewish middle class and working people — this movement must by no means suffer — must not go under.
The Jewish cooperative credit movement in Zagłębie stands at the edge of the abyss. Formerly, one took „revenge“ on another. If „my“ bank went under — then why should the same not happen to my neighbour as well? If I have worries and troubles — let my „enemy“ have no rest either. If I was left without honour and without a livelihood — let the other fellow feel such a taste too...
The feeling of Schadenfreude burned and glowed.
Instead of putting out the fire, people strove with gossip and hatred to make the flames flare up as much as possible, and — „let me die with the Philistines“.
The result:
Jewish Zagłębie is now as if helpless; there is nowhere to obtain a penny of credit. The merchant, the shopkeeper, the artisan are at their wits' end, and the cry is already going up — let us make our credit cooperatives healthy, let us help one another!
The merchants' banks have heroically withstood all the fires, and they do not want to, and must not, go under. No one can now come to the merchants' banks with any complaints; the merchants' banks are owed hundreds of thousands of złoty by their members, by Jewish merchants, by Jewish shopkeepers, and these are for the time being unable to pay; the money has „frozen“ — as it is called in bank jargon — and the bank needs fresh capital, modest sums, so as to be able in this way to make the „frozen“ liquid again.
And here there is a sacred necessity to obtain the help of the „Foundation“.
Among the surviving remnant we have also kept the Small Traders' and Artisans' Bank in Sosnowiec. To the credit of the Jewish artisan it must be said that he did appreciate the value of his institution and swam safely with it across the stormy sea. But with such a sum as the bank possesses one cannot nowadays meet even the most minimal needs of the Jewish artisan.
Therefore the „Foundation“ must not take this into account when it embarks on the second chapter of credit-cooperative history.
The „Foundation“ must understand our situation and reckon with the vital needs of the 100-thousand-strong Jewish community in Zagłębie.
Y. N.
My Chat with Winter. (A Short Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton.]
Yesterday I grabbed Winter by the lapels and said to him angrily:
— Stop, you Winter! What do you think — is the world a free-for-all? What do you think — that if „Dziadek“[?] [Grandpa — Piłsudski's nickname] is sitting in the warm countries, then there is no law and no judge? May one now pounce on us with cold right into Passover itself? Isn't the crisis enough for us, with the troubles, with the poverty, with the taxes, with the appeals — must we not even be rid of your frozen grip? Enough of your tricks, you Winter! Your time is over, take yourself off to your rest!
But Winter is a cold soul; he is little impressed by my fuming, blows on me a pre-spring frost of a few degrees and answers me thus:
— What are you spinning me a yarn for? What time, when time? I know my time and my reckoning quite well myself. Not the first year and not the last! I have my own constant signs. When the shops fill up, then I know that the festival of spring is coming and I begin to get ready to leave. But this year there is no beginning at all. Just take a look — in the shoe shops, in the drapery shops, in the haberdashery shops, at the jewellers and at the tailors and shoemakers and at the furriers — everywhere it is empty and desolate, Egyptian darkness, not a single customer so much as sniffs his way in; nobody buys, nobody takes in, nobody earns — so why are you pestering me that spring is near and that I must get ready to leave?!
Thus Winter argues with me, and sets about blowing frost and cold with fresh zest.
But I did not let go of him and explained to him briefly and sharply:
— Come with me, little brother, and I will show you with signs and wonders that Passover is near after all.
And while speaking I led Winter to the „Dobroczynność“ [the charity society] and showed him:
— Here, look and read the list of the hundreds of needy people registered for matzah; you see how the public „is preparing“ for the Passover festival? You say the shops are empty? How could it be otherwise, when nearly the whole town is waiting today for matzah from Passover charity [maos chitim]?! Now do you believe that Passover is near?
Winter took a look, shook his head and began to get ready to leave.
R—L.
The Blind Lamech

[Essay — war and peace.] By Dr. A. Coralnik.

If I were a painter, I would paint a war picture. And I would send the picture to Geneva, to the conference of the diplomats and "peace-makers", to[?] the League of Nations. I would have the picture shown[?] everywhere that people gather, where passion collides with passion and death plays on the threshold.

But my picture would not be like the thousand other well-known pictures: Mars, in armour and with a sword, rides on a horse and victims fall to the right and to the left. Death — a skeleton with a scythe, goes about cutting off heads. My picture would be simpler and truer. I would paint the tragedy of old Lamech.

Old blind Lamech walks along, and his great-grandson leads him by the hand. Coming towards them from the distance is old Cain, the accursed, the first murderer among men. Lamech asks the grandchild: who is walking there, whom do you see there — and the child answers: "I see some beast." The blind Lamech draws his bow, shoots and kills Cain, his forefather. And when Lamech learned whom he had killed, he struck his two hands together and killed his grandchild. And there stands the blind old man between two dead — the forefather and the grandchild both fallen by his hand, both killed because of his blindness.

And I wonder why this motif has occurred to no one. After all, it is so characteristic of the life of mankind. It is, after all, a key to the whole of human history. A blind man, bringing death, kills the past and the future and then stands in despair between the two victims of his blindness. An eternal motif, as old as mankind, as old as life. In any case as old as history. Recently the "Society for International Law" in Warsaw compiled a table and calculated that in the last three thousand four hundred and twenty-one years of history, three thousand one hundred and fifty-three years were "war years" and only two hundred and sixty-eight years — peace. When nation did not fight nation, army against army, then one group fought another instead, one class against another, a civil war; and no one, no one remembers a year or a day when there was no war.

Do you remember one? I don't. For as long as I have lived, I hear, read, see only war. Born a few years after the German-French and the Turkish-Russian war. In my earliest childhood — the great Chinese-Japanese war, then the Boxer[?] war, then the Balkan wars, the Italian-Turkish, the World War — up to this very day, when war is tearing at the gates of the world. And I name only the world wars. And how many "side-wars" there were in that time, so to speak in the intervals between the acts, to fill up the time? The Germans fought the Hereros in Africa, Spain fought America, France Morocco, Russia the Jews. And all this within quite a short time, and in a time of the highest cultural development, the time after the Hague Tribunal, after the Nobel Prize for pacifism, the time of the agitation for the League of Nations. And before that? Before we even existed?

The nineteenth century began in blood and cannon smoke, on battlefields. And hardly a single year passed of which one could say "peace in His dwelling", that it was quiet and calm, quiet not only on the battlefields but also in the hearts, in the minds; and if here and there there was a year of peace, it was only a year of revolution, of preparation, of gathering forces and collecting energy for a new war.

People in general look for an enemy. Each his own, one a distant one, the other a near one; one a lighter one, the other a heavier one, according to temperament, scale, means. Because not everyone can afford to have an open enemy. Rich and strong nations can afford it. The poorer ones must content themselves with a cheaper sort, or even with an "ersatz". And that is precisely why, for example, antisemitism in Germany, or in Poland, has now become so flaming, so wild, so barbaric. They are poor, the wretches; they cannot — for the time being — afford a proper, real enemy. They must, the poor ones, make do with home industry[?], and if one cannot allow oneself the luxury of beating Frenchmen or Russians, one beats at least Jews. It is both cheap and convenient, like manoeuvres in "peacetime". Preparation for the real battle, for "the day that will come", as Hitler says; the day of the new, great bloodshed; the day of the great slaughter.

And it will come. Sooner or later. It is almost a certainty. May it not be in our days. We, that is the generation that lived through the World War, are already somewhat sated. They, the young, the new generation that has not tasted blood, crave it, they thirst. Go out to the youth of today, wherever it may be, with banners and trumpets, sound a battle-cry, the old, primeval-human, primeval-animal shout: "Blood!" — and you will see how they will hurl themselves like [—][?] wolves. They will go when Stalin calls them under the red flag. They will rush to storm when Hitler waves the black flag at them. The youth of Japan — also human beings like us, also with blood in their veins — runs to kill and to die for the interests of Yokohama and for the business of a few Japanese industrialists; they run voluntarily to their death. And who knows. Perhaps they too have read Erich Maria Remarque's war book? Perhaps they too once swore "never again war"? But all these are words, fantasies, shadows. The instinct is stronger and it prevails. The instinct to kill.

And who invented the idea that "the people", that "the masses" want peace? Who says that only the ruling classes drive towards war? Napoleon was — the people, and Mussolini is — the masses, and Stalin, and Voroshilov, and Hitler — they are all "the people". All of poor parents, all workers' children and former workers themselves. But because they are the people, therefore also the people's instinct, therefore also blind.

Formerly one could perhaps still speak of a higher, hostile[?] power that drives people like sheep to the slaughter; [now] the responsibility for war — for the one that is and the one that is yet to come — is borne by the people itself, the great, tragic, blind Lamech, who shoots without a "why", driven by fear and recklessness — shoots blindly at his forefather and then, in his despair, kills his grandchild, destroys the bridges of his past and the approach to the future.

If I were a painter, I would paint a Lamech picture. And it would hang in a museum and people would talk about it, exactly as they talked about Stuck's picture, about Vereshchagin's terrible war picture (a heap of skulls beneath a mountain, and the inscription: "All is quiet at Shipka"). But from the museum to the barracks, from the barracks to the battlefield, is one leap, and they would make that leap all the same. The picture would not help either.
The Economic Boom in Eretz Israel

[Eretz Israel — economy; article.] Shabtai Weiss (Tel Aviv).
Eretz Israel now finds itself in a state of economic upswing — this should be said clearly and boldly, not for the sake of propaganda, but in order to describe the actual situation. Figures and facts will confirm this characterisation of the situation.
The building movement keeps growing. In the month of February 133 houses were under construction in Tel Aviv, employing 750 building workers (as against 540 workers in the month of November 1931). Around the building movement are concentrated hundreds of families who make their living from it, among them some quite large businesses, directly and indirectly. In the same month of February the local municipality issued new building permits for an area of 8000 square metres, among them large three-storey houses. There is also a strong Jewish building movement in Jerusalem, although building conditions there are generally harder and building costs higher. The situation is similar in Haifa and in the colonies. And nevertheless no empty flats are to be had; the demand for housing is great, and hardly is a house built when it is immediately occupied, even in the middle of the year, although here there is a special flat-letting season once a year, the so-called "Muharram". Where does such a phenomenon come from? First, there is in all the towns a large reserve of inhabitants (in Tel Aviv it is estimated at 10,000 souls) who until now have been living in cramped flats and, thanks to the improvement in their material situation, are moving into roomier ones. We are dealing not with a passing but with a lasting phenomenon. One can see it here quite often, how some of the immigrants who came here without means started their trade or craft on a very small scale, work their way up not badly in the course of two or three years, and move on to a higher standard of living. One can observe this phenomenon especially among the immigrants from the Orient (from Persia, Mesopotamia, Kurdistan etc.), who know the secret of thrift: on arrival they rent a small room for their far-from-small family and slowly move on to better living conditions. Second: immigration. True, the workers' immigration is as good as closed, but the immigration of capitalists (people of means, with 1000 pounds and more) is not restricted, and every ship brings a certain number of well-to-do immigrants from America, Germany, Latvia, and also from Poland. Third: natural increase.
The agricultural production of our mixed farms (grain, gamzin [?], poultry, dairy products etc.) is growing and developing, and finds ever more outlets on the home and foreign markets. Thus, for example, the dairy products of "Tnuva" (the largest agricultural cooperative in Eretz Israel) grew this year by 25 per cent, and everything sells well, and there is no need to warehouse them as in former times. Eretz Israel honey, for example, reaches as far as America and India. Other products are paving their way to the largest world markets and find buyers thanks to their good quality.
Jewish industry keeps developing and consolidating. The existing factories are perfecting their products, cutting their production costs and penetrating ever further into the neighbouring countries. New branches of industry are being added, which aim to take the place of products that until now were imported from abroad. Almost all the factories are continuing their work normally, and a large part of them are increasing their output. The number of industrial workers keeps growing steadily.
The cooperative movement in Eretz Israel shows great progress, and as regards credit cooperation one may say — tremendous progress. "Halva'ah ve-Hisakhon" (Loan and Savings Bank) in Tel Aviv, the oldest cooperative bank in the country, closed its business year 5691 with an increase of its own capital by 14 per cent, an increase of its deposits by 18 per cent, and a gain of more than 400 new members. The "Ashrai" (Credit) bank in Tel Aviv closed its financial year 5691 with the following results: its own capital grew by 44 per cent; the total of deposits rose from 125 thousand pounds to 153 thousand pounds; it issued loans to the sum of 370 thousand pounds, apart from mortgage loans. Its total turnover last year amounted to four and a half million pounds. And this bank was founded only eight years ago with a capital of... a few hundred pounds. These are only some typical examples of the general development. There is, it seems, not a single bank in Eretz Israel that has not lately gone through development and growth. The significance of this can be properly appreciated when one recalls what giant banks have collapsed in the past year in various countries of Europe and America.
Producers' cooperation too keeps developing, and likewise the transport and travel cooperatives. In these branches the cooperative form has proved very successful, and it will probably embrace ever wider circles. In the cooperatives mentioned, the number of members grew last year from 700 to 900.
And then there is the colossal development in the field of the orange plantations, these Eretz Israel "colonies" — or, as "Bustanai" [printed "Bustai"], the organ of the grove owners, puts it out of caution: if they are not gold mines, they are in any case mines of an honourable livelihood. And so there are already now 64,500 dunams of orange groves in Jewish ownership. Whoever wants to understand what this figure means, what an enormous Jewish asset it contains, should remember that up to the year 1926 Jews owned 10 500 dunams of orange groves in Eretz Israel. In the course of the last six years alone Jews acquired in Eretz Israel 54.000 thousand [sic] dunams of groves, worth three and a half million pounds sterling! This year the Jewish groves exported some one million four hundred thousand cases of oranges, which will bring into the country the sum of about 700 thousand pounds. According to authoritative estimates, Jews will plant a fresh 17,000 dunams of groves in the new year! Whoever wants to understand what this figure says should bear in mind that Jews have not yet reached such a planted area in any of the last six years (1926—1931), which were, as said, years of enormous growth in this field. The highest figure so far was reached in 1929 — and that was 15,000 dunams of groves.
And one more thing: when we said above that this year the Jewish grove owners exported approximately one million four hundred thousand cases of oranges worth 700 thousand pounds sterling, one must take into account that the Jewish groves have not yet reached their full fruitfulness. A grove yields in the sixth year after planting an average of 40 cases of oranges per dunam. Its fruitfulness develops steadily until, in the eleventh or twelfth year after planting, the grove reaches 120 cases of oranges per dunam. The Jewish groves are today, for the most part, in the first years of their fruitfulness. The same groves that this year exported one million four hundred thousand cases will in six years be able to export five and a half million cases. In all the years since the World War the average price of a case of oranges has been ten English shillings; if we are cautious and reckon in future with the possibility that prices will fall, and take as the average price only 8 English shillings per case of oranges, then the said production will bring into the country, in six years' time, the sum of two and a quarter million English pounds. It is easy to imagine what a tremendous effect this will have on the Jewish national economy in Eretz Israel.
And now the labour market. Let it be stated: in Eretz Israel there are now almost no unemployed. Some facts: in Jerusalem there are 70 unemployed. But if one considers that at the same time many hundreds of Arabs are employed in Jewish construction work in Jerusalem, it becomes clear to everyone that in the Jewish national economy there is in fact a shortage of working hands. Or the large colony of Hadera: all the unemployed, down to the last one, have been given work, and a severe shortage of workers is felt. And at the same time more than 400 Arab workers are employed in Hadera by Jewish colonists.
And when the situation looks like this in the various fields of the Jewish economy in Eretz Israel, then it goes without saying that the situation of Jewish commerce is correspondingly good. Jewish wholesale trade is developing and gaining strength. In the past year Jewish commerce has won new import branches, obtained various new sales agencies in Europe, and new shipping agencies.
• • •
The Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel now forms a source of strength that has no equal in the Jewish world. The great means and efforts invested in Eretz Israel are bearing their fruit. Like a blessed island the Jewish Yishuv in Eretz Israel now stands — with a tottering world around it. But the Jewish national economy in Eretz Israel thirsts for new forces, like a fertile field that thirsts for water. Eretz Israel longs and yearns for a new immigration, for new labour forces, for further capital — for its intensified development, for the building of the Jewish home and for the regeneration of the Jewish people.
Swapping the Roles...

(A merchant's little letter).
My friend! As you know, with us merchants everything has been going, regularly, for years now, butter-side down. One takes in nothing, competition grows, so the goods get cheaper every day, the takings get smaller still — and here sits over us an "ovshanr" [urząd — government office, here the tax office] that wants to know of nothing, just like hell, may it not befall us — only give, give, only pay and pay, without any consideration and without any mercy; there is no way to convince them that we really cannot haul on our shoulders such enormous taxes [podatki] as in those good times — they believe nobody and won't even listen. For instance, when it comes to income tax [dochodowy], they will not make the deduction for the minor [małoletnie] children that is due by law, because, you see, the commission did not confirm that I have children! So I start running about and arguing: how can it be?! I drag along the "vshanrtse"[?] [half-Polish word, meaning unclear], which I [?] at him with the registration books [książki meldunkowe], with the little children, may they be healthy and strong, and I show him black on white, plainly written: here, look, Panie naczelniku [sir, director], Beile Ratse [?] — one, Yosa Adel — two, Chaim Shmuel — three, and they are all still young children who cannot earn and still go to school — so why don't you deduct for me the allowances [stawki] that are due to me by law and in fairness?!...
You probably think the Pan naczelnik is impressed? Not at all! — "Szacunkowa komisja nie uznała, nic mogę nie pomożę" [broken Polish: "the assessment commission did not recognise it, I can't help"] — he answers me with contempt, and there is nothing more to be done with him. The "assessment commission" is a greater authority than [?] I with my wife and my children, whom I bring into the "ovshanr" together with the "vshandtse"[?]. Now go and do something...
And I have the same with the turnover tax [obrotowy] and the property tax [majątkowy]: I shout with all my strength that I cannot pay so much (in truth I can't pay anything any more), and he will by no means believe me, even if you cut your heart open and lay it down on a plate...
A week ago an opportunity came my way that I must not let pass and miss, so that now he will at last believe me a little. Now listen to what I did:
One fine morning, as I open the shop, two letters are lying there — one letter from the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office]. Since I had filed an appeal [odwołanie] against the taxes, saying that I have nothing, own nothing and take in nothing, the commission came to the decision that this does not agree with reality, that in truth I am an enormously rich man and must pay everything as the early authorities ruled, and — it's settled [lit. "expired"]...
The second letter was from Częstochowa, from a manufacturer of stiffening canvas [buckram]. Since I had at the time asked that my credit be increased, so that I could carry jute with stiffening canvas by the wagon-load, so that [printed "סדי"] the freight would come out three groszy per metre cheaper for me and I could withstand the dangerous competition — they write back to me that, since the factory had gathered information about me, it turns out that I am a quite small little man, and no large credits can be granted to me, and they enclose right away the reports from the information bureau...
Having received the two letters, I didn't think long and straight away swapped the roles, just as that young man once did...
A young man, a textile [manufaktur] merchant, held a bris (that was once upon a time — today that too is a rarity...), and, by the way, he had just sent back to a manufacturer a rag[?] of merchandise... So he sat down and wrote two letters: one letter to his father-in-law — since his little dove[?], may she be healthy and strong, had given birth with good luck and had a male child, he therefore asks him to come, for heaven's sake [?], on such-and-such a day to the bris, and he honours him with being sandek [printed "sandek-avot"]...
A second letter he wrote further to the Łódź manufacturer: since he had palmed off on him merchandise "which he cannot send", he therefore sends him the goods back, and he may grow old with them till a hundred and twenty years... But when writing the addresses he made a mistake in his great haste, so the letter in which he invites to the bris with the honour of sandek [here printed "sandek-amot"] arrived at the Łódź manufacturer, and the letter with the "merchandise which he cannot send", with which he should grow old till a hundred and twenty, arrived at the father-in-law... So you understand, of course, that the manufacturer came to the bris and the father-in-law stayed at home...
There — I did exactly the same: the letter from the urząd saying I am an enormously rich man I forwarded to the Częstochowa manufacturer: here, look what a great rich man I am...
And the letter from the manufacturer, with the bureau's information that I am a small little man, I forwarded to the naczelnik: here, look what a great pauper I am...
Perhaps he will at last believe me once that I am not able to pay such "colossal taxes"...
In any case, my friend, you see already that I did not sit idle, and, thank God, I did everything I possibly could, and perhaps the Almighty will help that in the present assessment, which comes round as always before Passover, they will loosen my tax-screw a little, and that, God willing, they will not [burden?] me for this year's Seder with such large taxes, which embitter one's life beyond bearing a whole [?] year. And they gnaw the marrow out of the bones, which really is no longer possible to bear,
If only...
Your friend Yosef Perlmuter [Józef Perlmutter].
Rasputin and His Jewish Mistress — a historical novel by Boris Maksimov (instalment 17)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin; instalment 17.]
Evening began to fall. In the room it grew darker. The sick boy now lay quietly, drowsy. The Tsarina sat motionless, staring with fixed eyes. Suddenly she recalled the old Archimandrite Feofan, who had been here an hour ago, and she remembered his words:
— Reconsider, great sovereign of "holy" Russia!...
And she thought: and perhaps? Perhaps one should follow the advice of the pious man? Perhaps God Himself speaks through his mouth and his advice will help? Perhaps what he says is true, that God is angry and does not want to listen to our prayers because unbelievers are found in the "holy" capital?
Then — and someone knocked at the door of the room. The Tsarina remained motionless and did not answer. There was a knock a second time and a third time, and since no "answer" came from the room, the door opened very quietly and Anna Vyrubova, the Tsarina's closest friend, entered the room. The Tsarina still sat motionless, apathetic, until Vyrubova came closer to her and the Tsarina saw her face.
Vyrubova, with intimacy and warmth, at once sat down beside the Tsarina, began to stroke her, caress her and console her with kind and faithful words. For a while the Tsarina listened to her in silence. She was still as if petrified. Soon, however, she was moved by Vyrubova's kind words. And — she burst into violent weeping. Her head fell onto Vyrubova's shoulder, and Vyrubova tenderly embraced her and drew her close. The Tsarina wept, and the tears washed away a little of the heavy pain from her heart. She felt a little easier. Vyrubova tried to calm her. When the Tsarina had become calmer, Vyrubova exclaimed with a quiet ecstasy in her voice:
— I have come to bring you great tidings!
With this exclamation Vyrubova at once drew the Tsarina's attention. The Tsarina became interested in her friend's words. Vyrubova spoke quickly, full of ecstasy: the Tsarina need worry about nothing any more... from now on everything will be good... Alexei will get well at once... and he will be healthy and strong...
And she exclaimed with enthusiasm:
— A new "miracle-worker" has appeared! A great "holy man" is now in Petersburg!... He will make Alexei well... one only needs to bring him here and Alexei is saved...
The Tsarina, who was tremendously superstitious and pious, became very curious. Her eyes, which until then had been extinguished and fixed, became a little livelier. Her heart began to beat more strongly and she asked:
— Who is the "miracle-worker" and where does he come from? Why has nothing been heard of him until now?
— From distant Siberia he comes... on foot he wandered until he came here... It is only a week since he appeared in the capital, and his name is already famous... I am sure: God has sent him here at the right time...
Vyrubova spoke in one breath, spoke stammering [?] and with great enthusiasm. He is a wonderful man, this Siberian muzhik... through his mouth God Himself speaks... he is endowed with great wisdom and possesses such power that he can perform [?] the greatest wonders... Yesterday she became acquainted with the "holy man". The priest Vostorgov introduced her to him and — she recognized him at once. This is that "holy" muzhik who once saved her life in Siberia... the Tsarina surely remembers... when she came back from Siberia she told her, after all... her life was in great danger... she was riding in a britzka and the horses bolted... began to run wild... she saw death before her eyes... she was on the point of perishing... a miracle happened: a "holy" muzhik came towards her and with a single shout he stopped the maddened horses... the Tsarina surely remembers it... isn't that so?
The Tsarina nodded her head and Vyrubova exclaimed with enthusiasm:

One Atonement for Many

[Satirical feuilleton — the economic crisis; the death of the "Match King" Ivar Kreuger.]
The whole world is racking its head over Kreuger's death. And this is not the "kula alma" [the whole world] of the Gemara, which consists of a couple of yeshiva boys on the bench, but truly all the stock exchanges, all the concerns, all the financial institutions, politicians and statesmen of the entire world are racking their brains: how did it come to this, that this world magnate, the friend of the Fords [printed "Ferds"], the Rockefellers and the Morgans, should suddenly go mad and put a bullet into his head?
So I want to reveal a secret here — only don't hand it over to the prosecutor — that it is in fact I myself who am guilty of Kreuger's tragic death, of course. I had many accomplices with me, but that does not lessen, but on the contrary, it only increases my crime, which was after all committed "in public". In modern parlance it is called: society is guilty. But I have no business with society, so I will confess to my own crime.
First of all, as soon as I felt that my pocket was empty, I began to save on matches. At first I followed the advice of a friend, a smoker, and began splitting a match in two. Later I realised that, fine, a papirosa [cigarette] I can reduce from "Maren" to "Szianti" [cigarette brands] — one must smoke away one's troubles. But a match is surely a superfluous expense when one can get a light from someone else.
And my wife took her example from me. Since there is no firewood in the shed [?] anyway, if she happens to buy a bundle of wood for heating and cooking together, she goes in to the neighbour with a splinter to light it, as grandmother used to do. In short, no match comes into my home. My budget has been reduced by one item, and Kreuger felt it in his business.
But he, the cunning merchant, had apparently already sensed that he would make no luck with matches. Matches are a beggarly article — so he threw himself at telephones. Here one deals with rich men, and near a fat pot it is good to rub oneself.
So I caught him [?] again. For twelve years I was a telephone subscriber; if I had now the money I have already paid for the telephone, I might perhaps have been able to crawl out of all my troubles. I had two telephones, one at home and one in the shop. But when I realised that with those 40 gulden [złoty] I can live for two weeks, I first took out the home telephone. And my wife and my daughters had to talk over their "randkes" [dates] and "pakers" [?] and plain "pszyjenczes" [?] on my business telephone. This year I did not buy a trade licence at all, the telephone became superfluous to me, and... my wives [sic] do indeed have burning troubles with their dates, but that is not what I am after.
And so a second branch of Kreuger's income was broken off.
He still had not given up, though. He was after all something like the banker of the world. Germany alone owes him 3 billion marks. And wherever you throw a stone, he had sown loans. From the interest alone he could after all make a living in abundance!
Then this happens. I borrowed three hundred gulden [złoty] at the Gemilut Hasadim [free-loan] fund on twenty-złoty bills with a good endorsement. The endorser went bankrupt and does not pay his acceptances, let alone his endorsements. I myself, of course, had no intention whatsoever of paying — it was after all already after the matches and after the telephones. And when I did not pay the "fund", an uproar broke out in the Warsaw "Joint" and in the Berlin Foundation — the whole apparatus was shaken apart and broken down. And since the "Foundation" sits in Berlin, there went out from it, like a plague, bank crashes all over Germany, and Kreuger saw neither principal nor interest any more — he was left with the bond certificates...
Let me tell you further how I stubbornly and systematically wiped out all of Kreuger's accounts: he dealt in paper — I stopped using paper for writing bills of exchange and stopped buying newspapers. He dealt in iron — I stopped even knocking a nail into the wall. Not to speak of building anything. He threw himself into trading in money, as it is called, stock-exchange speculation — I made a vow to have no money at all, neither metal nor paper, no form of coin whatsoever.
You think perhaps he was a schlimazel? Begging your pardon, you are mistaken. Whatever he would have taken up, he would not have found a place with me. Had he dealt in electricity — I have already signed the strike slip. Had he dealt in wedding rings — I have 5 daughters sitting at home and nobody even thinks of snatching them up. He did indeed deal in houses — so yesterday I already gave half a gulden to the tenants' association for its campaign about rent.
When such a time is now going on, a time of not buying, not giving, not having...
Is it any wonder that he, Kreuger, poor man, had to fall a victim?
Yet he did do humanity a small favour. Had he not grabbed so many businesses into his hands, we would now have had to have 20, 30, 50 suicides; now he has been the single kapore [atonement] for many.
This too is for the best!
Argus.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tzav)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tzav
The Portion
—o—
a) "Command Aaron" (6:2)
"'Command' always denotes urging... Scripture must urge especially where there is a loss of money" (Rashi).
In the "Yerushalmi" it is told: Rabbi Yohanan lost his money-purse; someone asked him a point of law and he did not know it. So they asked him: because you have lost your purse, have you also lost your mind? He answered: yes — the mind depends on the heart, and the heart depends on the... purse.
Yes: where there is a loss of money there is also a loss of mind; and with the burnt-offering, from which the priests get no benefit at all, it stands to reason that their thoughts will not be on it either...
Olelot Efrayim.
—o—
Rabbi Yitzhak'l of Warka used to say:
The Gemara deduces by a kal va-chomer (a fortiori) that pious Jews have wealth and honour. And indeed they are better off than the rich, whose money is in cash and who are full of worries lest it be stolen from them. Whereas the pious Jews, whose wealth exists only in the "kal va-chomer", can be sure that nothing will be stolen from them out of this iron safe — the kal va-chomer.. Osher Nifla'ot.
—o—
b) "And the priest shall put on his linen garment (mido)" (ibid. 3)
The priests — our religious leaders — live far more broadly than "mido", which according to the homily means "according to his measure". They lead a broad life at the community's expense. "And who has seen such a thing, who has heard such a thing... Our forefathers, the early tzaddikim, who are already in the World of Truth — they went hungry, suffered want and gave fat 'gakes' [?]"; today it is "they have given all their treasures for food" — for food, for making a living, they give away all their treasures: the Torah and everything that ought to be dear to them... Or ha-Me'ir (Rabbi Velvele of Zhitomir).
—o—
c) "And he shall carry the ashes... unto a clean place" (ibid. 4)
Even the ashes — the dross, the refuse of the Jewish people — must also have a clean place, for the worth of a Jew is beyond reckoning...
Beit Ya'akov.
—o—
d) "This is the law of the burnt-offering, of the meal-offering, and of the sin-offering, and of the guilt-offering" (7:37)
Sometimes studying Torah is truly a burnt-offering and a meal-offering to God, and sometimes — when one does not mean it seriously — it is a sin-offering and a guilt-offering, an outright sin. Botzina de-Nehora.
—o—
e) "That maketh atonement therewith" (ibid. 7)
When one brings a sacrifice, or repents of a sin, God does indeed grant atonement; but — like that merchant who settled with his debtor: because the man pleads with him and he sees his critical situation, he forgives him the debt out of pity. But he will no longer give him credit, even though he is sorry for him..
God does indeed forgive the sinful debtor, but He no longer trusts him... Mishlei Ya'akov.
—o—
f) "All the sons of Aaron shall have, one as well as another (ish ke-achiv)" (ibid. 10)
Among the sons of Aaron every Jew must be as beloved as one's own brother — "ish ke-achiv", a man as his brother; that is to say, love of Israel.
Tiferet Shlomo.
—o—
g) Parashat Parah.
A rabbi once gave a sermon on Shabbat Parashat Parah. A householder pays him a compliment: your sermon truly suited Parashat Parah.
— Why?
— Because the commandment of the red heifer has no reason (ta'am), and your sermon had no taste (ta'am) either...
—o—
h) "When a man dieth in a tent" (reading for Parashat Parah)
"You are called 'man' (adam), and idolaters are not called 'man'."
Rabbi Zadoc Kahn, the Chief Rabbi of Paris, once accompanied the funeral of a rich Jew. Many prominent Christian men also walked in the procession. Passing through the Christian cemetery, which borders on the Jewish one, Rabbi Zadoc walked along the whole time. On reaching the Jewish cemetery, Rabbi Zadoc stops and stays put.
A Christian, a friend, asks him the reason. He explains that he is a kohen and a cemetery is defiling.
— Well, and the Christian cemetery is not defiling? Don't you count us as human beings?
— Your Christian God, you say, did not die. His believers do not die either; they go straight up into heaven. So, they are not in the graves, and there is nothing to defile.. But we Jews — our Moses died, and we too die like ordinary people, therefore our graves defile...
The Spectre of Liquidation

When we acquaint ourselves more closely with the situation of our public institutions — those very positions whose conquest cost us so much toil and sweat — when we see how the danger of liquidation hovers over their existence, the fear threatens that one[?] fine morning these establishments, the ornament and pride of our public life in Zagłębie, will have to close.
Our communal workers have already exhausted all their abilities to make various savings, by cutting and trimming[?] budgets. At the same time as these savings, however, the income shrinks manyfold and far outruns the savings — and that at such desperate[?] moments, when they, the communal workers, put to themselves the bitter question: where will help come from at all, what will rescue us from all the troubles, headaches and countless woes? One begins to see that help in the so terrible word: liquidation.
If one of our communal workers sometimes dares to think about this terrible word and sees in it a rescue from his worries and cares, he must not be blamed, because it is not a mere whim on his part; it happens only after he has already tried everything, when he has already knocked on all doors and everywhere met with stopped-up ears and locked hearts.
Worried and despondent go about all those who, for one reason or another, stand at the head of some institution and have already grown together with it so much that it, the institution, has become part of their life, of their very self. They see that the yoke is too heavy nowadays, that one takes a great burden upon oneself at the present difficult moment when one runs a public institution.
The present time is hard for public work. Everyone has his own personal worries, which discourage him, which rob him of initiative, energy, the capacity to lead. The time is hard also because of the want and poverty, which advance with giant strides and already occupy an ample place in respectable homes too.
It would however be[*] many times harder if we did not strengthen ourselves under these circumstances, did not summon all our courage to drive away, to chase off this spectre of liquidation. And although the time is so bad, so bitter, because it is a dangerous moment, we must not remain apathetic[?], we must not lose courage; on the contrary: resolute and courageous, firm and with full energy, each in his place, each in his position should continue his work and not allow all this to be lost.
Let us believe that we shall get through the present hard time of crisis and with every possible means help the existence of all our public institutions.
Y.
New Small Inventions

From our correspondent at the Leipzig Fair, Z. Haber.
At the Leipzig Fair novelties are always shown that are important for our daily life. I will mention a few such small things here.
Waterproof clothes.
That fabrics can be impregnated to the point that they do not let water through is an old thing. But the fabrics had to be treated chemically already during weaving so that they would not let the wet through. At the present Leipzig Fair a firm from Germany exhibited a chemical[?] preparation of this kind, called "Imprägnal". With this liquid one can coat all articles — fabrics, shoes, hats, gloves and in general anything we want — and at once the articles become "waterproof". They let no rain through in any way. In this way one can put on any garment and go out in the rain; it will not harm it at all and it always stays dry.
New automatic machines.
Most widespread in the world are the vending machines that dispense sweets and chocolate. In the big cities vending machines for cigarettes, for postage stamps and for other things too have already been introduced. Now a firm brings out a machine from which one can obtain needle and thread in all sorts of colours, a thimble and in general everything one needs for sewing. It will now be possible, as soon as someone loses, say, a button torn off his coat, to get black thread with a needle and a thimble from a machine and sew the button on at once. Unmarried men will surely greet this machine warmly.
A means for cleaning glass.
Until now, when one wanted to clean glass, one first had to smear it with some paste or soap, then one cleaned it a little, and only after that did one make the glass completely clean. Now a product has been exhibited in Leipzig with which glass, mirrors, marble, porcelain and enamel can be cleaned and polished at once without any chalk or paste: it is spread on a piece of cloth, simply rubbed over, and the object is cleaned just as before, when one had to work on it for a longer time.
Curling tongs for ladies.
If a lady went on a journey somewhere, she had to take her curling tongs along in a separate parcel. At the Leipzig Fair curling tongs were exhibited that can be folded like a pocket-knife and carried in a handbag; a further advantage is that, folded up, the tongs keep their heat for several hours. It is therefore possible, when a lady goes to the theatre or visits someone, that afterwards, when she takes off her hat, she can arrange her hair as she likes with her tongs, which are hot and carried in the bag. — The ladies will surely use these little tongs everywhere.
A small home printing press.
A Dresden firm exhibited at the Leipzig Fair a model of a small printing press which is very cheap and very easy to use. It is especially important for those who need many small printed items, such as slips, labels, address strips and postcards. Writing paper can also be printed on it. One can also get all sorts of type for it, and anyone can print in a very short time all kinds of printed matter he needs. For associations too, which need invitations, notices and small hand-posters, the cheap apparatus is very good.
The Keren Hayesod Campaign at the Present Moment

"'Command' (tzav) denotes nothing but urging, both immediately and for all generations. Said R. Shimon: Scripture must urge especially where there is a loss of money."
(From today's Torah portion [Tzav].)

At a very hard time we are beginning the Keren Hayesod campaign in our town — at a time when all around there reigns terrible want, poverty, despair; Jewish livelihoods that held out for generations are tottering and being ruined one by one; the whole Jewish merchant class stands before an abyss and is threatened with being swallowed by the terrible chasm of the crisis; the antisemitic clouds grow ever thicker, the fire of the age-old hatred of the eternal people flares up ever more strongly and forces its way into every corner of Jewish life, eating away at the roots of old Jewish stocks that grew up over generations. And not only here in the Diaspora: there too, over the beautiful blue sky of the Jewish Land of Israel, a heavy cloud hangs; there too the hidden enemy, who thinks of destruction and ruin, lies in wait for us from every corner; the enemy's eyes are full of envy and hatred toward our splendid work of building — from which the enemy himself also profits with a full hand — and yet the danger is great because of the blind hatred stirred up by dark fanatical cliques [?]. And under just such circumstances, with just such prospects, we are beginning this year's Keren Hayesod campaign, and faint-hearted voices are heard: how can one still today come to the Jewish merchant, ask for money, contribute to the Keren Hayesod?

True! Certainly our loyal Keren Hayesod activists need extraordinary daring, an enormous faith in their strength to be able to encourage, to awaken the Jewish conscience, to plant in the hearts of the Jewish masses the confidence, the faith in their own revival and self-liberation. Armed with the one weapon, with the wonderful magic instrument, with the potent magic word called Eretz Israel, we come today — and precisely today, when it seems there is no way out, that, God forbid, all the appointed ends have already passed — we come to remind you of Eretz Israel, which after all is the only lighthouse in our dark life of exile. And we have complete trust in the broad Jewish masses, in their devotion, in their readiness for the greatest sacrifices for Eretz Israel. There is no destructive force able to break the firm faith of the Jewish people in Eretz Israel. We believe in the stiff-neckedness of the Jewish people, expressed in the Jewish saying "af al pi khen" ("nevertheless"): in spite of everything, in spite of everyone, the Jewish work that has begun to be built in Eretz Israel will be completed; to spite all enemies from without and from within we will double our energy and speed up the pace of creating and building.

And so, with the power of this faith, we come to you, Jews of Będzin, with an urgent demand, and we call out to you: free yourselves for a moment from the terrible nightmare that dominates you! Remember yourselves and your children!

We are not asking you for alms, not for philanthropy; Eretz Israel has already become nowadays a personal matter for every individual Jew, and no one knows when his day of judgement will come and he will need Eretz Israel. And even more must we remember our children! Our youth — and we must give our youth an idealistic enthusiasm that will be able to turn them away from other ideals that lead to national apostasy. And the more we elders show our enthusiasm, our willingness to sacrifice, the more we will thereby influence our children, our youth, who strive for and seek what is beautiful, pure, [just?] [printed "gshrefte", probably a misprint], who are eager to fight for a bright [?] future. And let every Keren Hayesod contributor bear in mind that with the contribution he gives to the Keren Hayesod he is not giving alms, but is thereby paying an honest debt for himself and for his children, helping to build a future for himself and his children; and who knows whether he is not already now benefiting — if not he himself, then his children who are already in Eretz Israel — from the Keren Hayesod institutions. Therefore, precisely at the present moment, we must remember the old rule: "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied" (Exodus 1:12). The worse the situation becomes, the more we must double our contributions, in order to speed up the building, to create a place of refuge for ourselves and for our children.

Nete Landner.
They Are, After All, the Privileged Ones...

[Letter in reply — society and family.] (A reply to the woman writer of the article in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 11, A. N., "You men make us nervous").
It is very convenient to look at the innocent faces of women when they, poor things, put on a pitiful face and prove with signs and wonders that if somewhere there is no domestic peace, if husband and wife do not live contentedly, if a man leaves his wife — then the only ones to blame for it are the "sweet men", the "dear males".
It is characteristic to see their claims, their grievances and complaints against the men, and their justifying themselves before all and sundry, and their wish to convince that for the woman's nervousness it is precisely the man who is to blame, because if he were to make even a bit of soul-searching, he, the man, would easily be convinced that the woman's nervousness and agitation, or even hysteria, is fully justified and well-founded"... This, then, is the content of the article in No. 11 under the heading "The men make us nervous".
When I, as one of the men, set about writing the reply, it is the consequence of a fact (as a result of the mentioned article) which I witnessed: how people lean on "even the newspaper writes" about the "wild men" who cause grief to the "poor delicate women".
Esteemed readers! Let us go out walking in the street with the aim of observing the bad times, i.e. of seeing the methods and means by which people earn a living today, what they occupy themselves with in order to draw a livelihood, and who are the "livelihood-givers", the "providers".
And what do we see? Here and there tormented men catch our eye; everyone runs and chases, each on his own path, each doing his work. One a lighter, nicer and better one, the other a worse and much, much harder one — each according to his ability, each according to his position and means. But the sum total of it is that the man toils hard and bitterly at "back-breaking labour"; he ploughs with his nose, with blood and sweat. And for what? Let us ask ourselves: for what the toil? For what the torment and self-torture? For what?
Is not the whole yoke and effort only to give the wife a livelihood? Is not the whole burden and load in order to satisfy her demands and to content the household?
...And yet, how many thousands of women there are who do not even know, or do not want to know at all, where the husband gets a living, and who do not lift a finger [literally: do not put a hand into cold water]... It does not concern them at all how much he took in today, what deals he, the husband, "laid the egg" on [?], whether he has even earned enough for cigarettes.
Very many women of this kind, unfortunately, we meet. But do you know the further behaviour of these women? Has anyone yet listened to the outbursts and polemics of these women when their "servant" has, at the moment, nothing to give them for the sum demanded for their expenses? Oh, then you may see that same fine woman — embittered, broken, nervous, crushed in spirit, groaning and wailing, weeping and lamenting over the whole wide world. Disgusting and ugly then are these scenes; sad and scandalous are the goings-on then at this unfortunate Jew's, when "the cow will no longer let itself be milked"... Or imagine it in a quite simple form: the man is tired, broken, troubles and worries without measure, from all sides [gshkaon — unclear word] and summonses [wezwania] for unpaid taxes [podatki?], and dates for distraint [zajęcie] or even an eviction [eksmisja] are not lacking either; frozen through [?] and broken from a whole day, and when he comes home agitated, [behuzer — unclear word] and angry — is all this not justified? Can one wonder that his mental state is so heated? Must not his wife calm him by every means? Must she not try to soothe his nerves? It is not enough that she gives no thought to the burden of making a living, nor even to cutting down expenses. For rouge and powder — only you still have to pay up [?] and give a kiss on the little mouth.
Do we find few such women? Instead of reflecting, of thinking, of helping the husband in his hard labours, they, the women, have in mind "quarrels" and "squabbles": this is not moral, that is not ethical, "nie taktowne" [Polish: tactless], "ja przecież [?] 'dama'" [Polish: after all I am a 'lady'], and respect for [?] "donkey-men", and debt, debt without end, "daj do kina, daj na szminki" [Polish: give for the cinema, give for lipstick], and to you, the "treasure-crown" [?] — a fig... For their nervousness is, after all, justly founded, meyl... meyl... [?]
They are, after all, the privileged ones!...
Ben Zion H—r
(The husband of a carefree woman).
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Meeting of the Kehilla Board

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 17 Adar 5692 — piątek 25 marca 1932 [Friday, 25 March 1932].)
Będzin

Meeting of the Kehilla Board.
With the participation of the Rabbi and members of the rabbinate, a meeting of the kehilla board took place.
At the meeting the Rabbi, in his report on kashrut matters, said that since a lot of meat is brought in from outside, and a large number of cattle are also slaughtered outside the town, a remedy must be devised to improve the matter.
During the discussion of this matter it became clear that kashrut in the butcher shops is neglected by the supervisors (ne'emanim) themselves. The matter was "settled" with the conclusion that "something must be done".
The meeting considered the proposal of Mrs. Sh., who wishes to give 8000 zł. on condition that after 120 years her plot (grave) be located next to that of her husband.
It was resolved to approach the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha about this, for their decision.

Cantor Żupowicz's Claim before the District Court.
The former Będzin cantor Mr. Menachem Żupowicz claims from the kehilla board a debt of 8 thousand zł. Because the board has not paid the debt, Żupowicz has filed a suit with the Sosnowiec District Court.
The trial takes place on 12 April. Summoned as witnesses are Messrs. M. M.[?] Zaks, H. Koniński, Avromel Liwer and the gmina (kehilla) secretary Mr. Frajlich.

"Hatikvah" Is Treyf to Sing...
On the programme of the festive service in the local synagogue, "Hatikvah" was, among other things, also to be sung.
But the whole programme, including "Boże coś Polskę", was performed — except "Hatikvah".
When one of the kehilla representatives drew the attention of the cantor, Mr. Piotrkowski, to this, he declared that he would not sing "Hatikvah" because he had been told so...

After Signing the Agreement, Someone Runs to the "Squire" to Intervene.
As we have already reported, the subsidy of 3 500 zł. from the Magistrate (municipality) for the religious chadorim was divided as follows: the Talmud Torah receives 1300 zł., "Mizrachi" and "Yesodei HaTorah" 900 each, "Beit Yaakov" 400 zł. The division was made by the representatives of the chadorim, and each of them gave his written consent to it. The next morning, however, one of the "close to the authorities" intervened with the Magistrate inspector, saying that "Yesodei HaTorah" ought to receive the same sum as the Talmud Torah, and that "Mizrachi" should get only a "trifle", because "in the Mizrachi school only rich children study"...

Mistaken Because of the Weather..
At a minyan on Małachowskiego Street, on Monday evening the Torah reader (ba'al kore), before reading the Megillah, recited the blessing "to kindle the Chanukah light"...

Magistrate Opens an Institution for the Mentally Ill.
The local Magistrate, not having the financial means to maintain the large number of mentally ill persons who are in psychiatric hospitals, has opened such an institution in Brzozowice[?], which is under the supervision of Dr. Wa-perzeyg[?] (possibly Wasserzug).
The institution houses a larger number of patients, who until now had been under treatment in the hospital at Świecie.

Jewish Youth Leave a "Strzelec" Performance in Protest.
On Saturday afternoon, in honour of Marshal Piłsudski's name-day, a performance was held, organised by the local "Strzelec" [paramilitary riflemen's association].
The performance, which was also attended by Jewish school youth, had a ridiculous[?] antisemitic content, as a result of which the Jewish spectators walked out of the theatre hall as a sign of protest.

On Making the Telephone Fee Cheaper.
The Merchants' Association applied to the telephone directorate in Sosnowiec with a request that, because of the critical times, the fee paid by telephone subscribers be reduced.
This week the Merchants' Association received a reply that the request had been forwarded to Warsaw, to the head directorate.

From the "Merchants' Association"
We are asked to point out that until Saturday the 26th of this month there is time to submit appeals concerning the new water-supply tax.
Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Trade and credit.]
On Cheap Credit for Merchants.
Under the chairmanship of the vice-president of the local Chamber of Commerce, a meeting of the trade section was held with the participation of representatives of Bank Polski, Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego, [the bank of the] Spółek Zarobkowych, the Credit Bank in Będzin, etc.]
After the report by councillor (Ratman) Sauber [Saber] on cheap credit for merchants, a discussion developed in which, among others, Messrs. Tenenbaum, Kabak, Tencer, Dr. Michalski and Kwiatek took part; they described the difficult situation of the merchants, which could be eased by granting them cheap credit.
On this question a conference called by the Ministry of Trade took place this week in Warsaw. The Chamber of Commerce was represented by Vice-President Gruszczyński and councillor Sauber. The Będzin Merchants' Association was represented by its president, Mr. Rubinlicht.
After the reports the Minister of Trade declared that a committee would be created, to be joined by representatives of all merchants' associations in the whole of Poland, and that the committee is to work out a plan for how to develop trade and in what ways the cheap credits should be given to the merchant class.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Artisans and taxes.]
Artisans' Representatives on the Assessment Commission
On the basis of the intervention of the artisans' representatives with the local tax inspector, the latter has given his consent that representatives of every guild (cech) shall be present at the assessments of turnover.
At the same time attention is once again drawn to the fact that artisans who want to benefit from the ryczałt (lump-sum tax) must register with the Artisans' Association. Otherwise they will not be able to benefit from the ryczałt reduction.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Health and charity.]
"Linas HaCholim" Establishes an Outpatient Clinic.
The new board of the "Linas HaCholim" society is showing activity with regard to its tasks. In particular, a vigorous activity is developing in the field of providing medical help to poor sick people in the form of medicines and night watches at the sickbed.
At its last meeting the board decided to open an outpatient clinic (ambulatorium). Negotiations on this are being conducted with a number of doctors in our town.
—o—
[Sosnowiec — Charity.]
Give Clothes to the Naked, Food to Hungry Sick Children.
Without noise or fuss, the women's section of the local "Dobroczynność" (charity society) is carrying on a broad activity for the benefit of the poorest stratum of the local Jewish population. Every single day 400 lunches are handed out; besides that, products such as butter, food and the like are collected, which are distributed every Thursday to Jewish sick children.
From time to time the section collects old clothes and linen, which are distributed among the poor population. Therefore, whoever has old things or linen should notify Mrs. Dr. Grodzińska by telephone, number 12-24.
Important for those who have relatives in Russia

The notice in our paper that the Craftsmen's Bank in Sosnowiec (Targowa 9 is accepting food parcels and provisions for dispatch to relatives in Russia aroused wide interest throughout Zagłębie, because until now sending provisions has been very expensive and has also involved great difficulties.
The Jewish Relief Society in London took note [?] of this and set up large food depots in several dozen towns in Soviet Russia, and has made sending provisions easier in such a way that one can pay a certain sum of money in Poland or in other countries, and on the strength of the transfer to the Relief Society the designated person in Soviet Russia receives his parcel of food and provisions.
The agency for Poland has been taken over by the Warsaw bank „Udziałowy“. The agency for the Będzin district has been given to the Craftsmen's and Small Traders' Bank in Sosnowiec, Targowa 9.
—o—
Eng. Gałat to be appointed deputy minister
In the coming days the President of the Republic is to sign the appointment of the present general director of the „Mandzhever Akladn“ [?] [works], Eng. Gałat, as deputy minister of communications.
—o—
Festive siyum ha-sefer in Old Sosnowiec
Next Monday the Jewish residents of Old Sosnowiec will celebrate the completion of a [Torah] scroll. Various festivities are being prepared for the dedication, which will take place in the local synagogue.

Members of the Communist Central Committee arrested
The local police have arrested 3 persons, members of the Communist Central Committee in Poland.
Among those arrested is also a certain Kagan, the son of a Łódź manufacturer.
The arrested are accused of being the organisers of the strike movement in Zagłębie.

„Rozwój“ sings its old song...
Sunday's K. Z. [Kurjer Zachodni] printed an appeal by „Rozwój“, which calls on Polish society, both when buying and when giving work, to keep in mind only the Pole and not „the strangers, who are our enemies“.
We do not know whom „Rozwój“ calls enemies — perhaps the very Jewish firms that fill the advertisement section of the paper...

Tram traffic declines
Because of the crisis, the traffic [ridership] on the trams has declined considerably.
—o—
Sosnowiec emigrants to the Land of Israel
On Sunday 8 olim, members of the local „Maccabi“, left to take part in the Maccabiah in the Land of Israel. Hundreds of people gathered at the railway station in honour of the departure and bade a warm farewell to those leaving for the Land of Israel.
—o—
For circulating counterfeit coins.
Two peasants from the Wolbrom [?] area, who had circulated counterfeit złoty coins, stood before the local district court.
The accused were sentenced to 18 months in prison.
—o—
A Purim ball at „Arlekin“.
Next Sunday the Jewish tailors' guild is organising a Purim ball at „Arlekin“. Great preparations are being made for the event; above all, the question who will be chosen as Queen Esther has aroused great interest. The merchants have forgotten the crisis, stopped taking an interest in what is happening in the Far East, in the presidential elections in Germany and in the Match King — all these matters have been pushed aside, and they are curious and eager to know who will be chosen as Queen Esther. In a word, Sunday's Purim ball at „Arlekin“ promises to be interesting.
—o—
A mysterious murder.
On Barbary street the 69-year-old Antoni Pasilek [?] was found murdered in his own flat.

They are already assessing...
Since Monday the assessment commissions have been at work determining turnover for the year 1931.
In the street poverty whistles. And the commissions sweat at their sittings...

The Jaworzno rabbi, who was elected local rabbi a few months ago, has already taken up his office.
The new rabbi's arrival took place with great honour.

Kehilla elections — in May
According to semi-official information received by the local gmina, new kehilla elections are to take place in May of this year.

At the „Huta Katarzyna“ a gas pipe burst, killing two workers.

Together with the coal strike, the workers at the „Strem“ factory in Strzemieszyce also went on strike.
This week a conference took place under the chairmanship of the Sosnowiec labour inspector, at which the strike dispute was settled as follows: workers earning more than 8 zł a day receive 5 [?] percent. Those earning 6 zł a day receive 4 percent less.

A Trumpeldor academy.
In the premises of the local „Maccabi“, in connection with the 12th yahrzeit of Joseph Trumpeldor, a memorial academy was held with the participation of Mr Jaskierowicz (Będzin).

On Jadwiga street in Dąbrowa a 3-year-old child fell under a tram. Thanks to the tram being stopped instantly, the child was saved from certain death. The wheels cut off all the toes of the child's left foot.

A Mother Burns Her Own Two Children in an Oven

[Gleiwitz — crime; child murder.]
In Gleiwitz [today Gliwice, then in German Upper Silesia] a terrible murder was discovered the day before yesterday in the morning, committed by a mother of her own against her two small children.
The widow Berta Haupt suffocated[?] her children in a pot, a little boy of two and a little girl of one. Then she put them into an oven to roast.
The cruel murder was discovered by the neighbours, who had noticed the terrible smell that came from Mrs Haupt's flat. Asked about it, Berta Haupt explained that she was roasting meat left over from the holiday.
Because of this the neighbours, seeing[?] that the children were missing, informed the police, which discovered the bestial deed. Of the little children there were already only a few bones...
When the devilish mother was led through the street by the police, a crowd of a thousand people wanted to lynch her.
The mother confessed. During the interrogation she stated that first she had cooked[?] the little boy and then the little girl. She had wanted to bury the dead bodies, but, fearing that the deed might be discovered, she burned the flesh of her children.
The inhabitants of Gleiwitz are shaken by the cruel murder. Large crowds of people gather in front of the prison building where the devilish mother is held.
