Shtadlan and Fighter

(Sketches in pencil).
Our tragic fate as a people, scattered[?] and dispersed among nations and lands, has always, everywhere and at all times, set before us, in all its sharpness, the problem of —
— shtadlanut [intercession] and — struggle!
Our rightless situation, our specific living conditions, created with them the favourable ground for the Jewish —
— shtadlan [intercessor]!
As a social-political activist, for the temporary rescue of individuals, or — at best — of a certain group, and drove out the Jewish —
— fighter!
for freedom and rights, of lasting and general national character, who found for his ideas and methods of struggle no understanding and no recognition on the Jewish street.
And at all times, under all conditions, we see the Jewish —
— shtadlan!
Self-satisfied, and proud of his activity, surrounded by recognition from those supposedly by him —
— rescued!!
And at the same time — the Jewish —
— fighter!
Downcast and humiliated, persecuted and rejected by those supposedly by him —
— betrayed!!
The Jewish individual, or the particular Jewish group, that has gained something through the —
— shtadlan!
cannot and will not have any interest in or understanding for other and more valuable achievements and interests, of a general national character, for which there fights, with admirable devotion, the Jewish —
— fighter!
for freedom and rights of lasting value.
And the Jewish masses of certain strata and groupings will not and cannot understand that in fact the —
— shtadlan and — fighter!
represent in our social-political life the —
— theses[?] and — antitheses!!
of our unbearable living conditions and of the attempts and efforts to get out of them.
In no case would[?] the Jewish —
— shtadlan!
achieve that little bit „on the tip of a knife“ that he achieves, if at his side there did not stand the Jewish —
— fighter!
for far-reaching, greater and more lasting achievements of freedom and rights.
And conversely — perhaps the demands of the Jewish —
— fighter!
would[?] long ago have been crowned with due success, if at his side there did not stand the Jewish —
— shtadlan!
who enjoys the spiritual and [—] gifts that are bestowed on him out of what —
— is due to us!
These strata and groupings of ours will not and also cannot understand that the difference between the Jewish —
— shtadlan and — fighter!
consists chiefly in a different conception of our relation to the great general —
— state table!
in the preparing and maintaining of which table Jews take a —
— great part!
and from enjoying which we are so systematically and ruthlessly —
— not admitted!
At a time when the Jewish —
— fighter!
stands up for our freedom and rights — downcast and humiliated indeed, but — with a proudly raised head and sternly demanding eyes, and boldly demands before the whole world his —
— place and — share!
together with all the equal and exalted —
— at the table!
at the same time the Jewish —
— shtadlan!
throws himself, with a grateful smile on his lips and a contented expression in his servile eyes, upon the —
— crumbs!
which are magnanimously flung down to him —
— under the table!
And when at times something comes up[?], for oneself and also for the surrounding world, the incessant demands of the Jewish —
— fighter!
who demands throughout his place —
— at the table!
— then against him, as counter-proof, is pushed forward the contented Jewish —
— shtadlan!
who is so grateful for being thrown something —
— under the table!
And that already serves as a justification both for oneself and for the other.
And tragic is the fate of a people, and hopeless are its prospects for the future, if the people does not understand and cannot properly orient itself in the problem of —
— shtadlanut and — struggle!
If self-satisfied and proud, surrounded by recognition, there remains with it the —
— shtadlan!
and downcast and humiliated, persecuted and rejected [is with it] the —
— fighter!
A. M. T. [„Emes“ — Truth]
What Will Be?

[Feuilleton — conversation; the economic crisis.] (A talk with a disabled veteran.)
Yesterday I go over to my invalid to buy a few cigarettes, and he turns to me with this sort of question:
— Tell me, sir [„panie“], what will be?
I remembered what Ecclesiastes says: "That which hath been is that which shall be." And that is indeed how I answered him.
But he did not calm down.
— No, sir! What has been will not be.
— How do you know?
— Just now [?] one of yours walked past, a neighbour from the house opposite, an old customer of mine.
He started with a pack of "Maden" [?] every morning, later went over to "Ergo" [?], came down to "Grand", waited on "Amanti". A pack, barely [?] — that was his ration.
— A few months ago he started buying them one at a time, then went over to 5 "Amanti", and lately he would buy two at a time for 7 groszy.
— And just now he walked past and pretended not to see — probably didn't have the 7 groszy.
— So you see [?], what has been will not be — it will be worse.
— Well, what can be worse than nothing? — I ask.
But my invalid is no fool.
— Of course it can. Today he has nothing for cigarettes, and tomorrow he won't have anything for bread either.
I want to try philosophising and say to him:
— You think there were never people before who had no money for cigarettes, or even for bread?
— There were, of course there were. But today there are too many of them.
— You know what? — he won't let go of me — as I sit here like this in my kiosk ["budka"] and look at the people running past in a hurry, I remember the war, from which I came out a cripple, and I think that life is a war. Fresh invalids keep coming out of it all the time; one of those invalids is precisely my customer who has stopped buying cigarettes.
— Very well put!
— Wait a moment. And when the number of invalids is already too great, the war has to be stopped...
— Well, how can you stop life?
— That is exactly why I ask: "What will be?" The invalids of that war got concessions for cigarettes and vodka. Those concessions are already worth almost nothing, because the public is stopping buying. But what concessions will they give the invalids of this war, which is called life? And who will give out the concessions, when everybody is already almost an invalid?
— So what will really be? — I now ask my philosophical invalid.
— Peace will have to come.
— What kind of peace?
— If life is war, then death is peace.
— So we'll all have to die out? That's no news, every person has to die anyway.
— So I ask indeed: "What will be?"
And so I left the kiosk, and neither of us found an answer to the question: "What will be?"
Avi Ver [signature; apparently a pen-name, "whoever"].
It Doesn't Feel Like a Holiday...

[Feuilleton — letter; trade and the economic crisis, Zagłębie.] (A letter from a textile ["manufaktura"] merchant)
By Józef Perlmutter.
My friend! [?] The sun is shining, the weather is dry. Purim is already over, and [?] the holidays too, and with us things are still somehow not cheerful [?]...
After such a long, hard winter, which froze [?] us completely, we had hoped for the pre-holiday season. But it came to nothing; there are just two weeks left in all until the holiday [Passover], and we thought to ourselves: perhaps, perhaps He will have mercy... But meanwhile the proper takings are nowhere to be seen, and even if something does get sold, that won't bring any great happiness either, because the Jewish customer was never the right consumer, one who could satisfy the merchant's appetite for takings, so that it could be called "sold" [?]...
I still remember the disdain that appeared on the lips of my late father, of blessed memory, when Jewish customers used to come into our shop. All in all my father ran a textile shop for thirty years in one and the same place, amid [?] a Christian neighbourhood, and made quite a nice living; but when Jewish customers came in, father would pass them on to mother, because he had neither the patience nor the strength nor the time to spend on Jewish customers. Firstly, he used to say [?], they don't mean to buy anything yet, only to see what's in the shop; and in the end, after he has covered whole tables with goods and talked his heart out, he will, after all is said and done, barely sell... a single rouble...
And secondly — father used to say — even if he does sell something to Jewish customers, he will still be left with nothing. It's like that puzzle they used to ask us when we were children: think of a number! "Got it." "Throw half into the water... give mother [?] her share... [?] until what's left is... nothing.
It was just the same with the Jewish takings, for from whom, after all, is the Jewish consumer recruited? From Malka Martel [?], the grocer [?], or from Chana [?] the butcher-woman ["jatkarka"], or from [?] of Turin [?], the [?] coal-dealers [?]... and [?] mother used to buy something from them and stay a little in debt; so the account came out that after a whole day's takings there lay in the drawer a few rolls [?] of copper ten-groszy coins, a little of it went to reduce mother's debt [?], and the rest was entered in the book as an interest-free loan...
And how lovely it was, my friend, to hear the back-and-forth when father bargained with the Jewish customers. I tell you, one really needed no theatre — all the comedies with all their pranks were nothing next to it! We children used to hold our sides laughing when two or three young ladies would drop into the shop, who were ashamed to speak Yiddish and couldn't speak Polish... So the language came out a hotchpotch of Yiddish-German and Polish together. Here, for example, something like this:
— Panie kupcze [Mr. merchant], show ["zeigen Sie", German] us something "na bluzeczkę" [Polish: for a little blouse], for a little blouse, just something pretty, "coś ładnego" [something nice], "żeby nie puściła" [so it won't run], so that it won't fade "po praniu" [after washing]...
And father would draw on his cigarette, shut one eye, and meanwhile repeat the whole speech and end with a question mark... and what that meant was, as they say: "Well yes, if you [?] will buy, I'll carry [?] it home"... And on no account would he take the goods out of the cupboard; only [?] as the goods lay arranged, they should choose first, and whatever they liked he would take out and spread out for them...
— Just look [?] at this merchant, "patrzcie na tego kupca" [look at this merchant], he doesn't want to show us any goods at all. "Nie chce nam pokazać towaru" [he doesn't want to show us the goods] — come on [?], "pójdziemy gdzie indziej" [we'll go somewhere else]...
Or a broad-bodied Jewish woman would drop in, a market-fee collector [?], apparently an acquaintance of father's.
— Reb Mendelshi [?], just give me something for a little boy, that will do [?] for a pair of little trousers...
But quite different — father used to say — is dealing with Christians. The Christian consumer consisted for the most part of pension people: an engine driver on the railway, a conductor on the tram, or he worked in a big factory or in the railway workshops, which were in the same neighbourhood; and however many people there were at home, they all earned, and on every 1st of the month they all got their pensions paid out in full. So if someone went to buy something, he would buy with full money, hand over a whole fifty [złoty] note and ask for change... They scraped together a bit of small change, borrowed a little, but a whole fifty remained in the drawer, and there was something to do with it. And father used to be full of joy at such takings... he could "give it a turn" [turn the money over], and that is after all the main thing with us in the textile trade...
If only the turnover doesn't go under, because [?] — as soon as, you see, the turning has stopped, everything stands still, not budging from the spot.
And the same thing, my friend, is felt now among us textile merchants. A hard, long winter is over, the Polish holidays [Easter] are already over, and all the hopes — like smoke...
I wish I could soon bring you better news, and above all, that the Jewish holiday eve brings the proper takings, so that the mood among us in Zagłębie really improves a little; meanwhile — not good...
Respectfully, your friend Józef.
Rasputin and His Jewish Beloved (19)

[Serialized historical novel — Tsarist Russia, Rasputin and the Tsar's household; installment 19.]
A historical novel by Boris Maksimov.

He is a loyal, devoted Orthodox Christian, and he — he is able to give the Tsar wise advice and counsel him on what must be done to root out thoroughly the revolutionary agitation among the people...
But most important of all is that Rasputin possesses a wondrous power to heal hopeless cripples, that he can work miracles, and he will surely make the "naslednik" [Russian: heir to the throne] well. Of that there is no doubt whatsoever. Vyrubova was sure of it. And she told: there had come to Petersburg a simple but dignified woman, a woman of the middle class and very pious. She came from Siberia, and she tells that in the region Grigori Yefimovich comes from he has long been famous and esteemed as a "holy" man and a great "miracle-worker" [Yid. "baal mofes"]. Day in, day out mothers came to him with their sick children; men and women who suffered from severe, incurable diseases — and he, the miracle-worker, cured them all and made them well... Blind people came to him led by others — and they went away on their own, seeing. Lame people came to him, brought on little carts, and they walked away from him striding on their own feet...
The woman who told all this is a widow. She herself had suffered from a terrible illness. Rasputin cured her, and in gratitude for his making her well she gave away her whole fortune, which was large, to charity, and came to the capital to tell of the wonders of the "holy" Grigori Yefimovich... whom she cannot praise enough... She says that there is no such "miracle-worker" anywhere in the world.
Vyrubova fell silent for a short while, looked at the Tsaritsa with shining eyes and [printed "in" for "and"] soon exclaimed in a joyful voice:
— And here is the most important thing I came to tell: yesterday, when the "holy" man came for the first time to the salon of Countess Ignatieva — the priest Vostorgov and I brought him there — I caught a suitable moment when I was left alone beside him for a while, and I told him how very ill the poor "naslednik" is... what terrible suffering he endures, and that the best doctors are unable to help him... how terribly crushed the Tsar and the Tsaritsa feel... He heard me out, stood silent, lost in thought, his head somewhat bowed. His face became very serious, his eyes began to shine with a strange [?] brightness and — Vyrubova was breathing in great ecstasy — then he answered me thus: "You tell the Tsaritsa she should weep no more, worry no more, I will make her child well and strong! The naslednik is a soldier, and he will have healthy red cheeks!"
— He said that? — the Tsaritsa asked again, and her eyes lit up with hope and inner joy.
— That is what he said, in those very words! — Vyrubova exclaimed, and her eyes glowed.
For the first time in four days a smile appeared on the Tsaritsa's lips. Now the Tsaritsa was completely under the influence of Vyrubova's talk and enthusiasm. Being deeply superstitious, she now began to believe with all her heart that God had at last taken pity, that God Himself had sent the "holy" muzhik [?] to protect the Tsar, herself and the little heir to the throne from the attacks of the revolutionaries: that he should save Russia and the holy Church from their hands and make well her only and beloved son Alexei. This belief lightened her heart. Colour appeared on her pale, wasted cheeks! Her eyes shone again. And when Vyrubova repeated the words the "holy" man had said, imitating the way Rasputin had said them, repeating his words with a peasant accent, the Tsaritsa could not help smiling. Rasputin's simple talk about "making well" and about "red cheeks" sounded so simple and so earnest that the Tsaritsa at once felt herself drawn to him... She felt a strong longing to see him. And she resolved at once to talk the Tsar into bringing Rasputin to court.
Vyrubova, seeing that she had succeeded in cheering the Tsaritsa and interesting her in "Father" Grigori, became more enthusiastic still. She now felt that she would manage to carry out her plan, to bring Rasputin into the court and promote [?] him further, and in forceful words she began to describe Rasputin's appearance, and especially his eyes and the wondrous glow of those eyes. She spoke with ecstasy of how there is an extraordinary power in his gaze, which overwhelms and subdues. When one feels that gaze of his, one immediately forgets that one is talking to a simple muzhik, and one feels that one is in the presence of a "holy man"; there is something divine in the gaze of his eyes.
Meanwhile it had grown dark in the room. Only a faint glimmer fell through the window-panes. The sick "naslednik" lay quiet, exhausted by his pains. The darkness and the stillness worked on the Tsaritsa's mood... She was now wholly governed by her friend's enthusiasm. And Vyrubova exclaimed in a whisper:
— Do you remember, dear Alix, how the holy Yohan [John] once prophesied to you that God would send you a friend who would help you and protect you from all evil? Do you remember? Believe me, dear, this is he! This is "Father" Grigori, whom God has sent you... He will protect you and guard you from every evil. He will save Russia and he will make your son well... I am sure of it. This is he, the "friend" of whom the "holy" Yohan foretold to you!
The Tsaritsa now believed every word. She wanted to believe... She sat lost in thought, gazed with wide-open eyes into the darkness of the room, felt hope growing in her heart — and then a strange thing happened to her: it seemed to her that she saw him, the new "friend"... There she sees him go up to the sick boy's bed, stand there with a radiant, pious face and raise his hands over the sick "naslednik" to bless him... From this vision a quiet joy rose in her...
Now Vyrubova no longer spoke in a soft whisper. She exclaimed clearly and loudly:
— I am convinced with all my heart that he will make your son well!
The Tsaritsa too began to speak in a louder voice:
— Oh, how good you are to me, dear Anna! You are, after all, the only one who is good to me... I thank you, Anna, for your friendship and for the wonderful [?] tidings you have brought me!
And she pressed Vyrubova's hand with warmth, gratitude and love:
— How grateful I am to you!
Vyrubova smiled. Her heart sang within her of victory, and she answered:
— Your words, dear, make me happy...
The "naslednik's" governess came in and put on the light in the room. Soon the Tsar came in too, and both of them — the governess and the Tsar alike — were enormously surprised to see the change that had come over the Tsaritsa. She had now completely recovered herself. She now looked in good spirits, was almost cheerful. To the Tsar she said:
— Dear Anna has cheered me up...
Vyrubova rose to greet the Tsar. The Tsar was deeply moved. He kissed Anna's hand and thought meanwhile: "She is our true friend... She is a precious soul and devoted to us with all her heart... And there are people who intrigue against her and try to make bad blood between us"... He looked into her face and gave a slight smile.
The Tsaritsa then said that today she would go down to dine together with the Tsar — something she had not done for the last three days. And she invited Vyrubova to dine with them. Vyrubova accepted the invitation with joy.
When they sat down at table, the Tsaritsa at once began to talk, telling the Tsar about the Siberian "divine" man Grigori Efimovich [spelled here without the initial yod], who had appeared in the capital, had amazed everyone with his simplicity and "holiness", and who assures that he will make the sick naslednik well... The Tsaritsa now spoke with ecstasy and with faith in the wondrous Siberian "holy man"... The Tsar, who was no less superstitious than the Tsaritsa, immediately took an interest in it.
The Tsaritsa allowed Vyrubova to repeat [?] to the Tsar everything she had told her about the extraordinary wonder. Vyrubova did so. Again she spoke with enthusiasm. Her face shone as she did, her eyes glowed. She is sure that the "holy man" will make the "naslednik" well... God has sent him at the right time... And the Tsar too was swayed by her; he too began to believe that the "divine" man who had wandered here from distant Siberia and appeared in the capital just when the "naslednik" lies so ill and needs help, is a messenger from God... The Tsar was a colossal egoist who regarded himself and his family as God's chosen, and so it was not hard for him to believe that God had sent His messenger to help the sick naslednik...
The Tsaritsa then exclaimed:
— Let him be brought here! Let the "divine" man be brought here and let him make our child well!
The Tsar answered briefly:
— Good... let him be brought here.
And the Tsar too felt that his heart had grown lighter. His mood became hopeful. Vyrubova at once jumped up from her seat:
— I will bring him here! He will be here this very evening!
— This very evening? — the Tsaritsa asked again.
— This very evening — Vyrubova exclaimed joyfully — why should Alexei suffer even one hour more than he must! I will drive off at once, bring him here, and I am more than sure that Alexei will stop suffering at once...
— Where will you find him now? — the Tsaritsa asked, feeling [?] that she was already waiting for him with great impatience.
— He is staying at the priest Vostorgov's house... It is now past seven o'clock... If I go at once, I believe we will be here by about nine o'clock...
— Good, dear Anna! — the Tsaritsa exclaimed — go at once and bring him!

If I Had 500 Pounds

[Feuilleton — the dream of emigrating to the Land of Israel.] By M. Kestenberg.

So I'm sitting there the other day, thinking. If I had, say, some 500 pounds... oh, how good I'd have it! Oh, what a life I'd make of it!...

"Well, guess," I say to my Chanele, "guess what I've got on my mind now — go on, try and guess..."

"You're thinking now," says my Chanele, "surely about some good match for our Pesele! It just won't get started [?]!"

"Then you're surely thinking about some new little business you mean to set up."
"Not that either!"
"Then you must surely be thinking about your brother in America."
"Heaven forbid!"
"Then you're certainly thinking about the rent money you have to bring [?] the landlord," says my Chanele, already worked up.
"Yesterday's day [idiom: nonsense]!" I answer.
"So what can you be thinking about?"
"Go on, guess!"
"I can't guess, I'm no fortune-teller!"
"I'm thinking now about what I would do if I had, say, some 500 pounds..."

"What do you mean, what would you do?" my Chanele cuts in. "First of all you'd look for a respectable match for our daughter and put down the fine [?] dowry; then you'd hand the landlord a few gulden so he'd stop grumbling [?]... Then you'd enrol Shmulik [?] and Meirl [?] in cheder; after that you could [?] see to [?] the needs of the house.. We simply have nothing left to sit on. One chair would need a leg mended and the other a board nailed on. And do you think perhaps the table wouldn't need replacing with a new one? Never mind. It has already served its time... And do you think perhaps the little ones wouldn't need new shoes? They're already going practically barefoot... Oh, we'd know what to do with such a sum of money!" — my Chanele ends with a sigh.

"No," I reply, "you haven't guessed it, Chanele, my crown. Not the first, not the second and not the third.. That's not what I was thinking of and that's not what I had in mind... It's not Pesele's match on my mind now, nor the landlord with the rent money..

Look, my dear little wife, if I had 500 pounds now, I wouldn't think long, wouldn't ponder long — I'd grab [?] sack [?] and pack and..."
"To Palestine [Polish: Do Palestyny], [—?]!"
"Well, Chanele, a bad plan?"
"Would that we both live to see such a year!" answers Chanele, and her little eyes sparkle with joy.

"If I had, you understand me, such a sum of money, we'd all move over there, I and you and Pesele. Oh, what a match she would make there! May we have such a livelihood — what a husband she would get! You know, Chanele, she shines like the sun, she looks like a princess... We really would all go over, all together pack up our bundles and move to the Land of Israel, buy ourselves a plot of land... put up a little house... for the time being of two small rooms. Plant a little garden with date palms, with fig trees, with oranges, and we would plant and sow [?] all day long, and every evening after work sit down to rest under the trees, and we would eat the fruit that our own hands had planted, and no one would point a finger at us... and no one would regard us as useless people... as unfree citizens, and no one would make up all sorts of libels against us...

Well, tell me, Chanele, is there any greater happiness in the world?"

And my Chanele, who had sat the whole time swallowing my words, wiped away the tears that had run down her face.

It seemed to her that she was in the Land of Israel, getting up at dawn, running out to the field, helping me sow and plant; the children are all still asleep, only Pesele, her treasure, her joy, is already up and has run out to the field to help Father and Mother; and she, Chanele, runs back home again to wake the little gang, make breakfast, send this one to school and that one to cheder...

From sheer happiness my Chanele bursts into tears [?] aloud, and tears come to my eyes too...
"Oh, where does one get 500 pounds?..."
A Concrete Plan for Middle-Class Colonization in Eretz Israel.

The problem of settling the middle class in Eretz Israel has lately been much studied by a special commission of the Executive of the Jewish Agency in Jerusalem. It came to the conclusion that the most suitable and most successful system of colonization is the orange plantations — pardesim (orange groves).
The Jaffa orange already holds today, thanks to its beauty and its richness in vitamins, the most honoured[?] place in this branch of production in the whole world, and can almost be regarded as a monopoly product. The high prices paid for it bring a net income of 15–20%. And that is why so much capital has been "invested" in orange plantations in recent years.
Planting orange groves, however, involves great responsibility and demands a great deal of experience and expert knowledge; mistakes in choosing and preparing the soil, with the young saplings and their care, can increase the costs and have a bad effect on the development of the grove.
Coming to the aid of the middle class who want to plant without any risk is the agricultural cooperative "Yakhin", which was founded in 1926, possesses 6000 pounds of its own capital, and has already planted to date close to 3000 dunams of orange groves, achieving very good results in the opinion of the great experts in Eretz Israel. "Yakhin" takes upon itself, on its own account and responsibility, all the work of planting a grove, starting from the purchase of the land, planting and irrigation, up to the management of groves that already bear fruit. The owner of a grove can thus, even while remaining abroad, prepare for himself through "Yakhin" a basis for a livelihood. This is especially important for those whose modest financial means do not allow them to wind up their businesses in the Diaspora completely until they have the possibility of a livelihood in Eretz Israel.
Recently the National Fund [Keren Kayemet] placed at the disposal of "Yakhin" some 500 dunams of land in Wadi Hawarith [Hefer Valley], with the aim of founding on it a colony for the middle class. Each person receives on lease from the National Fund 20 dunams net under a lease contract, and pays for the first 5 years 1 pound, and from the 6th year 2–2½ pounds yearly, as rent.
Anyone can obtain a plot in the colony if he is able to plant 10 dunams of orange grove, for which he must pay "Yakhin" for the planting under a special contract: in the 1st year — 245 pounds, in the 2nd — 160[?] £, in the 3rd — 95 £, in the 4th — 90 £, in the 5th 90 £; in total — 620 pounds, i.e. 62 pounds per dunam of grove, the wells already included.
When the owner comes to settle on his land, he will need, to set up the farm on the other 10 dunams (a house, stables, a cow, poultry, tools, etc.), about 350 pounds.
When the owner himself works his grove from the beginning of the sixth year, he will have to spend only on the work of animals and machines, organic and chemical fertilizers; then the account of his expenditure and income will be as follows:
In the 6th year, income: 500 cases of oranges at 5 shillings on the tree — 125 pounds; expenditure — 55 pounds; net income remaining 70 pounds.
In the 7th year, income: 650 cases of oranges — 162 £; expenditure 58 £; net income 104 £.
In the 8th year, income: 800 cases of oranges — 200 £; expenditure 62 £; net income 138 £.

The Problem of Physical Education (Freedom of Movement)

[Education — physical education; article.] By K. Jubel.

Movement is not an end in itself, but a means. No human being can do without it, just as he cannot do without eating or drinking. A person who is forced not to move is sick; he is dominated by a feeling of agitation and nervous irritability, from which he can free himself again only with the help of movement. Every limb whose freedom of movement is tied up withers away. Professional beggars often take a child to help them earn their living, and in order to arouse more pity they tie up a little hand, a little foot of the child — the child then grows up a cripple.
Movement is a physiological need of all living beings, but the strongest need in this direction is shown by young creatures. A child free of wrongly understood supervision, not disturbed and not fettered by imposed rules of "decent behaviour", runs, jumps, moves constantly. To curb the instinct of movement in children means to commit a cardinal error, means to hold back its normal development, to squeeze and crush the child's life-juices and strengths, whose natural urge is to grow and to ripen.
Not long ago a school headmaster boasted that in his school there reign quiet and stillness, as in a church. The children are forbidden to run and to shout in the schoolyard during breaks. During lessons they must sit with their hands folded on their chest or behind their back. With this "pedagogue" one cannot by any means agree; this is a false, a harmful method of upbringing, because this compulsion to sit without moving kills in the child the innate inclination to move, which is so necessary for maintaining the balance in the organism. All natural inclinations, if they are suppressed for a long time, die away. But it still remains to be known by which "modern pedagogical" means the above-mentioned "exemplary" quiet and order is achieved, for in healthy children such a lively inner urge as their urge to stir, to move, cannot so easily be suppressed and exterminated. In a whole series of so-called "powszechne" [state primary] schools the medieval corporal punishment still flourishes: children are still beaten and flogged, they are put "in the corner", made to kneel, and the dignity of the child is insulted and humiliated — but about all this in another article.
In combating certain inclinations in children one must distinguish between good and bad ones and not confuse the categories, not kill off such a good inclination as the natural urge to move. The lack of movement torments the child in the first period; the child suffers, endures terrible torments. With time, however, it gets used to it. But precisely in this lies the evil, because it has a fatal effect on the child's health.
In what, actually, does the blessed effect of movement express itself? The main thing is that it influences breathing, and breathing is the most important function of the organism. It has been calculated that a child who runs takes in six times more air than when it sits; this is an enormous gain, because air contains oxygen, which is after all the most important means of life. The oxygen penetrates into the blood, and physiologists know from experience that when one injects into a muscle that is temporarily tired, exhausted and unable to work a dose of blood duly saturated with oxygen, one immediately restores to it its former power and strength.
The main purpose of movement is therefore the development of the lungs. The larger the pulmonary alveoli, the more oxygen the organism absorbs. But the alveoli grow in relation to their activity, just as the muscles grow in relation to their work. In children who are forbidden to "romp", who must behave "decently", move "daintily, mannerly", so that everyone should see how "good" they are, the function of breathing is minimal, and consequently the lungs are all the less developed. If these children were at least permitted to speak and laugh loudly, for this too acts not only on the development of the throat muscles and of the vocal cords, but also on the lungs, and deepens breathing.
Objective conditions arising from our present-day struggle for life force us so often not to reckon with circumstances that are harmful and corrupting in the hygienic sense; one really need not, on top of that, produce special beds of Sodom for our youth. Freedom of movement — that is a sacred postulate which we formulate here in the name of our children.
With United Strength.

Y. L.[?]
(On the fund-raising campaign in Będzin.)

Someone once said: how dark Jewish life in exile would have been, were it not for the beautiful Jewish holidays. And indeed, in former times the Jewish holidays had a splendour and a joy that cheered and comforted the darkened Jewish exile-soul for long months. But the hard struggle for a bite of bread makes even the Jewish holiday ever more workaday, ever greyer, and Jewish life has become one long "weekday".

Only one more holiday has remained to the Jew, one that lifts him now and then above the vale of tears of bitter reality, that warms him with a ray of hope, of consolation. Eretz Israel is the only Jewish holiday in the present dark time. A greeting from the Jewish homeland, from the Jewish life sprouting there, an effort of help and support for the Jewish work of rebuilding in Eretz Israel, drives away for a while the mood of despair and makes one forget heavy cares. In the days when a Jewish community devotes itself to work for the settlement of Eretz Israel, one feels a kind of awakening, an uplift in the Jewish street; the extinguished eyes light up with a spark of hope, the languishing hearts beat stronger, the sleepy will grows taut, apathy and dejection give way to living energy, to joyful[?] deed.
•
Such Eretz Israel days we live through year after year at the opening of the Keren Hayesod campaign, when Jews are called upon to fulfil their duty to their people, to pay their tax for the great national work of building up the Jewish land as a home for Jews.

It seems there is nothing more frequent in Jewish life than collections of money; there is no other people in the world that must so often be roused and called upon to give, to sacrifice. What existence would the whole of Jewish life in exile have had at all, were it not for the voluntary sacrifices Jews bring to maintain their institutions? The state in which we live, and which we support with our taxes, gives us almost nothing for our needs, and we must drag on our own shoulders the whole burden of our cultural and social life, yes, even of our philanthropy and social welfare. And yet — and yet the collections for Eretz Israel are always an event; everywhere they are proclaimed. The ordinary Jew feels that this is a collection of an altogether different kind, that the collection of money is only the outward form of a higher collection, a gathering of the people's strength, a union of Jewish souls for an eternal goal. The Jew feels that with every grosz of his he brings something of himself, of his innermost essence, into an everlasting edifice that is to give the Jewish people a revival for eternal generations.
•
This year the Keren Hayesod campaign is being conducted among us at an especially hard time. All around reign want[?], poverty, despair. The Jewish masses struggle with their last strength for their existence. Economic positions which for centuries were held by Jews are tottering and slipping out of our hands. The clouds of antisemitism grow ever thicker. And some faint-hearted people ask: how can one come to the Jew today and ask for money for the building of Eretz Israel?!

How short-sighted they are, these questioners and discouragers, how alien to life they are, these supposedly practical people! When a fire breaks out, the most elementary commandment is to put out the fire, and the greater the danger, the more energetic the rescue operation must be. To despair and say: "Let it be as it will be" — only fatalists and degenerates can do that. People with a healthy instinct of self-preservation throw themselves into the struggle with the utmost tension of will, with all their strength, and save themselves. — If there is still a hope for Jews, and its name is Eretz Israel, then the strength of the whole people must be roused to action, steered in the one direction, in order to make of this hope a reality, an actuality.
•
And for the ten-thousandth time it must be repeated: Eretz Israel is being built not only for the Jews who live there, but for the whole Jewish people. Every Jewish family that takes root in Eretz Israel creates a workplace for at least one more Jewish family. Every dunam of land that is planted or sown, every workshop that is set up, creates conditions for new olim; for new immigrants. In this way the land is won by labour, little by little, for the whole Jewish people. The present Yishuv in Eretz Israel is merely our vanguard, the army standing in the first front line; the struggle of these front-line fighters is our struggle, their victory is our victory. May we abandon them to their own fate at so hard a time? If a Jew has not yet lost the last bond with the Jewish people, then there must constantly [printed "msdr", apparently for "kesseyder"] ring in his ears the old admonishing call of the first leader of the Jewish people:
— "Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here?!"
•
Not to despair at all, not to become dependent at all. We are climbing a steep[?], smooth mountain. There is no way back. If we do not want to tumble down into the abyss, we must go higher and higher, however tired we may be, however exhausted and languishing.

With united strength, with strained will — we shall reach the summit!

Będzin

The Council of Commissioners adopted the new budget.
On Monday the Council of Commissioners [Rada Komisaryczna, the appointed town council] held a session at which the budget for the year 1932/33 was adopted in third reading.
The budget contained an item for a new tax in the amount of 35 thousand złoty, which was to cover the costs of the water-supply installations.
Before the agenda, the majority of the council, especially the councillors Rechnic and Hampel, spoke out categorically against the new tax.
After the exposé of Commissioner Mr. Ruszczkowski[?] on the present crisis, [which] has burdened the activity of the Magistrate [town administration], the proposal for the new tax was put to a vote, and by a majority of votes the proposal was rejected.
After that, following a discussion, the ordinary budget, which amounts to 1.908,000 złoty, was adopted.
Then a conscription commission (komisja poborowa) was elected, consisting of Messrs. Szwajcer and Lubicz[?].
At the session the Commissioner announced that the loan which the Lwów company had wanted to grant for building the so-called "collector" [main sewer] is being withdrawn.

On unifying the price of electricity
A commission of representatives of the Ministry of the Interior and of the Ministry of Public Works is soon to come to Zagłębie. The commission is coming here with the purpose of fixing a uniform tariff for electricity and water in the towns of Zagłębie.

Resolved, as a protest, not to buy any fish.
From a larger number of local Jewish residents we have received a protest resolution against the raised[?] price of fish.
The resolution says that at the present time, when almost all products are becoming cheaper from day to day, the fish merchants have the audacity to raise the price of fish.
If the price of fish is not reduced, the Jewish population is called upon to refrain from buying fish.

How [—] the Magistrate [—] the [—] to the [—] / [cares?] for the [cleanliness?] of the schoolchildren[?] [faded headline]
In the municipal budgets up to now a certain sum was each time provisionally set aside as payment for the school youth who bathe in the municipal bath-house.
In this year's "economy budget" the item was struck out entirely, because the Magistrate's management and also the members of the Council of Commissioners recognised that the school youth can bathe in the bathtubs of the Institution for Health Affairs [the sick fund?]. There, where the most dangerous patients bathe...
As we learn, the headmistresses (kierowniczki) of the schools are against the schoolchildren bathing in such a place, where the nest of infectious diseases is.

This year's conscription is to begin in June.
In response to the many inquiries of our readers about the date of this year's conscription (pobór), we turned to the head (kierownik) of the conscription department of the local Magistrate, where we were informed that the Magistrate has not yet received any official order about it. But it is almost certain that the conscription will begin only on the 2nd of June (czerwiec).

Gentiles employed in baking matzos while poor Jews drag themselves from house to house.
In the last issue of our paper we touched on the question that only Jewish workers should be employed in matzo baking.
As some bakers inform us, only a very small number of Jews report for the work, and the bakers must employ non-Jews.
— It is no wonder; after all, we do not lack institutions that provide the beggars with everything, so why should they work...

House-owners are ready to give their houses away on lease.
The crisis has also made itself felt sharply in the rent. Simply put, the public does not pay any rent. How far this has already gone is shown by the following fact: several members of the House- and Plot-Owners' Association have approached the Magistrate with the proposal that the Magistrate should take over their houses from them on lease.

2 years' prison for passing counterfeit money.
Marcin Walczak and Jan Fink, well-known troublemakers (awanturnicy), were engaged in passing counterfeit 5-złoty coins. Their activity was exposed when one of them paid several times with counterfeit 5-złoty pieces for vodka[?] in Bonhart's[?] shop.
This week both were sentenced to 2 years' prison.

Tragic death of a drunken cyclist.
The 21-year-old Sikora, a resident of Upper Silesia, while in Będzin did not stint himself on drink. Riding home in a drunken state, Sikora rode into a cart and was seriously injured.
On the way to the hospital Sikora died.

Saved from death.
On Tuesday afternoon a drunken Christian tried to jump onto the tram while it was moving at full speed on Sutne[?] Street. The drunkard fell from the tram steps and by a miracle was saved from certain death.

Conference at the Small Traders' Association.
Last Sunday a conference took place at the premises of the Small Traders' Association in Będzin, in which representatives of all branches took part, numbering 150 persons.
Vice-president Mr. Józef Ros[?] opened the conference. In his opening speech he described the difficult situation of the small traders and proved with facts that only a firm and numerous organisation is able to relieve the distress by fighting for tax reliefs and long-term government credits for the broad masses of small traders.
The floor was given to the secretary of the association, Mr. P. Kener[?], who lectured on the law on turnover tax in general and on the lump-sum tax (ryczałt) in particular.
The vice-president Mr. D. Gutensztajn lectured on the question of credits for small traders and reported that the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce has begun an action in this field.
At the end a resolution was adopted, which states that the introduction of the lump-sum (ryczałt) tax means a great relief for small merchants and traders. This shows that the government has finally understood that the present tax system must be reformed. At this point, however, it must be stated that the turnover tax is in general not a just one, and therefore the representatives of the small traders are called upon to continue fighting until the complete abolition of the turnover tax.
The resolution also expresses thanks to the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, the Central Union of Small Traders in Poland, the board of the local Small Traders' Association and Mr. D. Gutensztajn for their work for the benefit of the small traders.

A soldier attacks the police with a bayonet.
Three Silesians (Ślązacy), who had fallen victim to card-sharps, reported to the police station in Czeladź.
When the police patrol sent out wanted to arrest the soldier Gorecki[?], who was one of the card players, the soldier threw himself at the police with a bayonet. Because of this the gendarmerie was called out from Będzin, and they arrested the soldier.

A maid who stole.
The servant Gertruda Fisz[?] stole various household items from the Kurland family on Mandżewer[?] [Modrzejowska?] Street and disappeared.

The Society for Knowledge of the Country [Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze]
is organising the following excursions: this Saturday a visit to the cable and wire factory in Będzin.
Sunday the 10th of this month — an excursion to Kraków. On the programme: a visit to the exhibition of M. Gotlib [Maurycy Gottlieb?], the Press Palace (Pałac Prasy), the Folk Museum and the theatre. Departure from Będzin at 9.10 in the morning.
This Saturday at half past five a general meeting will take place at the premises of the "Merchants' Association", at which delegates will be elected to the convention taking place in Warsaw.

Theft at the railway station.
At the local railway station the box of the automatic telephone, which contained 60 złoty from the telephone calls, was stolen in the middle of the night.

"Dobroczynność" is already giving matzos to the poor.
From Tuesday on, free matzos are being distributed by the "Dobroczynność" [charity society] to poor families.
The matzo portions are the same as in all years.

The turnover assessors have already finished the "work"...
On Tuesday the assessment commission for turnover tax finished its work. As is reported, the assessment is higher than in previous years...

10 Percent of the Artisans Have Been Assigned to the Ryczałt
The last deadline for appeals is the first of May
These days the tax offices have already sent out the payment orders (nakazy) for turnover tax according to the ryczałt (lump-sum) assessment for the years 1932 and 1933. Very often, however, it happens that the calculation is not accurate, because the reduction made by the appeals commission for the past years has not been taken into account. An even greater injustice has been committed in that 90 percent of the artisans who hold artisan cards are not on the list for the ryczałt tax.
In connection with this, an urgent meeting of the board of the Artisans' Association was held on Tuesday evening, and a resolution was adopted that a delegation should intervene at the local tax office concerning the injustices that have been committed towards the artisans.
The delegation, which intervened on Wednesday morning, obtained that the association should submit a list of the artisans who were not assessed according to the ryczałt law (ustawa) of 26 February (luty) of this year.
The Artisans' Association therefore calls on all artisans to apply in the course of the next few days to the association's secretariat with the payment orders they have received, in order to lodge the appropriate appeals by 1 May. After that deadline the appeals will not be taken into account.

Credit for Building Purposes
The commissioner Mr. Kuszniak [?] has intervened at the Ministry of Finance and with the management of the Agricultural Bank about obtaining credit for building purposes. As we learn, Sosnowiec will receive credit for building wooden houses of 4 rooms.
In the coming days the local magistrat (municipality) will draw up a list of those who wish to receive the credit. The list will be submitted to the Ministry of Finance in order to determine the amount of the credit.

Zagłębie Will Have Passover Matzot from the Land of Israel This Year
After a break of 2 years, Zagłębie will again have matzot from the Land of Israel this year. As we are informed, this year's matzot are of very high quality, because Baron Rothschild's large matzah bakery in Haifa has recently been completely reorganised. The matzot are baked with the newest machines, and thanks to this the matzot are distinguished by a very fine taste.
The news that matzot from the Land of Israel can be had in Zagłębie this year will undoubtedly cause great satisfaction.
Declarations (zeznania) of income for the year 1931

[Economy — taxes.] In the course of the present month every merchant who has traded and every craftsman who has run a workshop must submit a declaration (zeznanie) of income for 1931.

This year every merchant must take special care in writing the declaration. It must be written so clearly and in such detail that the declaration gives an exact calculation of his income; this will give him the surest and best chances of defending himself.

If a merchant fills in a declaration just like that, without a calculation — writing, for instance, that on a turnover of 70 thousand zł. he had 6 per cent profit and 4,200 income — then contesting the declaration is one of the easiest things.

It is different, however, when a merchant states in the declaration a calculation of how his yearly income came about. With such a calculation the office (urząd) must give him the reasons why it is being contested.

Therefore every merchant should make an exact calculation of his income. A dry-goods (textile) merchant, for example, can divide the income into 3 groups: the income from white goods, the income from "beytel" [?] goods, and separately from "siter" [?, perhaps printed cotton/chintz].

A leather merchant can likewise state the income from hard leather, separately from soft leather and separately from offcuts [?].

In the same way one can calculate in various ways, in several groups, the income from iron, from haberdashery, and the like.

———

Exempt from submitting declarations are merchants of the fourth and fifth category in all towns, as well as merchants of the third category who live in towns of the third and fourth class. Craftsmen of the 8th category are also exempt.

We advise, however, the merchants and shopkeepers who are exempt from submitting a declaration nevertheless to submit one, because it gives them better chances of defending themselves if they are assessed too high.

———

In answer to the inquiry of many merchants as to how one can convince the office to believe that there was a loss in this year, we give the following explanation.

For merchants who keep commercial books this is no great worry: one must believe them as to what the books show.

It is different with merchants who keep no commercial books. They must endeavour to demonstrate their loss in such a way that the offices will have to take it into account.

One must illustrate and substantiate the explanations and declarations with facts and documents. One must give an exact calculation, so clearly that one can see at first glance that there was a loss.

Since the merchants' main loss in 1931 came from the fall in prices, it is best to give examples of how much the goods cost when bought and how much when sold.

First of all one must state that the value of the stock fell. For example, on 1 January (styczeń) 1931 the stock amounted to 26,000 zł., and on 31 December (grudzień) 1931 it amounted, for example, to 21,000 zł.

Further one must show that goods were bought at such a price and fell in price so much that they were sold so-and-so much cheaper. One must also state the names of the articles, the purchase prices and the selling prices. To make the calculation even surer and clearer, it is good to explain with dates: for example, in January 1931 an article was bought for 3 zł. a metre, and in February (luty) this same article stood at 2.50, and the goods bought were sold below cost price.

It is good to attach to such explanations for the office invoices of the goods bought, which should prove that prices fell and that one never managed to sell the goods at the purchase prices.

Anti-Jewish excesses at Warsaw University

[Warsaw — antisemitism.] Anti-Jewish excesses at Warsaw University.
(By telephone from our Warsaw correspondent).
Yesterday the anti-Jewish agitation repeated itself: the incited Endek [National Democrat] hooligan gang threw itself with sticks upon the Jewish youth, sparing not even women.
The events began in this way:
At 1 o'clock midday there arrived at the Museum building at Krakowskie Przedmieście 66, where the first lectures were taking place, a delegation of Endek students from Wilno, which had been specially prepared in Wilno in connection with the first anniversary of the death of the student Wacławski, who fell victim in last year's events in Wilno.
After the lectures a meeting took place with the participation of the Wilno and Warsaw students.
At this meeting the speakers demanded that revenge be taken on the Jews. From words the hooligans passed to deeds: at once a wild hunt began after the Jewish students, sparing not even women, at whom they began throwing stools, sticks and the like.
At first the Jewish students tried to put up resistance, but seeing that they were in the minority, they wanted to withdraw; the Endeks, however, surrounded them on all sides and beat them murderously.
So that the Jews could not turn for help, the hooligans guarded the telephones in the Museum hall.
Later the excesses took on a wild character. Two Jewish women students who had called for help were thrown down the stairs from the first floor. One of them, 19-year-old Irena Buszycka[?], was wounded and a doctor had to be called for her.
With great difficulty the Jewish students managed to get out into the street, thanks to their having been able to alert the Rector, who came at once into the Museum and put an end to the events.
Police came and dispersed the assembled students.
The Pogotowie [emergency ambulance service] gave medical aid to the wounded Jewish students.
In the evening Jewish students, some 2000 strong, held a meeting, at which it was also resolved that a delegation should apply to the Minister of Education.

The Zawiercie Public Runs After "Evil Wonders"...

[Zawiercie — Society.] Zawiercie is boiling as in a kettle over the great "sensation" discovered last week by the carpenter Mr. Wolf Kinres. This carpenter made a table out of wood alone — not a single nail is to be found in this mysterious table, which "answers" various questions.
The "spiritualist séances" are held every evening in the presence of hundreds of people, men, women and children... Seven people sit down around the table and hold their hands on the table's edges for about 35 minutes; then the table rises and, by signs of knocking, the table "answers" all the questions put to it.
It goes without saying that there is no shortage of questions, but the main question that interests everyone at the present time is:
— How long will the crisis last?
The table rose and knocked 2 times, i.e. "the crisis will last another 2 years"...
To the question: when will the Messiah come? the table "declared": "in about 47 years".
As our correspondent writes, the table is a remedy for today's day-to-day troubles: people have nothing to do, so they spend at least a couple of hours at the "spiritualist séances" of Wolf Kinres's table...

On Guard Before a Catastrophe. XIV. (The Old Stock and the Student Youth. — Our Backwardness and Its Causes)

[Opinion / economy — crafts and trade.] L. Szpigelman.
It is no longer news to anyone, since we have said more than once and shown several times, that we are losing position after position, that our economic situation is already so deeply depressed, has fallen so unbearably, that in the prevailing situation we have no way out and we do not know how to save ourselves, how to remain standing on our feet.
We therefore must not remain indifferent to this chaos and look on as the branches of our economic tree-trunk — a field in which we were once of the noble lineage (yikhes) — break off systematically, and the ancient tree begins to stand bare and its roots begin to dry out, so that the tree stops yielding its fruit.
At such a moment one must surely take stock: where we stand and where the wind is tossing us. The older generation is no longer fitted to today's conditions; it cannot chase after the current, which spreads out broadly over a large area with tremendous speed and swallows up everything around it, so that one begins to lose one's way and sees no way out.
A large part of the Jewish population consciously realised this, and that was the reason why whoever had the means gave his children a secondary-school education, and with the matura people began to head for the temple of learning; they wanted to attain higher education, but the gates of the universities remained almost firmly shut to us Jews, and with that we are left without a way out: the older generation has begun to lose the ground from under its feet, and the coming generation, the youth already grown up, has no prospects at all, and the future looks to it very, very pessimistic, very, very sorrowful and clouded.
Well, as long as the years were still normal and business was still normal, the young gave up their studies and took up, some office work and some other white-collar professions. Now, when the times have become highly complicated, extraordinarily abnormal, there is nothing to be achieved in that field either; the youth wander about idle, and the element that until now was somewhat better situated has already forgotten how one can, under the prevailing conditions, earn both a livelihood and the most necessary needs that must figure in today's budget. The situation is thus without a way out, and one must not leave it hanging in the air; it must be resolved somehow, and one must adopt all possible and impossible means in order to examine this most dangerous situation in its full size and breadth, in its full light and nakedness. We must conceal nothing from the sad reality, however terrible and cruel it may be.
First of all it must be said that we underrate what we possess in the things we are occupied with. We know, for instance, that the Jewish craftsman finds it hard to make a living in the present bitter times; he goes about without a stitch of work, and when he does manage to obtain, after great interventions and string-pulling, employment — it happens that he cannot come out even with his capital; he has to put extra money into his undertaking and stays stuck in the middle.
Why is this so? Because he cannot calculate, he has not gone through any school, he is not qualified, and for that reason he cannot work out his accounts.
And something else: we quite often hear people complain that one should not deal with any craftsman; for thus — people say — it is well known that the artisan goes about without work and is simply happy when he gets something to do, yet as soon as he takes on a piece of work there is no getting along with him. One hour he works, and for two days he leaves the client stuck in the middle of the job. Of course this should not happen, but it is a rare thing for a craftsman to keep his word. Give him a piece of work, and though he has no work, he will drag you along for days and weeks and will never keep to the deadline. How often we hear people say that they never want to order [made-to-measure] what one can get ready-made in a shop, only because they are sick of begging for the goods or article to be finished at last, so that the customer already surely[?] gives up on the better finish and settles for a simpler[?] job, just so as not to have to waste time and effort in vain.
Our craftsmen do not progress in this field; they do not move with the times, they do not take conditions into account, they do not want to modernise their businesses, and because of this they suffer materially. People give them a piece of work only when there is no other way out.
If we think that things are better with us in another field, we are greatly mistaken. Trade in the shops and in small manufacturing, too, is inferior in the same way. They too cannot calculate and never know how to work out their accounts, and here too the fault, of course, is the school they did not go through. That school is missing for people at every step, and they suffer for it their whole life. That is why they overpay taxes, fall into debt, put money into the costing, and can never get out of it with whole bones. How many times do Jews pay taxes twice, and unjustified taxes, only because one time he does not have the receipts, and another time because he does not know what sort of tax he is paying.
At the same time the big industrialist or another large enterprise will not overpay a single grosz, because there the receipts are kept in proper order and an incorrect tax will never be paid, since they have specialists in this field, officials, who guard it like the apple of their eye. The poor craftsman (printed "bet melokhe" — a misprint for "bal melokhe"), on the other hand, or the small trader, overpays two- and threefold only because he has nobody to keep his tax assessments ("nakazy") and the receipts for sums he paid long ago; he pays a fine for it as well, so that he is reduced to poverty merely because of this disorder and lack of punctuality.
But what can these little people do so as not to overpay unnecessary sums two- and threefold? Can these people persuade themselves that they could hire people to keep all this for them as it is kept by big industrialists or in large commercial houses? Of course they cannot even dream of such fantasies, and therefore there is no way out here. Yes, it would have been quite a good way out if we were organised, if the organisation of every trade stood at the proper level — then it would be quite an easy matter.
But it turns out that socially we are still far from developed; people here are still far from understanding what communal responsibility, social accountability, is — which has been created all over the world in order to benefit the community, to help those who cannot help themselves.
How to remedy these dangers, both in the field of private commerce and in the sense of social life — in the next chapter.
Lawlessness and Fear (Sketches)

[Essay — Jewish public life in Poland.] Lately a heated debate has broken out in the Jewish press about our present political-social conditions and, especially, about the — — lawlessness! that has seized our entire life, about the takifes [the rule of the strong-arm bosses], in its various and most loathsome[?] forms, which floods the whole Jewish political-social life in Poland.
Something can be felt in this debate: that the tragedy of our situation has reached its — — culmination point! And that the conviction has ripened that one must at last say openly to the Jewish public that things cannot — — go on like this! That the coming tomorrow must be different from today, and that one must think over what is to be done.
And yet, even now, not everything is being said in this debate; even now the close connection between — — lawlessness and — fear! is still passed over in silence. In it lies our whole misfortune, the main source of our terrible helplessness, up to a boundless despair.
When we look closely at everything that goes on in and around us, we see that the entire Jewish political-social life is wrapped through and through with a — — spider's thread! which stretches from on high, runs through all our institutions and organisations, and by this barely visible but very strong — — thread! everything is bound together, everything entangled, and through it are firmly united the — — lawlessness! at the top of our political-social life and the — — fear! in the localities, in every town and shtetl.
The Jewish masses, the Jewish artisan, small trader and merchant, who on various occasions and in various circumstances happen to meet their various representatives — city councillors, kehilla parnassim, leaders of various organisations and all other kinds of — — „cooking spoons“ [busybodies who stir every pot]! — see and feel perfectly well what these — — representatives and providers! stand for with regard to the interests of the Jewish masses. They see and feel very well that in our present Jewish life, shattered to its foundations and poisoned as never before, a special — — caste! has taken root, of conscienceless careerists and swindlers who shamelessly build their personal — — prosperity! at the expense of the general Jewish — — misery and want! — closely bound to one another by one common slogan: — — „Guard me — and I'll guard you!“
We Jews, however, in our present inner brokenness and dejection, have moreover become, regrettably, isolated individuals[?]: each one thinks only of himself, and no one says a word out loud, because one is — — afraid!
And from this and because of[?] this there grows ever more, in all spheres of our political-social life, the — — lawlessness! This unbearable, oppressive and humiliating — — fear! takes hold, day by day, of ever broader strata of the Jewish population, and together with it the — — lawlessness! also grows ever greater in its scope and aspirations, thus creating a united front, over the whole of Jewish political-social life, of — — lawlessness and — fear!
And, fundamentally, — it is not at all impossible, and even not so very hard, to tear apart the — — spider's thread! that unites the — — lawlessness and — fear! that are so unbearable in our life. All that is needed is a little more courage, a little more understanding of the reality in which we find ourselves, and especially — of the slogan we so absolutely need: — — One for all and — all for one! And with common strength, at every step and stride, to stand up against the takifes, against careerism and machinations at the expense of Jewish — — troubles and — want!
And when we, stubbornly, sparing no one and nothing, bring into our — — extinguished and — trampled! political-social life small — — sparks! and a courageous struggle for our existence and human dignity, this will of itself become a great — — flame! that will burn up all the falseness and all the filth of our Jewish political-social life; and then life will change its heavy, dark forms of — — lawlessness and — fear!, under whose heavy yoke we are now so unbearably oppressed.
And when there is now so much talk about the necessity of mounting strong resistance to the — — lawlessness! at the top of our political-social life, there must at the same time also be proclaimed a merciless war against the takifes and the — — fear! in the localities, in every town and shtetl.
A. M. T. [„Emes“ — Truth]

World Antisemitism

[Essay / opinion — world antisemitism.]
By J. I. Segal [י. י. סיגאל]

The antisemites in all countries are now singing in one chorus. And among them there are all sorts of voices and little voices. And among them there are voices such as we had never heard anywhere before. We even wonder: do such ones really exist? Each time another one raises his lion's roar, or his still small voice, rises above the chorus and sings solo, shows what he can do. At times it becomes a real Katzenjammer of roaring and growling, nothing like that of any civilized — beasts. If the brilliant Wagner were alive now, he might perhaps have created a new work out of it. He might perhaps have caught signs of "revolution" and these black crow-croakings. God forbid that I should touch the honour of the genius, but falling into the ranks of the "song" of antisemitism, I remembered that he too, the great Wagner, had something against us; I grabbed hold of him like a drowning man at a straw, for one gets sick of dealing only with antisemitic nonentities like the present ones, who make a din up to the ceiling of the whole world-palace — so at least I grabbed hold of one decent person, of whom the antisemites themselves threw it up to us that he too is not alien to — Jewishness. At least [printed "patsh", read "khotsh"] we know that in him, in Wagner, there perhaps takes place a "and they struggled together" [Gen. 25:22], a Jacob-and-Esau fight, and when Wagner shouts and rails against Jews, we will assume that it is Esau inside him clenching [?] his fists, and when Wagner — plays, then it is "the voice is the voice of Jacob". That's how it must come out — how else? But, joking aside, antisemitism now sings in chorus. There are still a few countable countries that — keep silent. There is a supposition that they too are not silent. They murmur and hum under their breath everything the "chorus" says.

The only "luck" in this misfortune is merely that it is not the only hatred now raging in the world. The world is flooded with enmity and wickedness of one toward another. The measure of iniquities has been overfilled, of "sins" against the little bit of good and justice that has grown up on the black swamp of human malice and baseness. I do not know whether we ought to seek comfort for ourselves in this reason; it is a lamentable consolation, but it can somewhat still our burning sorrow, for it is hard to be alone in sorrow. It is a little easier when one sees broader, more distant causes and does not fall into too-deep self-accusation. Especially at such moments, when the beast has been let out of its cage and it races through streets and cities and overturns whatever comes in its way.

And we, in our great misfortune, are always in the beast's way; it will no longer let us pass, even if it has to make many detours in order to block our way — that is now its "manoeuvre".

And to this day we have not found any proper means of defending ourselves against it. After all we are speaking among ourselves, and the sad truth we may tell ourselves, even while holding our heads bowed in sorrow over our fate: we have, it seems, also lost a little of our certainty in political redemption. The last few years — such bitter disappointments in our protectors. But — something has become clearer to us: a certain feature on the face of world politics that has had a fatal effect on our national mood and consciousness. We have seen how we ourselves become a blind political instrument in the hand of a power that has only itself in mind and cares little about our existence. That is "something" more than disappointment and discouragement.

And now, in the antisemitic chorus, almost along the whole length of a world-line, with all the economic upheavals and the eve of upheaval, it follows the Judeophobic course; under every flag it grows. To the conservative [misprinted] camp it sends its black courier, and to the liberal, to the fascist and to the so-called socialist one, for a social-fascist is after all also a socialist. And a Jew — is treyf to it like a bourgeois. A Jewish person [misprint "mshnsh"] who works is not yet to be found in the world. All Jews are money-magnates. And if one does not see it on many of them, they hide their treasures. Where? About Jews one doesn't ask — who knows their hiding places, who can get to the bottom of their secrets. About Jews it is permitted to believe the worst and the most terrible. For the benighted masses there is an easy, elementary means: one incites them, one tells them tales of murders of Christian children, without whose blood Jews can by no means hold a seder or have a kosher Passover — that is for the mob. For the so-called intellectual a tale has already been invented about a kind of Sanhedrin, Elders of Zion, who sit and ponder plans for how to steal the world out of the hands of the goyim and run away — where to? — unless to the next world. Inquisitions there are indeed no longer today; we are, after all, a good few hundred years away from those — means; but other, sublimated ways have been found to burn the ground under one's feet. Hitler is the sheygets, the one who need not suffer any disgrace and really does not know what such a thing as shame is. Behind him, however, are silent those for whom Hitler is indeed their ugly plague, their disgrace, and their silence is perhaps fear. But we have already seen cases where the honest and humane knew no fear of the inhuman and came out openly and bravely against it and struck terror into the black gangs.

If even the better ones have already hidden themselves in a corner — perhaps we should not hold it too much against them; perhaps we should also put ourselves in their position, for they too are "guilty" in the eyes of the black forces. And in us too the instigator means not so much the Jew as the human being who bears the great sin of having thrown a spark of a higher moral feeling into the swarming vermin [?] of those crawling within themselves — destroying one another. We are often his bad conscience, and he might perhaps have loved us better if, along the roads of history, he had had before his eyes the grandiose picture of a whole crucified people instead of merely one single son of its own [printed: "zun irn"]. Antisemitism is still the most bloodthirsty in the forest of human settlement. It is only the savage that is still sometimes afraid to show itself in the ridiculousness of crawling on all fours, of climbing smooth walls, just to bark, growl and neigh at Jews, who hinder it a little from being an open beast; and — the poor thing, on top of all troubles, busies itself manicuring its nails with a little "scientific" file, when it sets about digging them into the body of a Jew, of the whole people.

We are now going through one of the antisemitic periods in history [...]
“Yo-Yo” (A Short Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — the yo-yo craze.]
In the street and in the garden, in the restaurant and in the pastry shop, in the theatre and in the cinema, in the kitchen and in the parlour — everywhere a game of “yo-yo” is going on; whole houses, whole streets, whole towns — everything is being seized and swallowed up by the “yo-yo”.
And although an editor must be a “kol-boynik”, a know-it-all, an expert on everything in the world, my readers will have to forgive me if I sincerely confess that I have no notion what the “yo-yo” game actually means.
