Free Lunches for Poor Pupils. Sunday — the First Lunch

[Będzin — welfare and schools.]
The women's committee at Public School No. 2 has set about active work.
Last week the committee carried out a "kilo" collection [a food collection by the kilogram], which was very successful. Thanks to this the school management has proceeded to hand out free lunches to poor pupils. The lunches will consist of a nourishing soup, meat and bread.
Next Sunday the first lunch will be handed out, and this will take place in festive fashion.
The lunches, although at the start they will be given out on a limited scale, will nevertheless to a certain extent relieve the great need of the poor children.
Steps are also being taken to increase the number of lunches, but for this the support of the Jewish public is needed.
It is therefore to be hoped that the Jewish public will continue, just as in the "kilo" collection, to give its attention to this sympathetic campaign, which is so urgent in the present severe crisis.

The Downfall of a Sosnowiec 'Don Juan'...

[Sosnowiec — town gossip.] If anyone thinks that Sosnowiec is a quiet town in the erotic sphere and that there are no 'Don Juans' among us, he is greatly mistaken — Sosnowiec is a town like any other and it has its own 'Don Juans' too.
About one such downfall of a Sosnowiec 'Don Juan' we are told the following:
The 'Don Juan' — let us call him 'Pan X' — happened to meet a young Christian lady, an office clerk, at a cinema, and struck up a conversation with her. Naturally, out of courtesy he walked his new acquaintance home.
When it came to saying goodbye, however, our young man did not want to go home. He tried to force his way into the young lady's room. The young lady at first tried to repel him with words, but when the 'hero' would not abandon the almost-conquered 'position', the young lady raised a real 'vayitsaku' (outcry) — people came running, and the 'Don Juan' left in great disgrace...

Shechita prices reduced in Będzin.

On Wednesday evening the Będzin kehilla council held a session, at which the proposal of the kehilla board to reduce the shechita (ritual slaughter) prices was discussed.
The board's proposal was: bulls 8 zł. (formerly 6,50), oxen, cows 6,50 (as before), small cattle [sheep/goats] 2,50 (formerly 3,80), turkeys 1 zł. (formerly 80 gr.), geese 60 gr. (formerly 80), hens, ducks 40 gr. (formerly 60), chicks [kurczak], pigeons 25 gr. (formerly 40).
The council changed the prices altogether. It was fixed: for bulls 7 zł., oxen, cows 5 zł., small cattle 1,50, turkey 1 zł.; hens, ducks and chicks according to the board's proposal.

An interesting trial behind closed doors.
On Tuesday an interesting trial behind closed doors took place at the Dąbrowa court. In the dock sat a certain shoemaker Diament, who was charged by his wife with abandoning her with a child and marrying a second time in Sosnowiec.
Seventeen witnesses were summoned to the trial, among them 13 Jews, who, after taking the oath before the rabbi, unravelled the whole story of the accused: that he had cast off his wife and child and married a Sosnowiec girl, and does not even want to bear the costs of his child.
At first the accused wanted to wash himself clean of everything, but when the judge took him under examination, he declared that „he had only married for the time being, merely a chuppah and kiddushin“...
The verdict: the accused must pay the wife 385 zł., and further he must pay 30 zł. a week for the wife and child.
As we are informed, the same man also tried his luck in Żarki...

To the attention of soda-water manufacturers in Zagłębie.
A communiqué sent to us.
At a meeting of the Upper Silesian Restaurateurs' Association the president declared to his members that he would build them a gas [carbonic acid] factory, but on condition that each of them undertakes to buy the product from him for ten years and, of course (this is the most important thing), also pays in several hundred zł. as a share.
The said[?] president justified his proposal by saying that of the gas factories existing in Poland only five are active, and they pay the remaining six factories a sum of 1 400,000 zł. a year for not working (!)
As all soda-water manufacturers know, all eleven gas factories in Poland are working nowadays, so there can be no talk of paying for not working. Secondly, since the entire turnover of gas in the whole country amounts to only two million zł. a year, it is groundless and ridiculous to claim that five working factories pay the others as much as 1,400,000 zł. for not working.
Besides, the government has already begun to revise the cartels' prices.

Peace Negotiations between Dąbrowa Kehilla Leaders at the Krymiłów Rebbe's in Zawiercie

[Dąbrowa — kehilla.]
As our readers know, during the election of the chairman of the Dąbrowa kehilla council a betrayal took place on the part of the allied Krymiłów Hasidim, and with their votes Mr. Hertsl Liberman was elected chairman.
As a consequence of that betrayal, the pensions of those officials who are Krymiłów Hasidim were reduced in the new kehilla budget.
The reductions had an echo at the Krymiłów Rebbe's in Zawiercie, who — as we are told — had a certain interest in seeing the opportunity exploited so that his Hasid Mr. Liberman would be elected chairman of the kehilla council in place of the outgoing chairman Mr. B. Fuks; and the Rebbe took steps so that his Hasidim should not come to grief over the chairman's seat, and so that peace should return among the camp of Israel in the holy community of Dąbrowa...
In this connection, last Sunday the presidium of the kehilla board was invited to a conference at the Rebbe's: the chairman Mr. A. Najfeld and the vice-chairman Mr. L. Rechnic, the council chairman Mr. Liberman, and, as “peace-pursuer,” the communal worker Mr. B. Rechnic.
The conference at the Rebbe's in Zawiercie lasted several hours (apart from the feast...)
With various arguments the interested party tried to influence the presidium of the kehilla board to stop “the war against the Krymiłówers” and let there be peace and tranquillity. The main motive was “not to hand power over to the Agudah,” which insults at every turn the rebbes who do not enjoy the Agudah's concessions. (Incidentally, the Rebbe was told of a “pathetic” remark made by an Agudah parnas during a kehilla meeting at the expense of the Krymiłów Rebbe, may he live long and well...)
As we have already mentioned, the conference of several hours has so far brought no positive result whatsoever, and the delegation left with the assurance that “we'll see that it turns out well”...
Be that as it may, the Krymiłów “betrayal” has brought kehilla life in Dąbrowa to the boil, and further results are awaited with great “suspense.”

On Exempting Empty Flats from Taxes

[Poland — taxation.]
In connection with the memorandum of the House-Owners' Association on the question of easing the tax burden, the Ministry of Finance has sent to all offices a circular concerning the tax on houses and on unoccupied flats.
In this circular the Ministry explains that under the tax regulations it makes no difference whether the house yields a profit or not; however, in exceptional cases, when the flats bring in no income at all — not through the fault of the landlord, but because the tenants are unable to pay rent — and the taxes could ruin the house-owner, the local tax office (urząd skarbowy) may exempt the house-owner from taxes on the whole house, or on those flats from which he has no income at all.

Murderer Kasiarek Sentenced to Death by the Kraków Military District Court

[Kraków — Crime.] In the military district court in Kraków, after a 3-day trial, the well-known murderer and deserter Kasiarek[?] was sentenced to death.
In October of last year ("p. y.") Kasiarek came to Mysłowice, where he stayed with the Wróbel family. After a while a love affair developed between him and Wróbel's wife, and so that the husband should not stand in their way, Kasiarek murdered him and threw the body into the Przemsza.
Kasiarek then went to Warsaw in order to obtain a different passport, so that he could return to his beloved in Mysłowice.
In Warsaw the plan did not succeed and he travelled back to Mysłowice. On the way, in the railway carriage, he murdered a certain Hałast[?], who was travelling from Częstochowa to Dąbrowa.
The Chevra Kadisha buried the victim in the Jewish cemetery, believing that he was a Jew. Later the mistake came to light and Hałast was removed from the Jewish cemetery.
This week the murderer Kasiarek stood before a military court, which sentenced him to death by hanging.

Where Will This Lead? (The Recklessness of Our Kehilla Leaderships. — The Decline and the "Fruitful Activity".)

[Zagłębie — Jewish communities; opinion piece.]
Often the thought comes to mind and asks us: do we have our own kehilla representations at all, do they do anything, are they interested at all in Jewish life and in its members? This thought occurs to us only when we read through a notice about the activity of our kehillas. Otherwise — had such a notice not slipped in among the general news — we would completely forget this "chief" [?] representation of ours. That is how they live and act within the Jewish community and in their Jewish world.

Yes, the community has altogether forgotten that these institutions were created for the Jewish population and shaped by it; and if one did not have to pay the budget levy (etat), and if one did not hear from time to time of its comic episodes, one would truly not know that it still occupies a place among us; one would forget its address and nobody would miss it, because it accomplishes nothing. It has already gone so far that nobody stops any more at its most ridiculous manifestations; one knows that nothing is realised there, nobody undertakes to do anything substantial, nobody carries anything out, and it is quite in order that what was regarded yesterday with sympathy and defended should tomorrow be left hanging in the air, or even fought against. Such absurdities, such cardinal errors or such indifference as one sees at the helm of the kehilla administrations one does not see even in the tiniest public institutions, which play no significant role in the wider society.

We see, for example, how in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] a president of the kehilla board is elected: the way one fools the other, the way they trip each other up — it makes you choke with laughter.

Well, Dąbrowa is a creature apart when it comes to fooling the other fellow and staging various contrivances that would never have occurred to any ordinary townsman. The Jews of Dąbrowa are specialists in arranging such spectacles.

But what joy do we get from the Sosnowiec kehilla leaders — how do they treat this representation, which was supposed to play such an important role in our Jewish life? What do these modern Jews do to make something of their kehilla representation? Is the institution not, for them, a kind of toy with which one can do no more than amuse oneself when there is time to put on a show? Is it not quite in order for them to defend [today?] what they fought yesterday? Do we ever see among them tact and restraint, perseverance and logic? Are their resolutions not annulled after they themselves [?] adopted them?

And Będzin, the heart of Jewish Zagłębie, the city that was crowned "a city and mother in Israel" — is the kehilla institution there set up any better than in the sister towns mentioned? Does it have more respect and reverence for its fellow citizens, for its members? Będzin always thought differently, felt differently, about the thing called Jewish communal work, Jewish public responsibility. Has not all this been desecrated in Będzin too, to the highest degree, to the point where it can be neither understood nor endured?

How far there is no sense of responsibility and no awareness at all is shown by the fact that last week the kehilla decided that first of all the members should be taxed according to the kehilla levy (etat), and only afterwards would they take up the budget. Have you ever heard of such a procedure, such a way of reckoning? We have always known that first of all one draws up the budget, bargains over it, takes off from one item and adds to another, until agreement is reached among themselves. Only then does one draw up the total, and once one saw the bottom line and learned where one stands in the world, one understood what large portions there were to divide. But it never occurred to anyone to cut portions from material that is in fact neither prepared nor worked out.

Such procedures, such notions are born only among people who have no understanding of, and no responsibility for, the public accounts [?]. People would laugh up their sleeves at such public activity. From this "logic" one sees clearly the lawlessness and demoralisation that have seized this field in the institutions in which all strata of the Jewish population are represented — the institutions that were supposed to be called local Jewish parliaments. They were supposed to be the tone-setters of the Jewish street, its pulse, the highest expression of Jewish public life.

It is a rare thing, how deep these highest representations of ours have sunk. People have become indifferent to them, nobody takes an interest in them, nobody gives them a thought; the critic has distanced himself from them, because everything there is already empty; there is no one and nothing to criticise, since nothing is born there that would benefit the Jewish population, the suffering or hungry Jew. So who could have trust in such oblivion, and who would demand anything at all of them, when all hopes and expectations have vanished far, far away into the deep infinite?

At the same time, however, a strange phenomenon is to be noted: exactly as they are helpless at any fruitful and useful work, exactly as no logical initiative can be born or realised there, we see on the other hand that the most unworthy deeds are carried out quite comfortably and modestly. Let it be a full 100 per cent damage to the population, let others fight against it — then they are rock-firm and will push everything in the world through; then various individuals will turn up who will stop at nothing in the world, as long as their own thing is carried through; however impractical and illogical it may be, however heavily it may weigh on the shoulders of the kehilla members, they will not take it into account.

Well, why should we fool ourselves — we know quite well that never was everything in the best order; we always made mistakes, and defects were found at every step, and people always had to grapple with them. It makes no difference — the truth may be told at any time and on any occasion — but it was never like this; anything similar could not even have been imagined. When a cardinal error was made, people stormed and pounded on the table until everything was turned upside down and inside out. Besides, public workers can always make mistakes, consciously or unconsciously. Such things cannot be thrown at anyone as if he were directly guilty — sometimes an error is made indirectly and perhaps unconsciously. But it never reached the present level; there was always a limit, which one had to reckon with, willing or not. Never was there what we see today; never did the limit vanish from the eyes of our representatives as we see it on every occasion nowadays, so that nothing and no one is reckoned with, and with the most incompetent and incomprehensible means whatever one pleases is pushed through on the one side, while on the other side matters that play a decisive and significant role in Jewish life are neglected.

What, then, will become of this chaos? How long can such a management be tolerated? Where will all this lead?

R. Let

[Będzin — Hasidism: Torah words and sayings of the Rabbi.] (For the 19th yahrzeit of the Będzin Rabbi, the great gaon R' Yissachar Berish, of blessed saintly memory.)
1.
Hard for a rabbi to satisfy everyone.
A rabbi from a big city once complained to the late Rabbi that his opponents reproach him that... he[?] mixes too much with people ("me'urav im ha-briyot").
The Rabbi answered him: it is written "Vayekan'u le-Moshe ba-machaneh, le-Aharon kedosh Hashem" ("They envied Moses in the camp, and Aaron the holy one of the Lord," Psalms 106) — but this is difficult: surely Moses was a man of God, so why is "holy one of the Lord" said here specifically of Aaron?
The answer is: there are two kinds of leaders. Those like Moses, of whom it is written "And Moses took the tent and pitched it outside the camp" (portion Ki Tisa), i.e. he lived outside the camp and did not mix with people; Aaron, on the other hand, behaved differently — he was a lover of peace and a pursuer of peace, etc. The community had complaints against both. That is the meaning: "Vayekan'u le-Moshe" — about Moses they talked: "ba-machaneh," they demanded of him that he be inside the camp, not set apart. "Le-Aharon" — against Aaron they had the complaint "kedosh Hashem": of him they demanded that he be holy to the Lord and not mix so much with people.
—o—
2.
"He that slaughters an ox is as if he slew a man" (Isaiah 66).
What connection does "slaughtering the ox" have with "slaying a man"?
But usually the sacrifice that was brought was according to the size of the sin. Therefore "he who slaughters the ox" — if he brings an ox as a sacrifice, then he must be "one who slew a man," i.e. he has killed a person.
—o—
3.
From the eulogy for R' Shlomo Shein, of blessed memory
Eulogizing the well-known Hasid and philanthropist R' Shlomo Shein, of blessed memory, the Rabbi said, among other things, the following: in Midrash Kohelet it says: "Man is like a breath (hevel) — if like the breath of an oven, there is substance in it" (if man is likened to the vapor of an oven, surely that has substance); "Kohelet came and explained: vanity of vanities. Like a shadow — which shadow? If the shadow of a wall, there is substance in it" (if a man's life is like a shadow on the wall, surely it has substance); "rather, our days are like a passing shadow." In what way do the vapor of an oven or the shadow of a wall have substance?
But "the breath of an oven" means the one who gives coal to poor people. "The shadow of a wall" means the young man who sways while studying and casts[?] his shadow on the wall. If a man is like "the breath of an oven" (a man is like his deeds), i.e. he donated coal and thereby was a "breath of an oven," such a man has permanence. A man for whom "the shadow of a wall," i.e. the Torah scholar, is his life — such a man has substance.
The deceased, who had both things in him — "the breath of an oven," giving coal to poor people, and "the shadow of a wall," supporting yeshivas and studying himself — has substance.
—o—

But "kapdi" is from the root of "the impatient one (ha-kapdan) cannot teach," i.e. gentiles get angry and punish because of cleanliness...

Put an End to the Tax Arrears.

[Economy — taxes.] In our economic journalism and in the statements of responsible editors a positive phenomenon can now be observed: the demand to liquidate the enormous sums of tax arrears. Not long ago we came out in the columns of our paper with a project for solving the question of tax arrears radically, by declaring an amnesty for merchants and industrialists. At the session of the Sejm the Jewish Koło [the Jewish parliamentary club] came out with the demand to abolish the tax arrears. The demand was argued with sound reasons taken from life. The Koło's proposal was that the tax debts be annulled for those taxpayers whose turnover in 1930 was not greater than 30,000 zł.; for these payers the debts up to the end of 1929 would be annulled. For payers whose turnover in 1930 was not greater than 15,000 zł., the tax debts up to 1930 would be annulled. For all other taxpayers the debts up to 1928 would be annulled. The project also covers debts for patents [licence fees], fines and interest.
A few days after the Jewish Koło's project was submitted, the head of "Lewiatan" [the Polish employers' federation], Mr. Wieszbicki [Wierzbicki?], also came out with a project for solving the problem of tax arrears. He too holds that the tax arrears are today an item that cannot possibly be collected, and so they are merely an obstacle to the further development of economic life. The "Lewiatan" project goes in the direction that for anyone who pays a certain sum of tax, 90 percent of the sum will be counted as one hundred percent of the tax, and the remaining 10 percent will go to cover [?] the corresponding sums of tax arrears. If someone owes no taxes, the ten percent will be credited to him as a payment on account of future taxes; for the ten percent he will receive a voucher with which he will be able to pay the due tax two years from now.
At the same time the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce came out with its own project for regulating the problem of tax arrears. The association of textile manufacturers also spoke up, putting forward the interesting project that persons responsible for the tax of an enterprise they once ran, which is now inactive, should receive a certain moratorium on paying the arrears of income, industrial and property taxes, on condition that they resume economic activity and continue to pay their taxes regularly. The interest and the fines on the tax arrears would in that case be annulled. From the current taxes, discount percentages would be credited. As arrears would be counted industrial and property taxes up to and including 1930, and income tax up to 1931.
Taking into account that agriculture too, though in a thin voice, demands that the tax arrears be annulled, we get a picture of the full solidarity of the whole of society on this question. Incidentally, the Ministry of Finance is probably also aware that it is an impossible thing to collect these taxes, which amount to more than a billion złoty, from the turnover or even from the property of society. Would it not then be better if the state rid itself of the dangerous and invalid [?] fiction of tax debts on paper, which are merely a burden on the feet of economic life and only lead to the citizen losing the will to pay even the current taxes? Do the decisive circles here realise that the optimism, or even enthusiasm, which such a decree would undoubtedly arouse is so precious in our times of apathy and crisis of confidence that the value of such a mood is considerably greater than a billion złoty of tax arrears?
W—r [וויר.]

on a well-manured, fertile soil,
for the blossoming of our home, the old-new one!

Take with you our heartfelt greeting and great thanks
to the pioneer brothers and sisters,
and tell them that you, halutzim,
we send to them as our gift...
Leizer Shikman, Sosnowiec.
The Most Pleasant and Cheapest Entertainment

[General — leisure and radio.]
Despite the general reduction in prices, cultural entertainments are still quite expensive for the pocket of the average worker. A decent seat in the theatre, despite all the price cuts and discounts, still costs a few złoty. Besides, going to the theatre involves such expenses as the cloakroom, the house porter, etc. On top of that it requires dressing up specially, which is often impossible, especially for women. A ticket to the cinema, for a good film, also costs up to 3 zł.; adding all the surcharges and taxes it comes to about 5.50 zł. And what then when we set out for the cinema or the theatre with the family! Then the expense already reaches a considerable sum in the household budget.
Under these conditions it is understandable that for the average intelligent [educated person] the most popular entertainment has become the radio, which is accessible to the broadest strata of the population. One can easily afford a not-large one-time expense to buy a radio receiver, which, incidentally, can be had on convenient terms. The later expense, a monthly fee of 3 zł., amounts to almost as much as one cinema ticket.
And what does the radio give us for the 3 zł. a month? It is hard within this narrow frame to enumerate all the pleasures and entertainments that the radio receiver brings us, which, as has rightly been said, is "the window onto the world". In any case everyone will find, or better said hear, something that will surely interest him. Thus one will await with curiosity the daily radio bulletins, which bring the latest news from the country and from the whole world; a second — the freshest sports news; another — a concert by an artist whom he has no opportunity to hear in a concert hall; yet another — popular songs from gramophone records and an orchestra from a modern dancing; "our dear little ones" — broadcasts intended especially for them, etc.
One could in this way enumerate the whole daily programme of radio broadcasts, from which it emerges that the radio receiver can provide people, with an interest in every field, with their favourite entertainment.
Heard and Seen

[Sosnowiec and Zagłębie — feuilleton.]
By Ben Amotz.
The "Żydek" Said...
A guardian of the law [policeman] walks into a newspaper stand and asks for a copy of a Jewish-Polish newspaper. He leafs through the pages, searches, rummages in every corner of the paper and — remains dissatisfied. He does not find what he was looking for in the paper.
Curious, I ask:
— What is the pan [sir] looking for?
And he, the guardian of the law, answers me:
— I am looking — he says — for a newspaper article in which, as we have been informed, the Christian faith was insulted.
— That is a lie — I say — we have not seen that in the Jewish-Polish paper, and it is altogether absurd to believe that such an article would be printed in that paper.
— I believe it — the guardian of the law goes on — but the "Żydek" ["little Jew"] explicitly told us that he himself read the article, he himself, the "Żydek"...
— Is that so? The "Żydek"? Yes, yes, a very good informer is the "Żydek"; everywhere he is a close in-law, all doors are open to him, to the "Żydek". All secrets are learned from the "Żydek". Someone goes to a spa, to a dacha, someone buys himself a little plot of land, a family lives like other people, a Jew earns a couple of guilders, a newspaper allows itself to say a bold word — at once the "Żydek" turns up where needed.
And when one of the wronged [?] comes to the same place with a complaint — how can this be? where is justice? — he is answered from "above":
— The "Żydek" said...
—o—
77...
No more and no less.
A few months ago a building for an old-age home was completed in Sosnowiec.
Individuals devoted their energies, individuals gave for the cause and — individuals pay monthly pledges...
I ask one of those who built the splendid building how the financial situation of this enterprise, opened only a few months ago, looks, and I receive a short answer from him:
— 77...
— he says clearly.
— That is how it is. To this day the institution, in which 17 old men and women in all are maintained, has no more than 77 members. On the whole of Modrzejowska [?] Street — he says — we have no more than 5 (read: five) who pay 2 and 1 guilders a month..
— Well, and the rest? Where are the rich men, the house-owners and the philanthropists? Sosnowiec, thank God, has a fair number of them, who even in the days of the crisis can still afford to support such a useful institution.
— Yes, there are many who can pay; on nothing at all do they economise — except on charity. We have demanded it of them many times, but our voice finds no echo among the Sosnowiec "notables", and that is why to this day we have such a paltry number of members:
— 77...
—o—
"Zehev Ehad".. [a misspelling of zahav ehad, "one gold piece"]
Yiddish or Hebrew, Hebrew or Polish. A quarrel without end, a problem which to this day has not been solved.
And do you know why? Because with us, with the "Thou hast chosen us" people, each group has its own version; each for himself creates — a new orthography.
Particularly great "erudition" in this field is displayed by the Jewish printing-house owners in Zagłębie. To read through a Yiddish poster is no easy matter. More than once one's face turns red with shame on seeing how the Yiddish word [?] is ownerless in the eyes of outsiders.
But this time we do not intend to touch on the painful question of the mangling of the Yiddish language; we mention it only in passing because of the "document" that lies before us.
The document proves once again that one can go about dressed in silk garments and not know how to say a blessing over a radish, that one can be a "fine" Jew and do the deeds of Zimri, that one can be an ardent Yiddishist and not know "mai dekamri rebbetzin" [garbling of mai kamri rabbanan, "what do the rabbis say"], and that one can be an ardent Zionist and a fighter for the Hebrew language, and, issuing a receipt for a guilder received for the Keren Kayemet, the collector writes that he has received:
— "Zehev ehad"..
—o—
"Lehakhisnikes".. [Spite-doers]
We Jews may boast that we are not vengeful and grudge-bearing; to every misfortune, may it not come — we answer "this too is for the best", we accept everything with love, far from revenge, and all bitter feelings we swallow with the excuse:
— "Probably that is how it was destined".
On the other hand we are great "lehakhisnikes": from a sly trick, from a "foot stuck out" [tripping someone up], we derive pleasure. How does the Litvak interpret it? "Ah lo padoh" — if my brother does not redeem, "yifdeh" — it is just as if I had redeemed...
Here, for example, take an issue of the well-known Jew-baiting organ "Kur. Zag." [Kurier Zagłębia], in which the lowest slogans [?] of "Rozwój" are printed, every sentence like a fiery spear against Jewish trade and craft — and right next to the hate, Jewish firms take the place of honour, and precisely those from the "national cheder"...
And when you ask such a Jew: how can this be? Where is Jewish honour? Jewish pride? Is it worth it, for the mere supposition that the advertisement will bring a Christian customer — to let oneself be spat in the face?.. he answers you with a cynical smile:
— "I do it deliberately, to spite the antisemites: on one side they raise the alarm — saying not to buy from the Żyds, and on the other side they have to advertise my business..."
— "Lehakhisnikes"..
The Jewish Good Fortune in Poland

[Poland — the Jewish situation; opinion.] The Polish embassy in London has got itself a Polish rabbi, who handed over to the public, through the JTA, its declaration concerning the situation of the Jews in Poland.
It turns out that Jews in Poland are well off, as if in God's own bosom; any better it must not get, because of the danger that Jews from other countries will emigrate to Poland. True, one could then shut the gates, like America, but that liberal Poland will surely not do!
And Jewish well-being is plain for all to see.
The strongest proof is that Jews pay higher taxes. Surely that is a sign that they do better business and are indeed richer.
And listen: Jews have 450 cooperatives with 174 thousand members, which hold deposits of 30 million and have a turnover of 132 million zł. a year. The People's Bank (Folks-Bank) has 160 thousand members, and the Polish banks have given the cooperatives credits — 35 million zł.
Such figures must not merely convince, but simply crush.
In short: in Poland there is no antisemitism.
A pity the embassy forgot to mention the affair of the dispersal of the „Abwepal“ [?; probably the OWP — Obóz Wielkiej Polski, the nationalist antisemitic „Camp of Great Poland“]. That would have meant that antisemitism did not simply vanish from Poland by itself, automatically, but that the government fought it stubbornly and drove it out with sticks.
No more. No privileges are given to the Jews, and no „state within a state“ are they allowed to make.
Should the Jews complain about it? On the contrary, they must be loyal, serve the Polish state faithfully, in order to earn the goodwill of the Polish majority...
Thus honey and milk flow from the lips of the Polish embassy in London through the declaration it has served up to us by the grace of Rabbi Yerukhem Leiner.
And the London Jews who read it were surely astonished. From other sources they hear quite different greetings about the situation of the Jews in Poland. Instead of the Song of Songs one sings Lamentations. Where does this contradiction come from?
And just so we too are astonished here. If Jews are so well off in Poland, surely we should feel it before the embassy in London does. Why, then, is nothing heard here, in the Jewish street, but groaning and despairing cries of woe?
We cannot deny the figures of the declaration, which are surely taken from statistics. But that the interpretation is a false one, of that there is no doubt at all.
Let us take the main point, the question of taxes and prosperity. On the face of it, it is very logical: taxes are paid by the well-to-do and not by the poor man. But the truth is that from year to year Jewish trade licences (patents) diminish by the thousands, because the crisis together with the taxes has sucked the assets dry to the bottom and left behind large deficits besides, which have found expression in bankruptcies and in outstanding tax debts, from which one can never disentangle oneself. The truth is that even the businesses that are still nominally functioning are almost empty of goods and of customers, and 90 percent of our shopkeepers and merchants do not earn a living even on a miniature scale, and they envy the employee and the official and even the worker who earns with his 10 fingers a few dozen gulden [złoty] a week, assured!
That is what the Jewish middle class in Poland looks like!
People will say: the peasant is even worse off, he barely has bread with potatoes. That is not right in essence, because the urban Jew would thank God seven times a day if he could have bread with potatoes in peace, without the dreadful headaches and constant trembling before the sequestrator and the komornik [bailiff], who do not let him get even the little bit of sleep at night!
Besides, the whole state looks after the peasant, to raise his prosperity. He is let off taxes, given credits to buy agricultural machines, cooperatives are organised for him, he is helped to export his products, and a moratorium has even been declared on his private debts — from which, incidentally, the small-town Jews, whose few groszy are stuck with the peasant, have suffered terribly.
And what is done for the urban Jew?
The few credits given to the Jewish cooperatives — if they are given — are like a drop against the sea of troubles in which Jews are drowning. And all those thousands of Jews who fall out of their positions can no longer rise in a resurrection of the dead. Into the monopolised and state-run enterprises Jews are not let in; to state posts they are not admitted. We would forgo the Jewish director in a state bank if instead a hundred Jewish caretakers (woźni) and watchmen (stróże) were taken on. We would not mind if the son-in-law of Prof. Schorr [?] were not a prosecutor at the Supreme Court — though it is an honour for us — if only no obstacles were put in the way of Jewish applicants. Jewish artisanry is simply going under because of the draconian guild laws, which in practice are much harder and more oppressive still than in theory.
The pathos about Jewish privileges and about a state within a state is incomprehensible to us; it is some misunderstanding dug up from the Polish antisemitic archives, long forgotten even by the professional antisemites.
The main thing is that Polish Jewry is going under. The living proof of it is the Jewish youth, which can in no way fit into the occupations and professions of their parents and wander about by the tens of thousands like roaming shadows, without a goal and without a perspective.
That is the truth.
P. K.
Little Feuilleton: Revolution and Swiss Cheese

[Feuilleton — Switzerland.] Switzerland has always been a city of refuge for all sorts of political „criminals“ whom their homeland had spat out.
The Swiss petty bourgeois had no business with politics and revolutions; the subversive convictions of the refugees were no concern of his. On the contrary, they are such obedient and quiet little lambs, pay their rent punctually, eat Swiss cheese with relish, shoot across the lakes [?], climb the mountains, sometimes they make a commotion about something, get heated and sweat over long debates — whom does it bother?
If the Swiss burgher did take an interest in world politics and revolutions, it was probably also for the sake of a livelihood.
Things have gone somewhat quiet in the world, domestic peace reigns in the countries, somewhere an amnesty has been declared — feh, that's good for nothing. The frequency of political „emigrants“ will weaken.
The Swiss reads his newspaper, looks at the telegrams with curiosity, and suddenly his eyes light up. In Tokyo a revolution, the Mikado has been overthrown — there will begin persecutions, arrests, people will flee, and here things will get lively. The empty room will be let, there will be a livelihood.
Switzerland, that is, traded in foreign revolutions; to the spirit of the revolutions it remained indifferent. From Poland a communist fled, and from the Soviet Union an anarchist; both were welcome guests in Switzerland, a landlord would gladly let the two of them a double room.
Even antisemitism was a matter of livelihood for her. She herself knew nothing of antisemitism; but the antisemitic persecutions of Jewish students in other countries made Switzerland downright rich. By the thousands the young Jews came down there, like locusts descending and devouring all the grain of the fields, guzzling all the milk of the cows. Only, a locust, when it has devoured, flies away and does not pay, whereas the Jews pumped whole treasures of money into Switzerland for her tolerance.
Should antisemitism somewhere in some country have grown old and the „numerus clausus“ been abolished, the Swiss would have grieved over it, because it would have taken away a bit of his livelihood.
And suddenly the Swiss himself has felt the taste of revolution in his own home, revolution with a bang and with a shot — with dead and wounded [probably the Geneva shooting of 9 November 1932].
And misfortune never comes alone: together with the revolution came antisemitism too.
Now the Swiss will know that revolution is not merely a matter of livelihood, a means of spreading Swiss cheese; but that one can get a bullet in the belly from it, and then one will never again be able to digest any cheese.
But one question remains: if the Swiss revolution should also lead to political emigration, and if Swiss antisemitism should also lead to a numerus clausus — then where are the Swiss emigrants and students to go?
Is there still a country in the world that has not been stricken with these plagues?
Let us hope that Switzerland will think better of it in time, that instead of making revolutions and manufacturing antisemitism it is much more profitable for her to manufacture cheese and to feed the emigrants and students and the delegates of the League of Nations.
Avi-Ver[?].
Captain Lerbas — by Maria Wielopolska

[Translated story — war.]
Over the Galiniawiec [?] swamps death descended. Far away the forest droned, taking leave of the fallen.
The shooting tore at the ears; cannon-balls flew among the bronze-brown [?] leaves and swept them away, as if with brooms, in murderous fury.
From time to time a fiery rocket ripped through the air. Terrified horses neighed with a wail that blended with the strange screaming of men.
Amid the monstrous cries men perished quietly, breathing out their last breath. Only the earth groaned; it was full of echoes, and it was hard to say over whom the earth was groaning — over the last human grief, or over the raging cannons.
Beside the swamps stood wagons, stood quiet and exposed.
No one knew what to do. The horses tore at the reins, stood empty [?]. They reared on their hind legs, drew arcs with their shaggy heads, sank deeper into the mud and floundered, wailed, heaved their flanks. The soldiers held the horses by the muzzles and stared into the dark forest, which was full of thunder and lightning. The soldiers knew that at any moment a witch could come out of the forest — death. In the dusk the forest spread out on both sides like the great dark pages of an opened book, and they, the soldiers, hungrily read from afar their own fate.
The end drew near. The shooting grew weaker.
Beside the military wagons stood Captain Lerbas. His face was dark, like the forest that was dying. His grey hair lay around his cheeks like a white polished frame around a Byzantine face.
"Halt!" he shouted from time to time, digging his feet and his rifle into the mud.
Behind him — wetness, an abyss. Before him — several thousand enemies and twelve cannons that would not stop firing.
Poles were perishing. Every bullet struck the moss-covered birches and echoed wide and far, and the echo fell back into the Jew's heart, into Captain Lerbas's heart; his faithful heart trembled within him, he knew that one must not stand here. But he had been ordered to, so he stood.
Suddenly he saw how, among the thin golden gossamer threads of "Elul summer" hanging in the dusk, Gramaika's uhlans were riding.
Colonel (Polkovnik) Krszyński sent an order that Lerbas was to get across the swamps with the wagons. Otherwise the enemy would seize the ammunition, the pay-chest.
The soldiers' hair stood on end [?] — no living man had yet crawled through those swamps. The forest did indeed smell of death, but the swamps — of wetness that squelched under their feet, and that was worse than death. In their eyes — terror, terror.
Captain Lerbas turned round and gave the command — march across the swamps. He unharnessed the horses, and harnessed himself and the soldiers to the wagons, and they began to drag.
"May the first cholera take it, Mister Captain! We can't go on!"
"Better to croak there in the forest than here in the mud!"
And the mud lashed, hissed, was full of foam. Night fell, the ranks broke, the wagons groaned, tilted now to the right, now to the left, and behind them cannons roared, louder and louder.
"Whoever leaves the wagon — a bullet in the head!" Lerbas ordered, repeating it over and over. "Hey, brothers, the fate of the whole unit lies in our hands — ammunition, money and uniforms..."
He had not finished when several soldiers let go of the shafts and the swingletrees and dashed for the forest.
"Stop, you scum!" Lerbas shouted.
The soldiers ran on.
The Jew turned pale, though fires flared up around his eyes. A dry hand rose, a shot rang out and the first deserter fell; terrified, the rest turned back and harnessed themselves to the wagons. They panted, sank in the mud and dragged.
As they dragged the wagons out onto the meadow, a horse black as night blocked their way. The horse was plastered with mud and could barely stand on its feet.
"By what right did you kill one of my [?] soldiers?!" shouted Rittmeister Gramaika down from his horse.
Lerbas let go of the wagon and, agitated, began brandishing his rifle and cried out:
"By what right? We were ordered not to run away, and anyone who runs away — I shoot him in the head!"
All at once the forest fell silent; there was heard only a sad song, a great song, and into that song, as into a goblet of blood, a shot fell — a single shot that rang out over the firing that had already lasted twelve hours.
The pistol in Gramaika's hand was still smoking. Lerbas trembled and doubled over, as if the swamps were dragging him ever deeper; he looked into Gramaika's eyes with a terrible sorrow. Then he fell:
"Lost! But you, Gramaika, did not understand me! I did not raise my rifle at you. I was only swearing by the rifle. Lost!"
He stretched out full length in the mud.
Far off, cannons thundered again. The forest trembled and groaned; frightened birds soared high, wanting to be as far as possible from the earth,
Let Us Talk It Over a Little! What We Wanted from the Jewish Sports Movement in Zagłębie, and What We Have Achieved

[Sport — Zagłębie; opinion.] The Jewish gymnastics and sports associations came into being in order to realise the idea of the physical renaissance of Jewish youth. People will say these are already threadbare, banal phrases that cannot be applied now, when sports and gymnastics associations in general, and the Jewish ones among them, have quite other problems to solve and settle.
Whoever now has the audacity to recall the idea of the Jewish sports movement, and the audacity to halt for one minute the insane pace of the wheel that is "being turned" by the fixers in the sports movement, will be taken for an idler.
We gladly take this idleness upon ourselves and hold that now there must come the outcry, the fist on the table from an authoritative individual, or an authoritative collective, who will say: enough, it cannot go on like this; the old watchwords of the creation and development of the Jewish sports and gymnastics movement must regain the upper hand and cool the tempers of our already overheated and inflamed sportsmen — those who regard this movement not only as a goal in the life of the individual but almost as the very existence of our whole people; cool a little those who hold that our heroes are the ones who distinguish themselves on the green field, and that no other domain of our Jewish life needs to be cultivated.
The Jewish sports movement was created in order to bring our spiritual condition into balance with the physical, in order to bring Jewish youth out of a state of fear, slackness, neglect, abjectness, sadness and despondency. Our sports movement was created in order to discipline our youth for the aims of the people, for the struggle for the existence and preservation of the people. In no way would it have occurred to anyone that a lofty idea would be debased into such things as shooting goals, combining with championship points, buying and selling players like slaves on the stock exchange. No one could have imagined that practising sport would become a profession, and that Jewish sports associations would assist in the whole game and outdo one another in these machinations and combinations.
On the one hand, it is said, the Jewish sports movement is centralised, at least the associations belonging to the Zionist trend. On the other hand, however, the central body looks through its fingers at all these things and does not want to bring before the public all the filth that has accumulated in the associations and that is so hard to root out. We understand the great difficulties now bound up with such a general cleansing. We know that this depends to a great extent on the surrounding atmosphere, but that cannot serve as an excuse. A beginning must be made. After all, one must protect the souls of the youngsters who are growing up and are already being poisoned, who think that this is what we demand of the Jewish sports movement. We also understand how important the appearances of Jewish sport in the outside world are, for prestige and representation, but precisely this must be safeguarded, made careful, so that it does no harm to the idea itself.
For those who have devoted their time and energy to the Jewish sports movement, the questions raised are of the first importance, and an answer must be found — and soon. How to approach the matter we shall try to talk over in a second article.
S.
Będzin Is Already Playing "Yo-Yo"

[Będzin — feuilleton.] The Będzin of old has died out and ceased. Its glory has departed, its splendour has departed. At twelve o'clock at night you will not meet a living soul in the street.
You will no longer come across the "bon vivant" — not even the drunken worker flirting with the street lamp, not even the one and only "night girl". For whom, after all?
And not only that, but our whole Europeanism in town is dying out — a second Sławków.
Just imagine. We Będziners have always been among the first followers and chasers after every new phenomenon.
When the "bridge fashion" came over — I mean the bridge game from England — "bridge clubs" were born among us at once, by the dozen.
And not only men's clubs, but women's clubs as well.
A new game was created — "ping pong"; the whole youth and all the old men together with the young flung themselves at "ping pong". The world of women, too, soon flung itself at "ping pong" — a game with little eggs like pigeons' eggs, "zig-zag", a little egg there, a little egg here, a sport reckoned, as is the custom, in — points.
It has already gone so far that in private homes "ping pong" has become a passing pastime, and husband and wife — and the whole household play at their own ping pong. Husband and wife therefore fight over who will score more points.
Lately, however, we have grown so much in modernism that it is worth telling about it, so that the world may learn of our level as regards Europeanism and world sport. Our Będzin, too, will become famous in the wide world's renown as a big city.
And do you know how this came about?
Why, we have taken up the "yo, yo" game.
The Americans invented a new game and gave it the name "yo-yo" — and it has become so popular here that only a select few do not know what the newest sport looks like and what is the nature of this thing.
Is this not a leap in our modernism? As everywhere in the whole world, here too great and small play it, schoolchildren of the cheder, in the schools and in the streets.
Picture a round, coloured spool pierced like a little ring, on which a coloured thread is wound — you give the thread a pull and the spool goes up, you let the thread go and it rolls itself back up into the spool. It seems to me that we cheder boys already played with such toys in the beginners' cheder, and that was not called "sport". Not "the newest invention", and more than once the "rebbe" whipped us for such games.
Today — grown-ups, adults play "yo-yo", in the café, in society, in gardens and parks, in associations and clubs. It seems the world has fallen on its head and people are crawling on their bellies.
They say: "an American invention". What little children played in the cheder — is discovered in America and called "sport".
We shall yet live to see the "etl-betl game" become a genuine American or English invention, and the games of our great-grandmothers: "etl-betl" — or even "reshele" — will enter the modern games of the day.
I still remember the "etl-betl" game [a string figure game played on the fingers, like cat's cradle]:
"I made a little cradle out of thread — and my sister took it from me and made a 'saw'. And my younger little sister took it from the elder one and made a 'lekekh' (honey cake). A girlfriend took it away again and made a ship, and a second girlfriend made a 'water' out of it."
And my grandmother — may she rest in peace — watched the game and said, laughing:
"You see, children, the whole of life is no more than an 'etl-betl game' — everyone's end turns out to be water."
P. W.

S. Lewin — Forlorn

S. Lewin.

Across the noisy street of the railway station, where trains come and go east and west, a Jewish woman was dragging a large wicker hamper; beside her walked two children: on one side a little boy with two small bundles in his small, thin hand, and on the other side a sick girl who could barely drag her feet.
"Where is the uncle who was supposed to wait for us?" the boy asked his mother again, his eyes still sleepy. He kept looking around, pressing himself against the wall. He had been travelling all night; when he woke up it was already day, and the people had begun to seem more and more familiar to him. The little windows and the benches too — he could have stayed there for ever. Now again new faces, angry ones; he pulls [as printed: "tsi"] his mother to step out of the way. People are hurrying, he is afraid they will get angry; he sees only automobiles and trams — there are no droshkies in Germany. The apartment houses (kamienice) and the streets .. and the policemen... everything different from at home... Well, where is "the uncle"? he asks again, afraid of the strange people in the strange city.
"'The uncle'?" the downcast mother repeats her child's question, and asks herself: "Silly boy... he's no uncle of yours, he is... a relative, really — not that either; he's a good man, we were neighbours, he owed all of us a favour; with Father, may he rest in peace, he was very close."
She sighed, took the address out of the silver purse, went over [as printed: "ibergeleygt"] the name again and began looking in every direction, to stop someone who would tell her where she had to go. Several times she stammered, as if begging for alms: "Khar leben"[?] .. but nobody stopped. Each time someone else got angry at her, telling her to get off the pavement with the big hamper and the bundles. The hurrying people pushed and shoved.
Suddenly the sick girl had her attack: her eyes rolled back, her face became even more of a mask, her limbs even stronger [stiffer?]; she began to fall backwards. Her mother caught her in her arms and sat her down on the hamper in the noisy street of the strange city. People began to stop and stand.
A fat German woman with a big umbrella made a pitying face: "Mein Gott."
The man for whom the unfortunate woman had an address had already been in Germany for several years. He lived with his wife and child in a furnished room in a poor district; the landlady with whom he lodged, a war widow, stuck to her own line: "Ich erlaube nicht!" (I do not allow it!)
A big city. So many houses, and three people have no place.
* * *
At the little window of the cellar room, which has iron bars, there is always someone different standing and looking out: sometimes the widow who came from Poland (she no longer sighs), sometimes the sick girl. Most often the boy. Of everyone one sees only the shoes of the passers-by and bits of coat-tails. The orphan keeps going out of the cellar and looking at gloomy faces, of Jews with long beards who turn about worriedly back and forth; the street reminds him of home. He goes back down into the cellar, because down by the little window he sees "his" town better. Where he had so many friends, and he cannot forget them. He promised Garfinkel and Glezer that he would write. But he hasn't done it yet. In the club (Verein) it was cheerful: they sang songs, romped about, held discussions and went on long walks. At home nothing was lacking, even after Father's death; Mother went on running the beer tavern; Silesians (Ślązacy) got drunk, sang merry songs, fell down as they walked and rolled on the ground, crazy Avrom played on a stick. The orphan cannot hold out in the cellar; he has come to hate his sick sister. In the former home he hardly ever saw her; since she fell ill — so long ago now that he no longer remembers when — she was no longer his sister; only sometimes he would recall what she looked like when she was still healthy, when she used to play with him; now he hates her. He would run back to Sosnowiec if he knew the way and were not afraid to walk so far alone.
He has to laugh when he sees the Jews with the little plush hats and in silk kapotes (bekeshes) turning about back and forth along the street. And the Germans — what they speak is like Yiddish. But he does not understand a single word. But why did Mother travel here? In Sosnowiec it was so good! He would come home from school, eat lunch and run straight out. The friends were already waiting at the door. Only one thing was bad: every day Reb Hersh came with the Gemara and would not let him go, and afterwards he had to do his lessons. But lately Reb Hersh had stopped coming. Mother sighed and dismissed one maid, then the second, and worked herself. From then on things got bad. A man from the Magistrat (municipality) began coming again and again, with a yellow briefcase under his arm, and he shouted; they no longer burned the electric light, only a night-lamp — only in the big room, and in the little rooms — when someone still came to eat or drink something — Mother lit a candle. Lately it had really been very bad. The women and the Jews who used to bring meat and baked goods shouted and banged with their fists, until a wagon drove up to the door with two policemen and the man with the yellow briefcase, and they took all the things out of the rooms.
But why did Mother fool him? She said: "We are going to an uncle in Germany and from there to America." And this Jew, to whom they dragged the hamper with the sacks, is no uncle at all and cannot help at all. And from the "uncle" in America still no letter comes.
The widow sits on the hamper standing in the middle of the room; she no longer sighs; her small grey eyes have sunk even deeper into her head and grown more glassy. The small forehead grows ever more dried out. In her brain everything shrinks together, goes out; only a few little flames still flicker: no gravestone set on her husband's grave, money left owing to the baker and the butcher's wife, the shame before the neighbours with whom she lived together so long. And what is she to do now? She has already been everywhere with the sick girl; nobody wants to take her into any hospital, it costs so much money! She has the last few marks, she has nothing more to sell; for the silver purse they will give only six marks. Wherever they told her to go, she went — not, God forbid, so that they would give her something, but so they would give her advice. They told her to go back home.
Go back home — — — —
A heavy sigh tears itself out of her. "Master of the Universe! For the sake of the two orphans help us in the strange city!" But hardly [printed "pmet" for "kimat"] anyone among the strangers hears the weeping of the despairing mother with her orphans, and they remain forlorn in the strange city.

Every merchant faces a penalty of up to 3 months' arrest.

[Poland — Economy and legislation.] The new laws which recently came into force have created such a situation that a huge number of business owners — over 200 thousand merchants and manufacturers — are each threatened with arrest of up to 3 months if they do not punctually fulfil the regulations.
The social-welfare laws oblige employers to deduct from wages the sums that must be paid for the sickness fund, insurance for white-collar workers and employees („ZUP“ [Zakład Ubezpieczeń Pracowników Umysłowych]), etc. Since the payments are very large, hundreds of thousands of merchants, craftsmen and manufacturers owe these institutions large sums, amounting to over a billion złoty.
Because of the severe crisis it is very hard to pay for the sickness fund and „ZUP“, especially since, besides the part deducted from salaries (pensje), the employers must also pay a large contribution for every worker and employee.
The social institutions have obtained a strong whip against the merchants and manufacturers: in the „Kodeks Karny“ [Penal Code], which is already binding throughout Poland, there is an article 58 which says that owners who do not pay into the social institutions the sums they have deducted from wages face arrest of up to 3 months, or a fine of up to 3.000 zł.
Whether this harsh law will help, in such a time of crisis, to make the merchants and manufacturers able to pay the enormous billion sum they owe these institutions is not known; but these social institutions are already setting about relying on this law. It has already been decided [printed „בעשטיצט“] that these social institutions will demand payment of the sum owed, relying on the consequences that non-payment carries under article 59 of the Kodeks Karny.

How the Turnover Tax for 1933 Will Be Calculated for Merchants and Artisans

[Taxes — turnover tax.]
We consider it necessary to explain to the community of merchants and artisans that from the New Year the turnover-tax rates will be changed for all branches. The greater part of the branches of trade and manufacture will pay much less than until now. This is provided for in the new law on turnover tax, Art. 7, paragraph five.
Under this new law, from 1 January 1933 turnover tax will be paid as follows:
1) Wholesale merchants who keep regular commercial books — half a percent.
3) Wholesale merchants who keep no commercial books, or whose books will not be recognized, will pay 2 percent.
3) Wholesale merchants of foodstuffs — flour, grain, etc. — who will keep no books, or whose books will not be recognized, will pay 2 percent.
4) Retail merchants of all branches of trade who, from 1 January 1933, will keep simplified bookkeeping will pay only three-quarters of a percent.
5) Retail merchants of all branches of trade who will not keep simplified bookkeeping will pay 2 percent.
Retail merchants are those merchants who hold the second category [of trade licence] and sell to consumers and also to small shopkeepers, but only in small quantities of goods. They will have to keep thoroughly complete commercial books, not simplified bookkeeping.
Simplified bookkeeping is only for retail merchants and shopkeepers who hold the third category, and for retail merchants who hold the second category but sell only to consumers and not to resellers.
6) Retail merchants of foodstuffs will pay three-quarters of a percent if they keep simplified bookkeeping.
7) Retail food merchants who will not keep the simplified bookkeeping will have to pay 1 percent from 1 January 1933.
8) For deliveries to state and municipal institutions one will pay half a percent if commercial books are kept. If no commercial books are kept one will pay 2 percent.
9) „Skup“ [buying-up] merchants of the first, second and third category who keep proper commercial books will pay half a percent. „Skup“ merchants of the third category will pay only half a percent if they keep simplified bookkeeping.
10) „Skup“ merchants of the first, second and third category who keep no books will pay one percent of turnover from the New Year, and they will be assessed at the discretion of the tax commissions.
11) „Skup“ merchants of the 4th category will pay only half a percent, without bookkeeping, but their turnover may not exceed 20 thousand zł. a year.
12) Enterprises engaged solely in „dostawy“ [supplies/deliveries] will pay half a percent with books, one percent without books.
13) Commission enterprises and commercial brokerage will pay 4 percent of earnings.
14) Forwarding (expedition) enterprises — one and a half percent.
15) Mills and oil-presses [olejarnie] that keep commercial books will pay one percent.
16) Mills and oil-presses of the 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th category may keep simplified bookkeeping, and they will pay only one percent.
17) Artisans who hold artisan cards [karty rzemieślnicze] will pay 1 percent. They need not keep any bookkeeping.
18) Manufacturers of all kinds will continue to pay two percent.

A merchant from Gniezno arrived in Königshütte (Chorzów) by the express train. At the station a certain Icchak Cajtenbaum from Tarnów paid a "visit" to his pocket. The trick, however, did not come off, and the pickpocket was arrested.
Escaped from court custody
On Monday a certain Szymon Apelbaum, who had been charged with a series of frauds, escaped from court custody in Königshütte.
Hitler's hasid sentenced...
The court in Königshütte sentenced a comrade of Hitler's to 10 days' arrest for shouting in the street in honour of Hitler.
A "Mizrachi" in Katowice
Last Sunday a founding meeting of the "Mizrachi" organisation took place in Katowice. At the meeting a fairly large number of members declared themselves.
The sensational trial in Katowice concluded
On Saturday, after several days, the sensational trial against the three directors of "Oswag"[?] for committing a series of frauds in paying taxes was concluded at the Katowice district court.
The director of the Pszczyna (Pless) concern, Ebelir[?], received a year and a half in prison and a 5,000 zł fine under "Urteil" [article] 313 of the Commercial Code. Director Anerman — 7 months' imprisonment, and the director of the Deutsche Bank in Katowice — 3 months.
On the strength of the amnesty, Ebelir is remitted a third of the sentence and also the money sum. Anerman — half the sentence, and the director of the Deutsche Bank is remitted the entire sentence.
Attack on a policeman
On Tuesday 3 persons attacked the policeman on duty at the "Emma" mine. One of the gang shot at the policeman and wounded him.
Shopping hours extended
On 3, 10, 17, 21, 22, 23 and 30 December the shops in Königshütte will be open until 8 o'clock in the evening.
The Campaign for the Yiddish Book in Zagłębie Continues! Communiqué No. 2

[Zagłębie — culture.] The campaign for the Yiddish book proclaimed by the PEN Club again recorded success this week.
Since it has not yet been technically possible for the delegation to visit, by 1 December, all those who are interested in the Yiddish book, the campaign committee came to an arrangement with Warsaw and obtained consent to continue selling at the cheap prices during the coming 2 weeks. The campaign committee announces this good news with pleasure.
The campaign committee once more reminds the better-class Jewish reader to hurry with orders. Such an opportunity will not repeat itself so soon.
The "revue scenes" at the budget session of the Dąbrowa kehilla council

[Dąbrowa — Kehilla.] On Sunday afternoon, under the chairmanship of Mr A. L. Fuks, a session of the Dąbrowa kehilla council took place to approve the new kehilla budget for the year 1933.
The course of the session was very "interesting", above all for the "gallery", which for several hours enjoyed itself thoroughly and was regaled by the personal abuse and tavern expressions, which were not spared even on the part of the Dąbrowa Jewish representation...
Thus, for instance, we are told, when one of the parnasim pointed out that the council was adopting the new budget within the framework of the "concessioned majority", which came into being thanks to the sovereignty of the Krymiłów Hasidim — or better said, to safeguard the pensions of the Krymiłów Hasidim, who are gmina (kehilla) employees — he received such an answer as one no longer hears nowadays even in a second-rate tavern...
After hours of shouting and interjections from the gallery, which took a lively part in the discussion, the budget was adopted, according to which the establishment (etat) will be higher by 15 thousand gulden.
The administration had proposed a reduction of the pensions, which could have brought about that the establishment amounts, as in the previous year, to a sum of 21 thousand zł. Then came the council, which handed out with a generous hand, rejected the reduction proposal and approved the establishment at 36.400 zł.
The council also adopted the administration's proposal to exempt the population of Reden from any fee for using the mikveh there.
For this purpose 3 thousand zł. was provisionally allotted for administrative expenses.
Great success of our townsman, the well-known Jewish artist Ziegler, in Warsaw

[Zagłębie — Culture.] At Garliński's art salon on Mazowiecka Street in Warsaw, the artist Shmuel (Samuel) Ziegler [Cygler?], a child of Zagłębie, has exhibited his pictures.
The exhibition is having a great moral and material success; the local press, including the press that is not friendly to Jews, devotes warm notices to the exhibition and speaks of Ziegler's artistic achievements on a very broad scale.
"Ziegler," writes the Jewish press, "is no new face in Warsaw; he used to take part in the collective exhibitions of the Jewish Art Society, where his excellent graphic works attracted general attention. But this time Ziegler has appeared as an entirely new artist; the graphic works at the present exhibition are proof that Ziegler has broadened [?] and deepened his art.
Echoes of the abuses at the Dąbrowa tax office (Urząd Skarbowy)

[Dąbrowa — Courts.] In the month of September (Wrzesień) Messrs Dudziński [?] and Skoczylas, officials of the Dąbrowa tax office (Urząd Skarbowy), who are accused of abuses in the performance of their duties, were arrested in Dąbrowa.
In connection with this the officials were arrested.
These days the investigation into the matter was concluded and the accused were released on bail.
A letter to the editor

[Dąbrowa — Letter to the editor.] Esteemed Mr Editor!
I ask you to print this letter in your esteemed newspaper, for which I thank you in advance.
In the last issue of the "Zagl. Tsayt." [Zaglembier Tsaytung], in the notice "Dąbrowa merchants' association without a president", I was called upon to take over the office of president of the Dąbrowa "Merchants' Association". It is truly incomprehensible for what purpose the interested merchants have gone public with this matter; perhaps they believe that the honour of my person being mentioned in the esteemed newspaper will lead me to change my opinion, which I have already declared many times to the delegation: so long as the administration is not recruited from persons capable of work, I will not take over the leadership of the Dąbrowa "Merchants' Association", because it is a responsible undertaking, at the present time when commerce is ruined and one must devote a great deal of time to alleviate the situation.
So I declare once again that the way out is to call a general meeting, elect a proper representation, and then I too will be one of the active workers.
With respect, B. Rechnic.
