On Guard Before a Catastrophe. XV. (Why Should the Thread Not Be Drawn Further? — Backwardness and Understanding of Sources of Income)

[Opinion / economy — crafts and trade.] L. Szpigelman.
We have thus already shown that the public runs away from the craftsman solely because he drags things out and delays beyond measure, and it becomes loathsome to keep going and waiting for the article that needs to be finished; and so people have grown used to this: at the first opportunity they shy away from ordering anything, so that whatever one can get ready-made, one goes into a shop and buys it.
It is no better with costing: they [printed "ויי", misprint for "זיי"] cannot calculate; it happens that the craftsman either botches the article and earns some 80 percent that way, or he has not calculated well and loses 20-30 per cent.
The merchant class, too, has not progressed in this field. Among the nations of the world we have a name as good merchants, skilled businessmen. We, however, know that we have our abilities, which we truly do possess — but neglected and made light of. True, we had the best chances to carry on our abilities, each in his own field, and if this was made light of, it is only owing to the fact that the parents did not want their children to occupy themselves with the same thing as they themselves, and that is the only reason that prevented the thread from being drawn further with success.
Thus we know that, for example, a tailor, a shoemaker, a carpenter — even though they themselves strove to raise their trade to a higher level, and preached and agitated at every opportunity that one must no longer be ashamed of their trade and that they are already far removed from the period when a craftsman was not permitted to go further than the "polish" [the synagogue vestibule] — nevertheless did not want to make their children craftsmen. It impressed them more that their children should become officials [printed "בשאמטע", misprint for "באמטע"], teachers and even [?] "luftmenshn" [people without a real livelihood], as long as not a craftsman.
With the merchant, too, the situation did not change: even though no one was ashamed of a merchant, he too did not want to hand his profession over to his children. Better that he be a doctor, a lawyer, an engineer — as long as not a merchant. The father never wanted to take into account that his child was perhaps not suited to the profession destined for it, that he might perhaps have been a better merchant than a doctor.
We therefore hold that this one thing is the reason why among us no one progressed in his own field, but we constantly went backwards, and our positions were quite easily seized by others.
It would have been quite different if everyone had seen to continuing his profession: the children would have perfected what the parents could not attain. The children, had they been trained in their field, would have risen as intelligent professionals to the desired height, to the proper level. The parents and grandparents would then not have recognised their own enterprises, whether it was a commercial one or a craftsman's one; each would have specialised in his own, perfected it beyond recognition, each would have used his abilities in his own line. Instead, the father remained standing at the same height, and the son — just when he could have developed, with his training, the intelligence of the business from which he drew his livelihood — the father tore him away from it; in this way everything became paralysed, so that at the first best opportunity, at a mere breath of a change in climate, others, more intelligent, seized the positions which could have been carried on by their [our] children.
We have no understanding for our past, we [printed "מיט", misprint for "מיר"] do not know how to value our laborious work; among us it is considered right today to smear over the signboard whose firm for decades proudly represented this or that article.
It is quite different in the cultured countries abroad. There firms pass from generation to generation; even strangers, when they take over a business, do not strike out the founder of the business — for them it is a relic, something sacred. And this is not only with big firms, but even with quite small ones. We walk past a quite ordinary watchmaker — which among us is not considered a trade at all — and we see on the signboard that the business has existed for four generations already. Actually we need not go far: we see this also near us, in Upper Silesia. In Katowice itself we find at every step such long-existing firms, and therefore it is truly a pleasure to take a look at an enterprise there. When one comes from the largest cities in Poland to Katowice, one is immediately delighted by the shine of the shop windows there, by the punctuality of the craftsman, by his exact reckoning and costing and his aesthetic and intelligent execution. At the first glance the training and the experience strike the eye. One sees that each one is absorbed in his trade like a true specialist, and therefore he works with love and devotion.
Under the German rule every Jewish citizen could do with his child whatever he wished. He could study without restrictions; nevertheless nobody was eager to study what he did not need. If the father was a craftsman, he perfected and trained him in his own field; a merchant, on the other hand, wanted his children to complete a commercial academy, so that he would have the possibility of continuing his business as an experienced businessman.
While an Upper Silesian firm, be it a craftsman's or a commercial enterprise, will think over how to achieve something in its business, whether with the help of various advertisements or with aesthetic and attractive shop-window displays, among us such an enterprise will not deposit even a broken two-grosz coin for that purpose.
It is no longer a secret to anyone that many inhabitants of Zagłębie do their shopping in Upper Silesia thanks to their [the Silesians'] understanding of advertising. Incidentally, one must grant them that the service and treatment are exemplary, which must impress an intelligent person — while among us such an expense is looked upon with disdain. Among us people know that without a licence ["patent"] one may not open a business, but they do not want to know that both the advertisement and the aesthetics of the business are an enormous necessity in order to progress.
We have thus come to the conviction, and we indeed feel it on our own shoulders, that all branches of our livelihoods are exhausted: both the crafts and the merchant class are beaten down and shattered; moreover, we do not know what to do with our youth, because on the one hand it cannot make its way to studies, and on the other hand there is an enormous surplus in all the intellectual professions — so that, willy-nilly, the most practical thing would be for everyone to continue his enterprises with the help of his children.
Let the children be given a real training, let each study practically and theoretically — it will do no harm at all that he will be an intelligent merchant or tailor; it will be of use to him in life and in the profession. In this way we shall strengthen our positions, for which we truly have abilities; we shall then know how to guard with full piety that which was founded by our forefathers, and that will indeed also be our source of livelihood.
Incidentally, we have no other way out either, and actually we would not have needed one, because we need not be ashamed at all of our professions, if only we knew how to handle them and in what way to value them. What we shall not be able to achieve, our children will attain with the help of their theory and intelligence.
Let us not neglect [?] [printed "צוליגן"] the buildings that have already been erected; let us rather repair them [printed "רעפערירן"], rescue them so that they do not collapse, rather than distance ourselves from them completely, having and seeing before us no other way out and no better future.
— That is what one must remember in the present catastrophic time.
Spiders, Apes, or Adam?

[Satirical feuilleton — economic crisis and pedigree.]
(A conversation about our pedigree).
By reason and by history, we Jews all over the world ought not to be so downcast and so frightened and so desperate about a crisis.
About an economic crisis, I mean, because a spiritual crisis has always been hard for us to bear. A spiritual crisis means for us going „kaput“.
But an economic crisis is nothing new for us. We are already used to it, it seems, as to a good brother.
For when did Jews ever have full and good years? One must search with a candle to find some joyful[?] page in our history from all the lands!
Only the gentiles, precisely, who to this day do not know us, are forever fooling themselves and envying our Jewish „wealth“, so to speak!
All gentiles, regardless of language and land, have always thought that with every Jew whole chests of gold and silver lie somewhere in the cellar. And for that reason alone gentiles like so often to give the Jew a thrashing, in case a bit of gold should fall out of him.
The gentiles think many more things about us. They think that all the Jews in the whole world are one piece of „Israel“, with one counsel and one opinion.
And therefore, they believe, to this day one cannot discover any „secrets“ of the Jewish people, such as, for example, at least such a „trifle“ as taking „Christian blood for Passover, for the matzot“.
Go and tell them, the gentiles, that with us every Jew is a nation unto himself, and only rarely is one Jew in agreement with another, and there is never any peace among Jews, and if such foolish customs as „blood“ and others really existed, they would long ago have ceased to be secrets, and the Jews themselves would already have told them to the world!
And just as with unity, so it is with wealth among us.
We know very well, after all, that we never have any unity; and we also know very well that all our years we toil for a piece of bread.
There is no other people that must use so much wisdom and spend[?] so much time and effort and be so capable of playing the worst roles, — and all for that piece of bread.
Nothing more: we do have individual Jews who are indeed very rich; and as rich Jews like to make a noise in the world. They hate to hide their wealth in the ground, but want precisely to display it before the whole world in various ways, good and sometimes not good, fine and sometimes very nasty; and since the gentiles have a habit of blaming our whole people because of one Jew — that is how the legend of Jewish wealth came about.
But, as the saying goes, nobody knows where the shoe pinches except the one who wears it.
———
In short, my readers, we all know that „His Majesty Poverty“, who has today been crowned with a modern name, „economic crisis“, is with us Jewish children a frequent guest, a veritable resident from time immemorial, and we need not now be as sorrowful as we are.
The only difference is that our grandfathers and fathers swung poverty like a kapparot fowl [shook it off with contempt], they laughed at poverty and at their troubles together, they wanted to forget about it and meanwhile occupied themselves with higher things, and that is how they pushed their little world along.
Our grandfathers and fathers always found means to forget poverty. A misnaged immersed himself in study, and then the whole world with all its fortunes was not worth even an onion skin in his eyes. A hasid cleaved in devotion to a joyful melody with a little „tikkun“ [a drink], and then he simply went off to the heavens together with his rebbe's „ascent of the soul“, and what does he hear of the world?! A plain Jew refreshed himself with a simple chapter of Psalms, with a groan and with a tear, until he was truly revived; away with worries! A maskil lost himself in thought over the Haskalah, the „daughter of heaven“. A Zionist dreamed of Mother Zion and sang „Hatikvah“, a socialist put up proclamations and abandoned himself for the redemption of the world.
———
To what end, then, have I come to talk about all this? Precisely against[?] this: that I want to spare you a little of your talk about crisis and have a talk with you a little about science, that is, what science now says about our pedigree...
But be calm, do not be frightened, my friends, I do not want here to touch on the pedigree of my family, or of yours. Today family pedigree is worth nothing at all; on the contrary, precisely the home-grown aristocrats are in dire straits.
The only drawback is that pedigree has here been reincarnated in money. And the respect one pays today to the golden calf is a thousand times greater than that old home-grown respect for pedigree. With money you can buy today „what“ you want and „whom“ you want...
But, as said, I do not want to speak here about family pedigree, but about our human pedigree.
From whom do we humans come? What, then, is our pedigree?
I, actually, can be quite content with the explanation of the Humash, that we all descend from grandfather Adam and from grandmother Eve.
And I even have many proofs for it, precisely from his weaknesses:
First. Remember that Adam was the first citizen of the world. That is, the president of the globe. One would think: a whole „ja tobie dam“ [Polish: „I'll show you“], and along comes such a plain little woman as Eve, and dupes him, and gains mastery over him! Exactly like us, his very grandchildren.
We can be in the world the greatest big shots and sages and philosophers, — but to the Eves we are [sic] and must be foolish slaves, and we let them order us about...
But then Darwin came and said that our pedigree begins with the ape. Certainly not such an exalted pedigree, as you say. But that is how his science would have it.
And now in recent days, at a congress of scientists, a scholar came out with another theory and said that we actually draw our pedigree from certain kinds of spiders, that is, that both our little man, and the ape, and all other creatures descend from these very spiders!
And if you please, one can certainly find proofs for this too. For example: our little man indeed has in him the nature of a spider. The spider likes to snatch a weak fly in its paws and suck out of it the last drop of life... And our little man likewise; the stronger likes to hold the weaker in his paws and suck out of him as much as is at all possible.
And however much we fume and rebel[?] against these spidery tricks of ours, it is still hard to break the habit!
But, after all these proofs, I like neither the ape family nor the spider family, and I will by no means acknowledge them.
And the reason is simple: from those spidery and apish grandfathers we can learn nothing at all, and we will surely find no consolation for the present crisis, but from grandfather Adam we have much — much — to learn...
———
If you wish, my dear ones, that your heart grow lighter, remember that you descend from grandfather Adam; and that grandfather, when he was driven out of the Garden of Eden, went through a much greater crisis than yours, and he did not even, poor thing, have the luck to have such a „provider“ as our Citizens' Committee...
Try to reflect on our pedigree, and you will see that one need be neither a „spider“ nor an „ape“, but a human being!..
Pini Baal-Loshn.
Let There Be Darkness

[Essay — mood of the times.] By Y. Y. Sigal. (Mood of the times.)
I do not stop listening to the beat of events in our restless days, and intuitively I sense and hear an unceasing saying and murmuring, as if from beneath the earth: Let there be darkness — let it grow dark. We do not see him, the devil, who commands darkness. We do not know where, in which corner he has hidden himself and curses from there the world and man. Perhaps he has not hidden or concealed himself at all. He is in every corner, and from everywhere he looks out, and upon everything falls his curse of darkness. And so, slowly, he creeps into each one of us and puts out there every spark of light. We see it only in others. Here it has already grown dark in this corner of the world, and here in another. Here this or that people's leader has ducked down under the darkness and huddled under the black, protective wings of Ashmedai [?], and here another one. Little by little, little by little, darkness seeps into everything and everywhere where generations of geniuses kindled light. Great sufferings, endless torments were the oil that made the torches of light burn in the dark alleys of human life. We came onto the earth, set ourselves apart from the beast, moved out of the primitiveness of the forest — so we read, we the scientifically enlightened, we read the Bible and smile into our moustaches.
We left the forest and entered — the city, became civilized and turned into decent people. Then we went with the lantern of culture in hand, bent into the corners and cracks under beds and cupboards, and from everywhere drove out ignorance, obscurity and darkness. We became civilized, "refined"; the bathhouse goy and the doctor, the "prophet" and the simple man of the people — all of them pricked up long ears to the radio, which has almost brought heaven down to earth.
This estrangement, this turning of one's face away from the other — is what characterizes our time. We do not need to see before us the light of the human being, the beautiful, the high and the sublime: the person, the personality; we need only the material he gives out of himself. It is the narrow relationship we have to the ox, which we slaughter and whose blood and flesh we eat. We already have almost that same relationship to one another; earlier it was only in the material market, now we have carried it over into the spiritual one. We have handed over the spiritual, the beautiful, culture, to the merchant, to be a servant of the lawful swindler, of the politician. Our own "I" has become inferior in our own eyes. We do not want it. We want to spit it out of ourselves. These are hard words, but one must say them out loud at some point, one must write them down when one stops for a moment before the abyss of the events that encircle us. Just as one cries out in fright when one suddenly sees that a great disaster is rolling toward you and will crush you under its wheels — one sees a terrible darkness approaching and cries out: light. So Goethe cried out when he saw death approaching, when darkness began to obscure the world for him.
I sat in the cinema these days and saw and heard Mussolini speak to his crowd. I saw how he imitates a Napoleonic gesture, I saw how he sees Bonaparte's shadow before him and plays history as if before the mirror of a bygone epoch. I heard his mighty, iron Italian, and it became clear to me that this political Caruso knows man better than the Spinozist Einstein. He knows with what force one conquers the world. He has been in the chambers of civilization and knows [printed "rvis"] that it is all play and imitation of the genuine and natural. An outward play; so he too plays his false role — in Napoleonism [printed "Rapoleonism"], and — writes history. A chapter of history that tells how he undertook, in his own way, to kill off the personality, to harness human culture to a wagon of stones in order to build a new Caesarean Rome. How the muscles of his face trembled with that "great" dream of his as he spoke and said his "strong" word to the powerless world.
And — the darkness draws ever nearer and its shadow falls on the still distant, rescued positions that the man of the spirit still guards with such trembling piety. And if an unjust, cruel war brought bloody revolutions, both together will bring a world civil war. The talked-up, pointless hatred of people against people, country against country, will be transformed into a real and perhaps just hatred of man against man.
For the bitter day is drawing near when we shall truly be guilty toward one another. It will become such a two-times-two-is-four reckoning that we will be guilty to one another — a brother, a sister, a father. We are guilty of it already now, for a long time already, only we have so far kept our conscience on a chain. We have stuffed its mouth with political bones. But it will wake up in us with burning eyes and with inflamed blood, and no false justifications will hold before it.
The whole matter of belief in God is, at its deep core, belief in man; the religious, the mystical, the legendary — is the light that burns and shines with the power of the reality-naphtha. It has been made into an all-too-earthly reckoning, and the sun has been forgotten... One makes a materialist balance-sheet of history and does not understand its meaning — — —
Ford's mission is to make of man a — horse, a little machine on four little wheels that hurries over stone-paved streets and must reach as quickly as possible the village of — meaninglessness.
Let there be darkness! Let it be dark, put out the soul in man, and let the devil carry it off on his shoulder into those spheres and to those people who believed in it and foretold to man a bright day.
In 2 Corridors

[Feuilleton — satire.]
The Polish ambassador to America, a gentleman in a top hat, a dinner jacket and a pair of white gloves, stood in the corridor of the “White House” in Washington.
Chaim Moshe the grocer from Zawale Street, a little Jew in a worn-out[?] coat and twisted shoes, stood in the corridor of the tax office on First of May Street.
The ambassador could not go in to President Hoover right away, because ambassadors of other states stood ahead of him, and he had to take his place in the queue.
Chaim Moshe the grocer also could not slip in to the tax chief (naczelnik), because other grocers stood ahead of him, so he had to take his place in the queue.
An ambassador into Hoover’s room, an ambassador out of Hoover’s room.
The other ambassadors asked those coming out of the room whether one could get anything out of Hoover, and what sort of mood he was in?
A grocer into the tax chief’s room, a grocer out of the room. The other grocers asked those coming out of the room whether one could get anything out of the chief, and what sort of mood he was in?
After standing a couple of hours before the door, the Polish ambassador’s turn came, and he went in on tiptoe to Hoover’s room.
— What did you want?
— I wanted to ask the honoured American President to postpone the instalment for me, 10 million dollars, which I must pay today, the 15th. I am simply not able to give such a sum of money. The crisis is severe, unemployment is great, so how can one take 10 million dollars out of the treasury today?
— Yes, it really is not good at all, — says Hoover — everyone is badly off, but pay one must. Meanwhile pay something in, and afterwards we will talk about postponing the instalments.
After standing a couple of hours before the door, the turn came to Chaim Moshe the grocer, and he went in on tiptoe to the chief’s room.
— What did you want?
— I wanted to ask the honoured tax chief to postpone my tax instalment, 10 złoty, which I must pay on the 15th. I cannot take such a sum out of my little shop, the crisis is severe, there are no takings, my children are unemployed, so how can one give 10 zł. today out of the poor till-drawer?
— Yes, it really is not good at all — says the chief — everyone is badly off, but pay one must. Meanwhile pay something in, and afterwards we will talk about postponing the instalments.
Everyone is badly off, but Chaim Moshe the grocer is evidently worse off than his “colleague” the ambassador, who also comes to ask for an instalment to be postponed.
To Chaim Moshe the tax chief can send the “wagon” [the bailiff’s cart] to take away his last belongings, but Hoover surely won’t send a “wagon” across the ocean to Europe...
Why should the ambassador be afraid? That I do not understand.
Yosef.
Because of the Critical Times

[Advertisement — calendar.]
Everyone knows, after all, that one must make reductions, one must save and cut back on every expense, because in times like these every grosz counts.
Our friend Igelsztajn is an expert at calculating, so for the year 1932 he bought some calendar a few groszy cheaper; but because of that he is now saying for the tenth time[?] that one has to know what to save on, because saving a few groszy on an article one needs for daily use does not really pay, taking into account the defects and inaccuracies he has run into all year with the calendar he bought; therefore our friend Igelsztajn has come to the conviction that one should buy only a proper branded calendar, which is published right here in Zagłębie and bears the name Zaglembier Calendar “Di Vokh” [“The Week”].
Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.
The statutes are already here...
It was at the time when the barns had been filled with fresh grain and the townspeople had already come back from their summer-cottage (dacha) resorts, that among some Sosnowiec public figures the idea ripened
— to create a "Beit Lechem" [a "House of Bread"].
So meetings were called, generous hearts responded — how could it be otherwise[?]: in such a hard time, when the number of the impoverished grows from day to day, when families who still live in big apartments go hungry, one surely may not sit quietly, may not be indifferent and stop one's ears so as not to hear the tones of lament; and unanimously, all with one voice, it was resolved
— to create a "Beit Lechem".
Sosnowiec, however, does not possess the kind of activists who believe in "saying and doing". The Sosnowiec public figures never hurry when it comes to matters of mitzvah. There is a theory:
It is because of the Sosnowiec people that our Sages of blessed memory did not institute a blessing over acts of kindness and charity — for the pious man, to whom one came about a matter of charity or kindness, would first run off to the mikveh, and the non-pious one would hold Tarpat [689] thousand meetings over the proposal, until
— until the needy man's soul had expired..
Such a fate has also befallen the plan to found the institution named — "Beit Lechem". They, the initiators, are not worried; meanwhile the crisis has grown stronger and seizes new positions, and when the registered applicants come to them with the question:
— When at last? When will the institution finally start operating?
they are answered with words of comfort, that there is not long to wait now, because
— the statutes are already here...
—o—
For a piece of bread..
This takes place one morning at the Old Market [in Będzin].
On the spot where the "Golden Drop" once used to drip, all is hush-quiet, a living cemetery, where several times a day a scene from "At Night in the Old Market" [I. L. Peretz's play] is performed...
The scene takes place up high, on the first floor. The actors, without make-up, come out on a balcony and the "play" begins...
— May you croak like a dog...
— May an R... grow on you...
— You'll die without a shroud
— An evil sickness on your head.
And when the repertoire of rebuke and of one's own composition has been exhausted, there is a pause, and the "spectators"
— applaud...
And as I watched this sad scene, I thought that the leading role here is played by someone whom our rulers do not want to see or to know — namely
— Jewish want...
Like hungry wolves the merchants lie in wait to snatch a customer; let him out of your hand for a moment — and he never comes back.
And the upshot?
Jews stand on the balconies and curse one another with vehement curses — over what?
— Over a piece of bread...
—o—
Times of reduction...
The clock at the Będzin railway station is already getting old. It was never a great creature to begin with; rarely, very rarely did it happen that the clock did not suffer from "constipation", but lately it has been taking really big "rests" ("odpoczynki") and stopping for several days...
When I drew my neighbour's attention to it, he told me that apparently I had forgotten that we live in times of reduction, so the clock too has reduced its working hours.
2 days it runs and 4 days it stands — that's enough for Będzin.
Do the factories and the mines run properly, then?
— Times of reduction...
—o—
4 for 10 groszy...
A cry from a child's little throat cutting through the air.
And at once a small boy with black eyes stands before you, in whom you see the tragedy of our present time: torn little shoes, in his hands a box of toffees ("iris")
— 4 for 10 groszy...
And the little peddler tells you — the cry [sic] — of an unemployed father, of a sick mother, of a cold, poor home, of months of hunger and want, of a home with children waiting for the little peddler's profit..
A young little soul is telling you this, one whom fate has prematurely thrown into the cauldron of suffering, a little soul that grows up before its time, and you feel the poison that penetrates into its heart, and you see at once how the soul of a child grows old
— 4 toffees for 10 groszy..
He carries them around to sell for the sake of other people's pleasure.. he offers sweet, cheap wares, and he himself is hungry...
I want to chat a little longer with this little breadwinner, but he is in a hurry: one has to — he says — run, sell the box, take fresh ones and sell again. One has to, one must after all earn something
— 4 toffees for 10 groszy..
We Are Being Smothered with a Kiss...

[Opinion — taxes and the Jews.] We Are Being Smothered with a Kiss...
— Help, the taxes! Help, they are smothering us with a kiss!
That is now the cry that resounds from all sides in the Jewish business world in Poland.
That is also the cry of the Jewish taxpayer in general.
The "innocent" emissary of the tax office — the sequestrator [bailiff, sekwestrator] — is now the terror of the tax-paying population. A terror that before the War nobody knew of.
Before the War it was the policeman who came to the taxpayer to demand the tax, and if he was given no money, because there was none, he drew up a protocol: "That the person assessed has nothing to pay with, and with that the matter was over.
Today's tax collector wears no police uniform, but his power when demanding the tax is, for that, much greater. If you have nothing to pay with, he is not content with a protocol alone: he simply writes down your things [for distraint] and then even carts them off to the tax office.
His power goes further still: he has the right to enter the bedroom at night and search the pockets and the drawers.
Today the taxpayer is not looked upon as an oppressed man who cannot pay. Such a thing is not even imagined. He is looked upon as a malicious criminal who can — but will not pay.
And with such a man one does not stand on ceremony; such a person may be visited even in the middle of the night, even on his day of rest.
Nobody investigates his situation. If he does not pay on time, one sees in it not a sign of inability but, on the contrary, further proof that he is a "rich man — a swine," and at once interest is charged and a heavy fine is imposed on him, several times as large as the tax itself.
That is how the tax offices work here.
The taxpayer is turned, poor as he is, into a Canaanite slave [an utter bondsman] of the tax office: he has not yet paid off the principal, and already "peni" [late-payment penalty] is growing on it, and already he must pay an instalment of the "kara" [fine], and the "penia" goes on growing.
The taxpayer can never pay himself out, because he is looked upon as a "rich man, a swine," from whom one must tear, and the more the better [the greater the mitzvah].
And one suddenly remembers that tax is due from him from as much as eight years back, and one digs up debts from years ago of which the taxpayer himself has no idea, and payment orders [nakazy] are sent in even for the year 1924.
People here keep shouting about putting an end to tax arrears [zaległe], but it is a voice crying in the wilderness.
And one gets the impression that they are always looking for new sources, always digging up new springs from which to draw money, because for the later years they have already squeezed the money out of the taxpayer.
And it goes so far that even children's little bits of furniture are listed for distraint.
Nothing is taken into account any more. The sequestrators have an order: money! And they must procure the money, deliver it!...
Of course taxes must be paid; that is the means by which the citizen sustains the state and fulfils his duty towards it. Nobody has anything against that, nobody disputes it.
But the way it is done here, indirectly [?], with respect to the Jewish taxpayer is a model not to be seen in any country in the world.
The citizen has been turned into a little money machine which must, day and night, on Sabbath and holidays and even on Sunday, deliver such-and-such a quantum of money. He lives in sheer terror of the sequestrator. What feelings can accumulate in such a citizen, other than bitterness?
The citizen has nothing else to think about but the sequestrator: here he comes — and where will one find the few guilders [złoty] for him — not tax, but interest or fine money.
The citizen is turned into a little calculating machine: day and night he must keep books, keep accounts with the tax office, perhaps buy "iron chests [safes] for his receipts [?]. So that he [the collector] should not demand a second time. Guard his payment orders. In short, he must live not for himself, not for his wife and children, not for his shop and his business — but for the tax office.
The citizen has been turned into an eternal "liar." When he says he has nothing to pay with, he is not believed. When he says he is a poor man, his words are given no credence. When he says he earns less, that means he is cheating.
That is how one looks today upon the pride of the state — upon the citizen.
Not to mention when it concerns the Jewish taxpayer.
And on top of that it is demanded that, as a result of such treatment, we should nevertheless not cry out, that we should nevertheless be content and quiet, like a kitten.
We are to keep silent even when we are being economically smothered with a kiss.
But silence too has its limit!
A. Y.
The Law on Associations

[Poland — legislation: the Associations Law.] The Law on Associations.
On the first of January [styczeń] 1933 the law of 27.X [19]32 on associations comes into force, replacing the decree of 3.I 1919 that has been binding until now.
The new law introduces very important changes into the regulations in force until now, standardises the registration procedure, and tightens control over all associations, which must adapt themselves to the new regulations if they wish to go on existing.
The first part of the law provides that only adults from the age of 18 may belong to associations. School youth may not belong to associations.
Under Art. 6, political associations may not conduct any gymnastic or sporting activity.
Trade [professional] associations of employees do not fall under the law, but they must fulfil certain formalities of the law: such as reporting to the administrative authority the composition of their boards and other information about their activity.
The new law provides for 3 categories of associations:
a) ordinary — which may be founded by a minimum of 3 persons on the basis of a written application to the starosta [district head] — and statutes.
b) registered — which may be founded by a minimum of 15 persons on the basis of a statute, which must be registered.
Under Art. 20 the registering authority (the voivode [provincial governor]) has the right to refuse to register an association if it finds that there is a danger to public security, peace or order, and also when the authority finds that the registration of the association in question is not in the interest of public benefit...
Every registered association must have a board capable of legal action; otherwise the authority has the right to appoint, on its own initiative or at the request of an interested person, a curator for the association.
General control over associations has been considerably tightened.
c) Associations of higher public utility are recognised and approved by the Council of Ministers and receive their statute officially. To these associations, which can receive various privileges and special rights, minors and school youth may belong.
Contravening the provisions of the law, or the demands of the authority, as well as failing to fulfil them, is punished by administrative procedure with a fine of up to 500 zł.
R. Rechtman.
Commercial Books. What Are the Economic Organisations Doing?

[Economy — commercial bookkeeping.] Commercial Books.
What are the economic organisations doing?
The question of keeping commercial books has now caused great confusion in merchant and shopkeeper circles.
In the new Penal Code there is a paragraph which says that if it is proved that someone does not keep commercial books, while he is obliged by law to keep books, he is punished with 2 years' imprisonment.
The commercial law still in force here dates from Russian times; it contains instructions on the keeping of commercial books. The Russian law explains that the mode of bookkeeping is divided into 3 categories. But the Polish law on the division of the patents [trade licences] into categories is entirely different from the division in the Russian law, and therefore chaos now reigns in this field. Even lawyers are still splitting hairs over it. The question will probably be clarified by a circular from the Finance Ministry.
For the broad mass of shopkeepers and merchants, however, the matter of keeping books is still entirely foreign; they do not know where to begin. If the law on bookkeeping comes into force from the New Year, the necessary preparations surely have to be made already now.
In several larger towns the economic organisations have held consultations on this and have opened instruction courses for shopkeepers.
We think that in Zagłębie too there ought to be a meeting of the economic organisations with the participation of lawyers. Courses for shopkeepers should also be arranged on the model of other towns.
Why does such passivity reign over this painful question for every shopkeeper, merchant and manufacturer?
Y. R.

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayetze

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Vayetze and its Haftarah.] The portion.
A) "And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee whithersoever thou goest" (28:15)
"The Rabbis said: He answered him on everything, but on livelihood He did not answer him. Said R. Isso [sic]: He answered him on livelihood too, as it is said: 'For I will not leave thee.'" Midrash Rabbah.
When God answered Jacob "For I will not leave thee" — that He would not forsake him, that Jacob would always be with God — that is also an answer concerning livelihood, because if one has no livelihood, one is not with God either... "Poverty makes a man transgress the will of his Maker." Beit Shmuel Aharon.
B) "And he lighted upon the place" (ibid., 11)
"Vayifga" — he prayed there. (Hullin 91)
Rabbi Eliezer Yitzhak, son-in-law of Rabbi Itchele of Volozhin [Wołożyn], saw one of the yeshiva students praying hastily, and he admonished him: one must pray slowly and with devotion — at the very least the way one counts money.
The student gets clever and answers:
— To what may the matter [print: "adabber"] be compared? To a man driving a wagon. If he drives slowly, all sorts of urchins [shkotsim] grab hold of the wagon. But if he drives fast, the urchins don't manage to jump on. So too with praying. When one prays slowly, all the stray thoughts grab hold of him, but when one prays fast, they don't manage to catch hold of him.
Rabbi Eliezer Yitzhak replies:
— But I am afraid that you drive so fast that even the single urchin — you... doesn't manage to jump onto the wagon...
—o—
The Holy Jew used to pray fast. The "Seer" asks him: Why do you hurry so in your prayer?
— Because I love praying, so I grab it and swallow it.
— But I too love praying — the "Seer" asks again — why don't I swallow it?
— Because — the Holy Jew answers sharply — your praying is fire, and swallowing fire, one gets burned...
C) "Bread to eat, and raiment to put on" (ibid., 20)
What else is bread for, if not to eat, and raiment, if not to put on?
But indeed, sometimes a person uses his raiment "to eat" — he pawns it for bread; and sometimes a person indeed has bread, which he uses to sell for medicines. So our father Jacob prayed not to come to that.. Nahalei Dvash.
D) "So that I come back to my father's house in peace" (ibid., 21)
Whole from sin. Rashi.
From where does Rashi infer that "peace" means "from sin"? Because, following the wording of the verse "and will give me bread to eat," it should also have said "and bring me back in peace" (vehashivani), not "so that I come back" (veshavti). It must be, then, that here piety is meant; therefore Jacob could not say "vehashivani," because piety depends not on God but on oneself alone. "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven." Matteh Moshe.
E) "I will surely give the tenth unto Thee" (ibid., 22)
The Patriarchs, our Sages say, observed the whole Torah, even eruv tavshilin. Yet we do not find the Torah telling of a single commandment of the Patriarchs other than the commandment of tithing. Because giving charity is indeed a greater feat than all the commandments that require no money... Imrei Hen.
—o—
"I will surely give the tenth unto Thee" — because [if one gives on the principle of] "tithe so that you may become rich," or gives charity by calculation, it will be only "I will give the tenth unto me" — for my own sake; but it must be "unto Thee" — for the sake of the commandment, without calculation. Tiferet Yehonatan.
—o—
There are two pieces of advice for getting rich:
"Tithe so that you may become rich" (Shabbat 111 [as printed])
and "Honour your wives and you will become rich" (Bava Metzia 59).
For if one honours one's wife and follows her stinginess ("a woman begrudges guests"), giving no charity and helping no one, one can also become rich... But it is better to acquire the same riches through "tithe so that you may become rich" — through charity itself... Lahmei Todah.
F) "So he fled with all that he had" (31:21)
Jacob does not simply leave the land abroad — he flees, because abroad, together with Laban's household, the Shekhinah cannot rest upon Jacob. Midrash.
G) "Wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?" (ibid., 30)
The teraphim used to tell Laban everything; so[?] he thought that Jacob had stolen them, because, stealing silver and gold, he had to take the teraphim along too, so that they would not tell Laban...
Like that thief who robbed the tavern [kretchme] and had to steal the horses as well, so that there would be nothing to chase him with... Kiflayim le-Tushiyah.
The Haftarah.
H) "For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just do walk in them; but transgressors do stumble therein" (Hosea 14:10 [print: "yr"])
There is good food that tastes good only to the healthy; the sick it makes ill... "Transgressors stumble therein" — because they are not healthy, therefore the ways of the Lord harm them. Kokhav mi-Yaakov[?].
Jewish Personalities: Rashi

[Children's page — Jewish personalities.]
In the Children's World.
A special section of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" for our little ones
compiled by Sh. Libaszon [?].
—o—
Jewish Personalities.
Rashi.
2.
One of the greatest personalities of the Jewish people was the great scholar Rabbenu Shlomo Yitzhak [sic; = Shlomo Yitzhaki], Rashi, who created his commentary on the Talmud, the Bible, etc.
Those who write Hebrew know that Rashi was the one who created the Hebrew language and its style.
There were even others who tried to create a commentary on the Talmud. But no one succeeded with such a commentary except Rashi. He was a great pedagogue, possessed of great pedagogical abilities to teach the people, one of the greatest men of learning, whose equal we do not find in our theological literature.
Rashi himself was very plain; he did not show off his learning and used to flee from honours. He hid himself away in a corner, so that no one should know of him and he could do his work quietly and modestly.
But the great world nevertheless sought out the giant of the generation and recognised him as one of the greatest scholars of Jewish learning.
From Italy, France and Germany letters reached him with various questions, and Rashi studied everything thoroughly and gave each his answer, which was always a satisfying one.
Rashi came from a very distinguished family on both sides. He was born in Troyes ("Triver") in 1040.
He received his learning in the yeshivas of Germany, where he was a constant attendant of Torah scholars.
After Rashi had finished serving the scholars in the various yeshivas, he returned home to his birthplace, where he took up the post of preacher. He was one of the greatest lovers of peace, always thinking about peace for the people.
Rashi died in the year 1105.
The Pious Man and the Robbers

[Children's page — story.]
Once a pious man was walking through a forest from one town to another. He was carrying money with him. When he came to a place where the forest was very dense, two robbers with axes stopped him and threatened to kill him if he did not give them the money.
The pious man answered:
— I am not afraid of death, for everything is decreed by God; but to keep you from a sin I am giving you all the money, and I give you my word that I have no more.
The robbers went off into the forest with the money, and the man went on his way.
Without meaning to, he felt his pocket and found a złoty there — and he, the pious man, had given his word that he had no more.
Quickly he turned around and ran back to where the robbers had gone. He soon caught up with them and, handing them the złoty, he said:
— Here is a złoty, which I did not hand over to you.
The robbers were deeply ashamed before the man's piety, and after they had given him everything back down to the last grosz, they swore never to be robbers again.
Yakov Altshuler.

Milk

[Children's page — health.]
Milk makes big people out of little children. In the Austrian "Youth Red Cross" we read the following lines by a well-known doctor:
"You would surely like to grow big soon, children? Big and grown-up? Then there is nothing better than drinking milk. Do you know that little newborn babies drink nothing but milk; anything else they cannot tolerate at all. You, of course, can already eat and digest everything; but milk can nevertheless be of great use to you.
There is a definite reason for this: milk contains almost all the nutrients the body needs. Namely: proteins, fats, carbohydrates, water, vitamins and mineral salts, even calcium too, which is needed to strengthen the children [sic; perhaps 'the bones'].
The way these nutrients are present in milk makes it easy to digest, that is: the intestines absorb it, pass it into the blood, and in this way all the substances reach the cells and tissues. Only iron is absent from milk, and it is needed to strengthen the red blood corpuscles. That is why you eat green vegetables or fruit, because they contain iron. The fluid of the milk flushes thoroughly through the whole body.
("Dos Kind")
On Learning Yiddish and Jewish History

[Children's page — children's letters.]
When I was little I was, unfortunately, not interested in learning Yiddish. But when I got a bit older I found out that the language is very beautiful and that it is the language of all my own people, and I began to learn Yiddish.
Now I am also learning Jewish history, which is very interesting. I am getting acquainted with my ancestors and how they lived in olden times. Many of the things are indeed only legends, but in the histories of other peoples too there are many legends.
In any case, the Yiddish language and Jewish history are very interesting. And a Jewish child who learns other languages and foreign histories must surely know the Yiddish language and the history of our parents and ancestors.

Once There Was a Water-Man...

[Children's corner — story.]
(A story written especially for Zagłębie children)
By Leyzer Shikman.

Grandma Rokhl loved us, her grandchildren, very much. And we, her grandchildren, used to repay Grandma Rokhl in the same coin.

We children used to spend a great deal of time at Grandma's house. A kind of loving closeness bound us to one another; so dear to us were her presence and everything around her in the house: the little kitchen cupboard with the neatly arranged flowered plates, the earthenware and iron pots; Grandpa's little tinsmith's workshop with all sorts of tools and implements; the broken ottoman on which Grandma used to sit, her footstool, the little bookcase of holy books, the portraits of good Jews, and, in wintertime, the little iron stove under whose ashes potatoes were roasted for us children.

All of this drew us to Grandma Rokhl's house as if by a magnet...

Grandpa Hirshl too was fond of us; every year before Purim each of us received from him a Haman-clapper [grager] that he had made himself, also[?] dreidels for Hanukkah and little money-boxes for saving money — and, of course, Grandpa was the first to drop a groszy into each and every box, which at the same time already counted as Hanukkah gelt too.

Nevertheless, we loved Grandma Rokhl much more than our grandfather, because Grandma loved to chat with everyone, whoever it might be — believe it or not, it is all the same; she hated silence. "Silence," she used to say, "is for a stone, not for a human being."

Grandpa, on the other hand, was by nature a silent man, a man who hated talking. That is exactly why Grandma called him by a nickname: "M-r-u-k" [Polish: grump, a man of few words], and he, Grandpa, in turn called Grandma: "M-a-t-l-e-r-i-n" [chatterbox]...

Grandma Rokhl was a great master at telling stories. When she told a tale, it had to come with all the little frills.

She had a great treasure-chamber of every imaginable little tale: she told of demons, spirits and "not-good ones," of the World to Come, reward and punishment, or of Elijah the Prophet disguised as a patriarch or a beggar.

We children liked Grandma's little tales so much that even at night, in our dreams, we used to live through them anew.

Once — it was on a winter's day — it was delightfully warm at Grandma and Grandpa's house. Grandpa sat beside the red-hot little stove with his elbows on his knees, and we children sat around Grandma, who said:

"Well, children, now say good night and off home in good health; tomorrow, God willing, come back here again, and there will be new tales."

But for us, as always, it was hard to part from our Grandma; it was as if we were inside a magic circle in her presence.

We began to plead:

"Grandma dear, our crown, tell us just one more single little tale, and then we'll go home."

"All right," she agreed, with a gentle smile, "just one more little tale I'll tell you." And she promptly asked:

"Have you ever heard the tale of a... w-a-t-e-r-m-a-n?"

"No," we all cried out with one voice, "we've never heard such a tale."

"This tale happened in the town of Będzin," Grandma began, and her old eyes took on a youthful sparkle (for whenever she mentioned the town of Będzin she mentioned it with such holy reverence as if she were — to make a distinction — speaking of Jerusalem). "It was many, many years ago. My grandmother — that is, children, your great-great-grandmother, may she rest in Paradise — was living in Będzin then, and she used to stand, Grandma did, in the Old Market with tinware that my grandfather, may he rest in peace, your great-great-grandfather, had made himself: watering cans, graters, mugs, carbide lamps, lanterns and similar things of that kind.

One time — it was a market day — my grandmother had sold her bit of merchandise and went home joyfully to eat the hot meal Grandpa had brought her. But something terrible happened: as soon as she put her hand into the money-bag in which lay the whole day's market takings, she saw, to her great misfortune, that instead of money she had a bag full of... s-c-a-l-e-s!..."

Grandma Rokhl looked at us with great wide-open eyes, giving her last word a mysterious meaning.

"Another time," Grandma Rokhl went on, "it was a Friday afternoon. Some Będzin boys had, as usual, gathered at the Przemsza river to bathe in honour of the Sabbath. It happened that right by the water's edge there stood a lantern that my grandfather, may he rest in Paradise, used to make himself. Well, one of them went right up to the bank where the lantern had been set. The other boys, suspecting nothing at all, stayed standing a little further off.

But at that moment, when the boy reached for the lantern, in the blink of an eye there suddenly came out of the water a figure that looked partly like a man, partly like a fish, and on top of that had a long tail as well.

This strange man-fish figure seized the unfortunate boy by the throat and vanished with him beneath the water.

Of course, the other boys, frightened to death, ran at once into town with heart-shaking wails, announcing the terrible news of a water-man who had lured an unfortunate victim into his net...

And it was then, on that fateful Friday, that it became clear to everyone why in that money-bag, instead of the money that had been put in, there had turned out to be — scales! Because, you must understand, children," Grandma Rokhl went on to finish her story, "the water-man himself used to come to the market disguised as a person, in order to buy up various objects with which he dazzled his victims, for year in, year out he had to take one for himself."

Grandpa Hershl [sic; earlier "Hirshl"] suddenly woke up, startled by the racket we rascals made as we left the house, and began scolding Grandma Rokhl, the chatterbox...

———

What's New in Zagłębie?
Będzin
Cantor Żupowicz Wins His Lawsuit Against the Kehilla Administration.

[Page header: "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 50, page 7; Friday 9 December 1932 / 10 Kislev 5693.]
On Tuesday, for the third time, the Sosnowiec District Court heard the case against the local kehilla administration, which had been sued by the former cantor Mr. Żupowicz with a claim that it pay him the pension owed to him and 6 months' compensation.
After hearing the witnesses — the Dozór [kehilla board president] Mr. A. Liwer and the secretary Mr. Frejlich — the court upheld Mr. Żupowicz's claim.

Brazen Attack on Zawale Street.
140 zł Stolen.

On Monday at 6 in the evening, as Mrs. Chawa Szenberg [?] was walking along Zawale Street, several persons ran up to her and tried to tear from her the handbag in which there were 140 zł.
When Mrs. Sz. defended herself, one of the attackers struck her hand and gave a yank, and only then did they succeed in carrying out the attack.
The "Unwanted Shochet" Is to Be Given the Post of Ne'eman...

As we are informed, official circles have approached the shochet Mr. Yechezkel Wajcman asking him to stop the "illegal slaughter"; in return he would be appointed ne'eman [supervisor].
Mr. Wajcman rejected the proposal.
Applications for Patent Discounts.
The Small Traders' Association asks us to point out that the deadline for applications to benefit from the discount on [trade-tax] patents for the coming year ends on the 15th of this month.
Departure of a Group of Young People by Car to Eretz Israel.

The report in our paper that on Sunday at 8.30 a group of young people would leave by car for Eretz Israel aroused enormous interest among all strata of the local Jewish population. Already from 8 o'clock crowds streamed to the starting point at "Hakoach" on Kościuszki Street, from which the departure took place. But owing to the poor organization the departure took place with an hour's delay, which caused strong dissatisfaction among the large crowd assembled.
Dr. Rosenfeld's visit to Będzin.

[Będzin — Zionism — sport.] Last week the vice-president of the Maccabi World Union, Dr. Rosenfeld, stayed in Będzin. On the first day the distinguished guest gave a short lecture in the hall of the "Merchants' Association" on the significance of "Kfar Maccabi". On the second day a consultation was held with the board of "Hakoah"; the "Hakoah" orchestra was also presented to him, and Dr. Rosenfeld promised it would take part in the Winter Olympiad in Zakopane. Afterwards the board, together with Dr. Rosenfeld, was received for tea at the home of Dr. Rechtschaft [?], where they spent time until late at night.
On the third day an impressive academy (gala) took place in the packed hall of "WIZO", where the lecturer Dr. Rosenfeld spoke at length on the significance of sport and of "Kfar Maccabi".
A windowpane smashed.

[Będzin — violence / police.] On Monday evening a young Christian smashed a pane of the shop window of Mr. Kupczyk's store on Kołłątaja Street. When the owner of the shop tried to detain the Christian, he fired a shot, as a result of which a panic broke out in the street. The policeman who arrived took the "hero" off to the police station (commissariat).
A ball of Jewish academics.

[Będzin — society — ball.] On the 31st of this month the Jewish academics in Będzin are holding a grand ball in the splendid reception halls of the Jewish gymnasium named after [?] Mr. S. Fürstenberg. The ball, which falls on the last day of Hanukkah, will be a real attraction for all lovers of dancing and entertainment. A special orchestra from Katowice is being engaged.
1½ wagons of rye flour for poor Jews.

[Będzin — relief for the poor.] Thanks to the efforts of the guardian (opiekun) Mr. A. D. Bolimowski [?], the Citizens' Committee at the local magistrate (town council) gave one and a half wagonloads of rye flour, which was distributed among the poor Jewish population.
Shooting on Modrzejowska Street.

[Będzin — police / violence.] On Saturday night two persons came up to one of the plain-clothes (secret) police, began to pick on the policeman and later also started to beat him. The plain-clothes policeman, defending himself against the assailants, first fired into the air, but seeing that this did not help, he shot at the assailants and seriously wounded them.
The post office as debt collector.

[Będzin / general — post — economy.] A new scheme is being prepared that will allow smaller sums of money to be collected through the post office. Any interested party who wishes to collect from his debtor a sum not exceeding 30 zł. will be able to buy a form for 30 groszy, state the sum and the debtor's address, and the post office will then collect the money and hand it over to the interested party. This reform will be of great significance for businesses that trade on instalments. The scheme, which is to be put into effect from the New Year, will take the wheat bread [i.e. the livelihood] away from a whole series of debt collectors.
Premises for a kitchen for the children of Public School No. 8.

[Będzin — welfare & schools.] The several notices in our paper addressed to the local Magistrate concerning the provision of premises for a kitchen for the poor children of Public School No. 8 have had the proper effect. A suitable room is being given over in the premises of “Piast”, and from next week the children will already be receiving breakfasts and lunches.
The Tenants’ Association rises for the “resurrection of the dead”..

[Będzin — organisations.] Next Sunday the local “Tenants’ Association” is calling a larger meeting, at which the question of reviving the “Tenants’ Association” will be discussed — something that is an urgent necessity at the present moment. It is desirable that those who have been invited should come to the meeting.
Keren Kayemet evening at WIZO.
[Będzin — Zionism.] On the 25th of this month, the second day of Hanukkah, the local women’s organisation “WIZO” is holding its traditional evening in aid of the Keren Kayemet [Jewish National Fund].
Sosnowiec: The “angels of peace” at the budget session of the Sosnowiec Kehilla Council.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] On Sunday morning the local kehilla council met in session for the purpose of fixing the new kehilla budget. In the presence of 13 councillors and a large number in the gallery, the vice-president Mr L. Szwajcer opened the session and read out the agenda.
Before the order of the day the floor was taken by councillor Mr Dawid Zylberberg, who complained about the state of the kehilla and proposed that a rabbinical commission be elected to bring about peace in our kehilla, and that the budget be postponed for the time being.
The proposal was supported by councillors Messrs Chaim Dancyger, Unger and others.
Against the proposal spoke board member (dozór) Mr Nachemja. “One can talk of peace,” he said, “only when the vanquished comes to beg for it; but when the peace is comparable to one of the ‘Pińczów wisdoms’ — we cannot take it into consideration.”

The “Kurier Zachodni” Does Not Like the Jewish Officials in the League of Nations
(From the Polish press)

[Press review — antisemitism.]
Having stopped inciting for a while after the recent sad student events in the larger Polish cities, our local antisemitic organ of the Endecja [National Democrats], the well-known (from the advertisements of the Jewish national firms) “Kurier Zachodni”, has taken on the handful of Jewish officials in the League of Nations.
Under the title [?] “It did not work out with Mr. Rajchman”, the writer of the article wants by every means to discredit the three Jewish officials who work in the Polish [staff of the] Secretariat at the League of Nations.
Here is what is written:
“In the Secretariat of the League of Nations Poland has only five officials in higher positions, of whom three belong to the Jewish race. We did not use the opportunity at the last reorganization of the bureau at the League of Nations to increase in this way the share of Polish citizens among the officials.”
“The tactic which our delegation adopted was a fatal one. The effort was concentrated entirely in the direction of obtaining the post of [deputy?] Secretary-General for Dr. Rajchman, a native of Warsaw, who holds the post of director of the Hygiene [Health] Section at the Secretariat of the League.”
In the further part of the article it is related that, despite the fact that Dr. Rajchman is a well-known personality in international spheres, his election was a fatal one, because “Mr. Rajchman has fallen out with the opinion of the Catholics of the whole world; namely, in the spring and summer of this year the official organ of the Vatican, ‘Osservatore Romano’, published several articles in which the personal activity of Mr. Rajchman is censured as contrary to moral and Catholic principles. The reason for this is that in a report prepared by the Hygiene Section and signed by Mr. Rajchman there is a sentence which means using means against births.”
That is the whole sin which Dr. Rajchman committed, and the article ends:
“We would surely have had greater success if instead of Jews we had put forward the Catholic character of Poland.
It is high time to break off the harmful sympathies.”
It appears that all the hate articles against Jews — including the appeal in bold type of the “Rozwój” not to buy from Jews, which is printed every day — do not help at all (proof: the Jewish advertisements, even those about memorial services [azkaras] at the Jewish cemetery, are printed on the other side, after the “Rozwój” appeal) — so be it: when it does not go on the internal front, they turn to the foreign front...
S. Szach.

The truth about the new kehilla budget in Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — Community.] Esteemed Editors! Allow me to print in your esteemed paper the following reply to the so-called President of the Council, Mr. Liberman, regarding his letter in "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 50 about the Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] kehilla budget.

1) It is true that the majority of the Board outvoted me at the first meeting and set the budget at 126,935 zł., of which the staff establishment [etat] at 62,195 zł., because the majority of the Board was against my proposal to reduce the officials' pensions. The same thing happened when I presented my reduction proposals at the Council plenum: the Council, too, would not agree to them, for other reasons — because, under the deal over the president's chair, the craftsmen had to be paid off with a subsidy of 4.500 zł. Nor could any injustice be done to the officials, since most of them are, after all, Krymilów [?] Hasidim... And the upshot was that the Jewish population ended up burdened with a staff establishment of 36 000 zł. It goes without saying that the assessment was bound up with great and unpleasant difficulties, and I sent the budget back to the Council.

At the Council plenum a "miracle" did indeed happen, thanks to which the staff establishment was reduced to 25,500 zł.

This came about because the "domestic peace" among the allies broke down, which led to the president and his allies leaving the meeting, and then all the reduction proposals were adopted.

2) As to your complaint, poor thing, that you cannot work in a kehilla whose president submits a votum separatum against a high budget and declares that he will try to have the budget not approved — I would like to ask: does the Dąbrowa population pay 8,500 zł. so that you were elected President of the Council? Mr. Liberman! "Adorn thyself first" — you too exert yourself "where needed"; the only difference is that I seek the good of the community, and you — out of personal ambitions...

Finally a small remark: you need not yet use the title "President of the Kehilla Council"; there are already very many such "presidents" in Zagłębie, and not one of them has yet allowed himself to attach the title "president" to himself...

Respectfully, Abraham Najfeld [Neufeld],
