On Jews and Their Children

[Essay — Jewish parents and the upbringing of their children.]
A Jew would sacrifice himself for the sake of health, and — may it not befall you — a Jew is a bit of an invalid. In the "pitele" [?; probably "middle"] years a Jew by nature has some ailment; a Jew has a liver, kidneys, a bundle of bones... A gentile, they say, has them too, only it is as if he did not know about them... A Jew knows, poor thing, about his 248 limbs... he feels them, poor thing. He knows their place, where they are located, can touch them with his fingers: right "here... ouch"!
Such a Jew, who has neglected himself since his earliest youth, never looked after himself, such a darkened, long-suffering Jew — wants to be healthy. One goes to doctors in one's own town, one travels abroad to a professor, and the farther one travels, the greater the pains. The regular family doctor did indeed let out a bigger squeal there, where it hurts, than he, the patient himself; but he was compassionate, one of our own, homely... That could still be borne, but the little old professor — he pinches as with pincers... It would all have been worth it — if only there were a hope of getting well...
In the same way a Jew "educates" his child... A Jew will sell himself, he will give away the bite from his own mouth, deny himself the barest necessities, and educate his child, have it taught.
Jewish fathers and mothers, when they take their little boy to be enrolled ["andingen"] in the heder or in school, are moved to tears. Grown-up fathers and mothers stand and tremble over the little "Kaddish" — before the teacher has even opened his mouth he is showered with such gratitude and love... He is a fool, the teacher, for how little he asks for his Torah — he fools himself... They would have given more! They will pay him off, "Yosele's" teacher — a trifle! It seems good. Iaz [?] — but it is the opposite. Father and mother do tremble over the child, but not as over a living being — as if it were not a child at all but a toy; they do not know it, they do not see the child in perspective, where its traits of character become more [—?], more prominent. They say to one another: "When our child grows up" — but it is no more than a saying, a phrase of the kind; they do not believe it; after all, Yosele is Yosele for all eternity. They themselves, thank God, are already people advanced in years, people who have absorbed something into body and life, who have a character of their own, a full content; they live out their lives in formed ideas and thoughts rooted somewhere deep, in traditions of their own and in a language of their own. Yosele, though, babbles in some other tongue and in some other manner. The new (I do not want to say: the alien) that the child has made its own is still only half the trouble; the danger lies in its growing away from father and mother, from their milieu and their rich content. Meanwhile one still plays with our Yosele — what don't grown-ups do for a child: one crawls under the table, one harnesses oneself like little horses — but when Yosele stops playing, he will not understand those close to him.
Life has already proved it. But no one learns the lesson! It is such a Jewish attitude, a specific one, to a child: a warm attitude, devoted to the utmost — but not a serious one.
Jewish fathers and mothers see everything in Yosele — the prettiest toy in the house, the biggest doll — only not the human being, the Jew, the Jewish human being with the double bookkeeping. Living in water is hard; for a fish it is one of the easy things... One has to get used to the double bookkeeping; if one bends something in the complicated account, there will be an error, an ugly error.
Jewish fathers and mothers call a mohel for their eight-day-old babe and think that they have made him Jewish once and for all, and done their duty. But making Jewish is a constant process. It must not stop until the last breath of this "Judaized" boy who lives out in the wide world.
A Jewish boy who lives out in the wide world has debts to the world which he must pay. But he also owes something to himself. It is a double bookkeeping: Jewish-and-worldly, but a healthy one for us, a healthy one, a digestible one.
Jewish children pay the world what is due to it, and their own is cheated. Their own debt the fathers and mothers have twisted — not, God forbid, out of malice... One denies oneself — some out of coarseness, others out of poverty of spirit and without the slightest flight of imagination. What is lacking in [?] everyone is the feeling of responsibility for the growing child, for its individuality, which must not be wasted at a tender age. We are distinctive. But we lack the reverence for that distinctiveness, which we must share with the little ones in their earliest days.
As said — average Jewish parents treat their children, if not entirely as something "thing-like", then as a less living being than they themselves, with less responsibility for their future — a responsibility not content with the career one makes, but with the growth of the personal within the human being, the personality.
Our parents' attitude to their children takes its revenge later, just as Jewish health takes revenge, which has been neglected and made light of...
In a Jewish home it is cheerful at first; in a Jewish home there are children, one's own; when the children grow up in Jewish homes — it becomes gloomy there, they cease to be one's own. Father and mother do not recognize their own. Yoseles. I mean the converted and the half-converted Yoseles. I mean those — nearly all — Yoseles who, as if suddenly, crawl out of their childish skin and, as if suddenly, are transformed in their parents' homes into people. For people one must prepare; a person must be awaited like the Messiah. One must make oneself ready for him, expect him, receive him. A person — if he comes unknown and unexpected — is a stranger to us in Jewish homes. Strange young fellows walk about. In Jewish homes it is not homely; in Jewish homes where there are elderly fathers and mothers and grown-up children — it is not homely... Doors open and close, people come in, people go out, and one does not know what and who... It makes one's head swim — strangers turn about, strange manners, strange tongues, young fellows who have indeed only just taken off the schoolboy's cap, with fresh matriculation certificates in their breast pockets; there is laughter, the young fellows laugh — but it is not laughter, it is mockery. Where are our children? Children... We had children and it is as if they had vanished; a longing rises in the heart, a sad, despairing longing for children — as for health.
Jews do not spare their health and later want to be healthy. Oh, how they want to! Before our eyes nature plays out an act of revenge. It is terrible, but not ridiculous. It is not really they who fail to spare themselves — the hard, abnormal conditions of life have not spared them; therefore the phenomenon is not at all comic.
Jews love their children enormously. Jews do more than their strength allows for their children. One sacrifices oneself for "education". But in relation to their child they lack a sense — the sense of self-respect; the seriousness with which one leads a child into a life of its own, a healthy life. That is why it is so ridiculous when fathers and mothers, having given body and soul to their children, suddenly lose them.
Such an act of revenge! And it is not nature that plays it, not her sin — it is our own sin that destroys us.
What could be more terrible and... more ridiculous?
Y. S—n.
The Old and the Young Jan (a sketch from the 'Lemberger Morgen')

Jan was a drunkard. He lived in the village. He drank at the Jewish tavern, and when he used to get drunk, he would smash the windowpanes of the Jewish tavern-keeper.

Jan had a little son, a successful boy with a good head. The teachers at the folk school loved him very much, and when he finished the village school the teachers explained to his father that he should send his son away to study in the big city.

When he [the father] used to get drunk and smash windowpanes in the Jewish tavern, his little son was deeply ashamed of his father, the drunkard and brawler. From shame he could not look the Jewish tavern-keeper in the eye.

When Jan had drunk away his whole fortune, he left the village and became a caretaker [stróż] in the big city. His little son's dreams came true. In the big city he studied at a gymnasium and afterwards at the university.

Because of the World War the Jewish tavern-keeper, too, came from the village to the city. Here he opened a little shop. He no longer wanted anything to do with liquor and drunkards.

During the recent events in Lwów [Lemberg] the windowpanes of the former Jewish tavern-keeper were smashed again. This time not by old Jan in a drunken state, but by young Jan, entirely sober.

The next day old Jan walked past the little shop of the former publican and present-day shopkeeper, and he was ashamed to look him straight in the eye.
Once the young Jan was ashamed — today the old one.

The young one, in time, stopped being ashamed.
The Jewish Students

Dr. Jakub Wygodzki.

As is well known, a great, epoch-making historiosophical study has established the fact that the pogrom against Jews which Endek hooligans carried out in Wilno last November must be regarded as an act of revenge on the part of the Jews for the Spanish Inquisition... Who took revenge on whom here, and why, is hard, very hard even to say; to understand it is downright impossible — but precisely for that reason, precisely for that, the said study has become so famous...

And here the Jewish students come forward first of all. People do not even say it so explicitly; but everywhere the awl pokes out of the sack, wherever one tries to hide it... In all the public speeches of certain circles, in all the street sheets of the worst, man-eating sort, their deep hatred of the Jewish students finds expression — because they dare to put up resistance to the honourable young gentlemen of the squirearchy, who have made the beating of Jews in general, and Jewish students in particular, into a kind of seasonal sport!..

If you look from the side, objectively and calmly, at the average Jewish student, he arouses in you the greatest astonishment: he goes through such a thorny path, such seven circles of hell, of which no other student has the slightest notion!

Already at the gymnasium, a Hebrew or a Jewish gymnasium, he is only very rarely able to obtain a matura, a full-rights matura that would open for him the road to university. What extraordinary energy and work the future Jewish student [printed 'rer' — a misprint] must put in here to get the real matura — is beyond imagining!

Finally, when for the most part his remarkable abilities, diligence and stubbornness overcome all obstacles, and he at last receives the long-yearned-for state matura, which others get so easily and so quickly...

It soon turns out, however, that even this matura does not open for the Jewish school-leaver the road to the university itself, but only to the numerus clausus, which was silently introduced at all universities at the demand of the 'Greens' — the antisemitic students supported from the side.

Through the dense sieve of the numerus clausus only a relatively quite small part of the Jewish students passes. The remaining, larger part must either renounce higher education or pack up and move abroad, where he must not only study the higher sciences but also toil hard to earn a piece of bread...

The 'lucky ones', those who remain in the country at the Polish universities, begin their studies by receiving blows and being thrown out of the lecture halls, dissecting rooms, etc., because 'their fathers let themselves be burned alive for the sanctification of the Name [printed 'kadosh'] by the Inquisition'..

When they have, thank God, got through all the insults and humiliations, and when their colleagues from abroad have already had their diplomas nostrified [?] — in a word, when they step out into life with their diplomas, they are entirely ignored by the state: Jews get almost no state posts, free professional practice crumbles more and more from year to year, and making a living from it gets harder and harder...

These everyday phenomena are no surprises but typical, unmistakable signs of Jewish life. Surely the Jewish young people who strain every nerve to obtain higher education know them very well; they know quite well what a hell they must go through until they get their diploma — and what meagre practical benefit that diploma can bring them!

And yet they stream in such great numbers, and yet they spend their last strength [printed 'pokhes' — apparently a misprint for 'koykhes'] to overcome all obstacles, just to get into the university!.. So deep in them sits the need for education, the thirst for knowledge! Let all those 'practical' people take note [?] who never stop raising an outcry about the 'overproduction of academics', about the need to introduce in the free professions a restriction on admission to universities and to return to the medieval 'guild' with its 'class-appropriate' life and its artificial partitions, which the French Revolution, it seems, so thoroughly dismantled... Let these 'practical' people be convinced by the example of the Jewish students that, far more important than a means of livelihood, the university is a source of knowledge for true students, who feel a thirst, a burning hunger for knowledge!..

What is to be admired in the Jewish student is precisely the absence of a general hatred toward his constant persecutors. The Jewish student, despite all the false accusations from which he constantly suffers — such as the 'numerus clausus', the cadaver question, etc. — despite being excluded from every 'bursa' [student hostel], 'academic house', 'fraternal aid', and so on, feels no hatred whatsoever toward Poles in general, whereas a very large part of the Poles feels this hatred and often displays it toward Jews in general and Jewish students in particular!.. In general, I know of no other people that bears a grudge as little as the Jew, in whom all the justified anger toward the adversary subsides [?]. As soon as the latter himself falls into trouble, you immediately hear: 'a pity', 'nebekh', and so on. To accuse the Jewish students of constant hatred toward the Poles, who 'never did them anything but good', is a double lie.

Certain Polish circles, at the very least, have almost always behaved, and behave to this day, with hatred toward Jews, which is expressed in severe persecutions. In turn, Jews certainly do not behave toward these circles with love. But an eternal, constant hatred of the persecutor is alien to human nature in general and to the Jewish nature in particular...

The antisemitism so widespread in Poland is, after all, an expression of a strong hatred of Jews, which shows itself in evil deeds!
Among Jews there has never been any anti-Polonism, and there never will be!..

If you look further at the deeply earnest attitude of the Jewish students toward learning — toward general as well as Jewish national culture — at their diligence and decency on the more than meagre means of livelihood they have, you must come to the conclusion that we can be proud of our Jewish students, and that we can calmly entrust to them the future of the Jewish people.
Old Jewish 'Main Privileges' in the Former Polish Kingdom

[History — Polish Jewry.] Dr. Moshe Schorr [Mojżesz Schorr].
A.
The Jews of the Polish Republic now stand on the threshold of a new political epoch, and it is therefore worthwhile to leaf through the 600-year Jewish history in Poland in order to see what rights and privileges Jews once enjoyed there.
What we now demand of the Polish government under the slogan of "equal rights" is in no way a new demand, but the demand to get back that status for the Polish Jews which was assured to them over many generations by the Polish kings and lords.
Not only are the present demands nothing new; on the contrary, this is a struggle for the restoration of those Jewish rights in Poland which are deeply rooted in the tradition of Polish Jewry.
Tolerance and fairness were [the hallmarks of] Polish-Jewish relations in the time of the old Polish kingdom, from the beginning of the 13th century until the end of the 18th century.
In the towns and townlets of the former Poland the Jews were the foundation of the burgher estate; with their activity they fulfilled an economic calling. The Jews were then the juridical property of the king; to him alone were they subject, and he was also the protector and defender of their life and property.
And even if the Jews entered into certain agreements, or modified their rights through agreements with other factors, the king still remained the highest instance, on whom the fate of all Jews depended at all times. Whatever those others had decreed concerning the Jews, the king could annul or uphold according to his own will.
Yet, notwithstanding that every monarch, when he issued a certain ordinance concerning the Jews of a particular town or province, expressly stressed in his decree that the privileges were granted "for ever", nevertheless a new king could not annul, or add to, the grace of his predecessor.
Therefore the greatest concern of the Jews at that time was how to win favour and goodwill in the eyes of the monarch.
And indeed we see that every time a new Polish king ascended the throne, the Polish Jews hastened to present him with a petition to confirm the old privileges, or to add new ones to them.
At first the number of Jews in Poland was quite small. There were only a few larger communities there, such as Poznań, Kraków, Sandomierz and Lwów (Lemberg). Each community kept its own Sabbath [i.e. went its own way].
And when the coronation of a new king took place, each community sent him its own special intercessor (shtadlan) to obtain from the monarch privileges that were valid only for their particular communities.
Such confirmed privileges bearing the king's seal are found today in the archives of almost all the large Jewish towns in Poland, and almost all of them have the same wording and the same content.
These are the so-called "main privileges", the oldest of which stems from Prince Bolesław of Kalisz of the year 1264, and which end with the confirmations of later princes around the 14th and 15th centuries.
A radical change in the mutual relations among the Jewish communities in Poland occurred in the middle of the 16th century, when the Jewish population of the country was considerably enlarged by the newly immigrated Jews who sought protection in Poland from the persecutions waged against them in various European countries because of the new Reformation movement.
And precisely at the end of the 16th century the foundation was laid for Jewish autonomy in Poland, known under the name "Council of Four Lands" (Va'ad Arba Aratzot), and its successor the "Council of the Land of Lithuania" (Va'ad Medinat Lita) (from the year 1623), which for 200 years was the representative and advocate of all the Jews of Poland and Lithuania.
At the same time there also appears on the scene the type of the Jewish shtadlan, one of the nobles of the people, chosen by the "Council", with the authorization of all the communities to be their representative in all their needs and demands before the king and his counsellors.
The centre of all the communities was then rich and honourable Kraków, "a city and mother in Israel" in the full sense of the word, which was also the capital of the country.
From that time there have been preserved in the archive of the Kraków community the "privileges" which concerned the whole of Polish Jewry. Of these "fundamental privileges" only a few have survived; the most important of them is that of the last king, Stanisław August (1765—1795), and it is known as the collection of "main privileges" of the year 1765, the year of his accession to the throne, and is to be found to this day in the archive of the Kraków community.
This scroll is a parchment volume of 16 leaves; through the middle of the volume is drawn a silk cord with a large state seal, and the whole is laid in a small tin casket. On the title page is written in Hebrew: "Privilege and confirmation from all the former kings and from our lord the mighty king, the pious Stanisław August, to all the Jews in the lands of Poland, and in particular to our community, the holy community of Kraków, written and sealed in the year one thousand seven hundred sixty-five [1765]".
This declaration is the most important document we possess from the earliest times up to Stanisław August, in which is reflected the attitude of the last Polish legislator towards the Jews.
The core of the whole collection is the enigmatic privilege (without a date) of King Casimir the Great, which was issued for the Jews of "Great Poland" (Wielkopolska) and was confirmed 100 years later by King Casimir Jagiellon, at the request of the Jews of Poznań, in the year 1453[?], after a fire had broken out in the town in which many old documents were burnt.
Concerning this document a discussion arose among scholars as to its authenticity, because some suspected that it was a forgery on the part of the Jews of that time (in the Middle Ages it was a common thing to forge documents in other circles too), since it grants the Jews such broad privileges as are apparently not to be found in the earlier privileges of Prince Bolesław and of Casimir the Third; in particular it speaks there of holding their own land, i.e. of taking possession of land which had been taken from the Christian nobles for unpaid debts, and of the oath of the Jews regarding the blood libel, and of other broad rights for the Jewish court of law, etc.
We dealt with this question in the foreword to our edition of the "Collection of Main Privileges" and in the Russian-Jewish periodical "Yevreyskaya Starina". There we demonstrated in detail that those are right who regard the document as genuine, and that the suspicion of forgery has no basis whatever. This, by the way, is not the place to repeat it all.
A Little Feuilleton — My Little Glass

[Feuilleton — a drinker's satirical monologue.]
Ah, my little glass, my dear! You are more faithful to me than anyone. You feel my heart! You, only you can understand me and feel with me.
Come here, dear little glass, let us tip ourselves over!
One must be drunk nowadays, drunk as a beast, honestly.
Yesterday I gave a speech at a conference on peace, on brotherhood among men. Ha-ha-ha! M-E-N! Who invented that foolish, unworthy name!
Men!
I am ready this very minute to hand in my resignation, if only someone would show me even o-n-e two-legged creature worthy of the name "man".
Ah; my little glass! Let us empty you — then you will look like the soul of today's politicians, of the present ringleaders [„redl-firer“] among men.
Something has been stirring in the world lately: somehow people bang their heads against the wall, somehow they wrinkle their brows; apparently they want to create a new league of nations, a new union of states. Well then, let them fool around there [„dreyen a mah“]; I will hold on to my little glass, which knows nothing of any politics of diplomacy.
Yes, I will take myself off into a desert, somewhere beneath the Mountains of Darkness, and there conduct my own politics. I will surround myself with hard, pointed stones and will... Ha-ha-ha! They think, my colleagues, that I am already giving up my place to them? Oh, no!
I am not one of those who let themselves be led by the nose. No one will take my place, because no one loves the truth as I do, because no one hates today's culture as much as I do; because no one has been so deeply disappointed in today's civilization as I have.
They think they are sober, that all wisdom lies in their heads; so I want to throw the bitter truth in all their faces and cry out: liars, that's what you are! You are all swindlers! You are all fallen creatures! Because you are too sober, and think that everyone else is drunk.
If only people could, at least once in their lives, grasp life so sharply and simply — sharply and directly — as a drunkard can!
But to whom am I talking?
You will all perish like beaten dogs and will not look the truth in the eye. Each of you lies on his own little dung-heap and guards it more than his own soul, pardon the expression [„mshteyns gezogt“]; you would rather sell your dearest possession (if you own such a thing) than lose a part of your coins.
You look at the sun through gilded spectacles — so how can you see its rays?
Phooey, phooey!
There is no one to talk about and no one to talk to.
Come here, my little glass [printed „pushele“], y o u do understand me.
You do take in the sun's rays.
L'chaim, brother!
Rebus.
Heard and Seen — by Ben Amotz

[Feuilleton — "Heard and Seen": sketches from Będzin and from the press.]
Let it be done thoroughly...
At a lunch in the people's school for Jewish boys in Będzin.
A very important undertaking has been taken on by the "Women's Fund" [„froyen-kasa“] at the school.
— Be mindful of the children of the poor, be careful with the poor children. At home poverty reigns, it drives one out of the house — so one runs into school, where it is bright, warm, and one is served breakfast and a respectable lunch too...
— Do the children get lunches every day?
— No, I am told, 3 times a week; the means [printed „pushes“, read „koykhes“] are not enough to give every day. It depends on the public: the bigger the campaign grows, the more [printed „ber“, read „mer“] days the hundred poor boys will get lunches at school.
— Completely free?
— For five groszy... We do not want — the headmaster explains to me — a feeling of charity to take root in the children; a small payment, five groszy, only not for nothing.
A very important undertaking, especially in the winter months, and yet I would like to draw attention to: 1) taking care also of the aesthetic, or better said the hygienic, side: on the tables around which the children sit there should be a tablecloth, at the very least white paper, because the decorative side of the table says a great deal, especially to children.
2) During lunch there need not be half a dozen women as "onlookers" [„tsushoyerins“] and often also as — "servers"...
Because children enjoy it when no one, whoever it may be, lords it over them while they eat. Besides, special duty-rosters [„dizhurn“] are appointed each time, who can be relied upon to fulfil their tasks properly.
And 3) — if it is feasible — a comfortable hall, so that the children do not sit squeezed together [?]. If one is caring this way for the well-being of the poor child — let it be done thoroughly...
—o—
Poor England...
There is a proverb: "If someone loses his fortune, he also loses his mind".
And in connection with what did this come up [printed „vshe“, read „zhe“]?
This week I read a newspaper item that: "the Yiddish language has been recognized in England as a literary language"...
I read and am astonished — is it possible? By mistake, or have the English already lost their wits? And if the pound has taken a blow [„zrike“], what's all the fuss? Is the world already ending? Does one already lose one's right mind and "recognize Yiddish as a language"?...
I was curious, of course, to know whether the item was true. So I decided that the barometer of the item would be our Jewish institutions. There, I was sure, I would find out whether I should believe the item or not...
And that is just what I did: first I visited the Jewish communities [„gmines“], then — the Jewish banks, private and cooperative, and finally the hundred-percent popular associations — the small traders' and artisans' associations...
And there, in our institutions, I did indeed see the naked truth: that I had been so naive as to believe the foolish item that "Yiddish has been recognized in England as a literary language"...
Because everywhere I found the common folk [„amkho“] standing and arguing (pardon the expression) with the clerks (of the female sex...)
— Po polsku [„pa palskiemu“ — in Polish!]...
The complaints were complicated: one about a protested bill of exchange, the second about a reduction on licence fees [„patentn“], the third — how to obtain an artisan's card; but the young ladies did not want to give up their "intelligentsia manners" [„mores“] and gave the "bill-endorsement clientele" [„zhirovskie klientele“] to understand — "po polsku"...
With a shamed face and in disgrace I left our societies and institutions, and recalled the above-mentioned proverb: that "when one loses one's money, one also loses one's mind"...
— Poor England...
—o—
Happy are you, Będzin...
To everything a season.
Everything has its time. There is no eternity on earth; "one generation passeth away and another generation cometh" — a generation goes, a generation comes; "the sun also ariseth" — the sun rises, "and the sun goeth down" — and the sun sets..
We Będziners are at the stage of "the sun also ariseth" — the sun rises"...
This time we do not mean it in the economic sense; the content of human existence is not for the body, for bread, "for man doth not live by bread only"; the essence of human life is — spiritual nourishment.
And in this field we are far from having fallen behind; on the contrary, we have a great gain to record; we are progressing, the "culture" in our town is spreading wide, wide, all the way across to the other side of the "Przemsza" [river]...
Once, in those "dark" times, we were so naive as to give Jacob Gordin the title [printed „situlirt“, read „titulirt“] of dramatist; later we gave the title to Adler, to Turkow and other "shni-kes" [?] such as Lampel, Dr. Baratov [?]...
Even now there are still, even today, a great many towns where the above-listed stars are received with enthusiasm, and the Yiddish theatre public still lives by their word...
An exception is the town of Będzin: here one is "no longer impressed" by foreign artists; we have our own, a whole pleiad of "stars" and "dramatists" who are beloved and esteemed by the broad masses, even by the suckling babes, who come to hear them every Saturday afternoon at "Ga-vashtshi" [?]...
And my heart melts with pleasure when I read that: "On Saturday afternoon the sexual life between man and woman will be performed, in the leading role the beloved dramatist Shebna Pimsenholtz"...
After reading the posters [„afishn“] I give praise to His dear Name for the great kindness He does us, that we are not beaten with two sticks: if our livelihood limps a little, we have in exchange an abundance of "culture"; spiritual springs burst in upon us from the
— Podzamcze [?] street...
— Happy are you, Będzin...
The Jewish Craftsman — and Government Works

[Poland — economy, craftsmen.]
For various reasons, both political and economic, the middle class has lately been treated with more attention than before. Whoever follows the question in its full scope notices this quite clearly. Here too, it seems, government circles, for the reasons mentioned above, are compelled to go along with the current.
Clear proof of this is the draft law intended to regulate supplies and works for government, municipal and insurance institutions, which the Ministry of Commerce and Industry sent on 22 June of this year to the Council of the Chambers of Crafts for its opinion.
The law contains 3 articles.
The first article deals with:
The need to establish the manner of awarding orders for work and supplies, as well as their acceptance by the State Treasury, municipal administrations, insurance institutions, government monopolies, government enterprises and enterprises administered by the government.
Article 2 states:
“In all craft works, craftsmen and their organizations have priority in receiving the works and supplies, provided the offers they submit do not exceed by more than 10 percent the lowest offer.”
Article 3 states which ministries must come to an understanding in order to award all the works or supplies they need. As we see, then, the draft law provides very broad concessions for craftsmen, both in their priority and in a price 10 per cent higher than the industrial offers.
True, the craftsman cannot compare himself with the industrialist in his mode of production, but that is not what concerns me now.
The law, if it appears, may truly bring about a great revival among craftsmen. Craftsmen in Poland produce — with very few exceptions — only for internal consumption. And however much government circles exert themselves on behalf of exports of craft articles, one cannot point to any great successes. And what internal consumption looks like is clear to everyone. Indeed the craft workshops stand without work, not only in the building trade but in almost all trades. And the craftsman’s family ponders how to improve [?] tomorrow. Particularly, of course, the Jewish craftsman feels this, who in recent years has been the “best” and biggest taxpayer.
And the question arises: to what extent will the Jewish craftsman be able to benefit from the new law?
It is enough to look at the list of trades given by the journal “Rzemiosło” which may come into consideration for government works, and to see that almost all the trades in which Jews are engaged are listed, for example: building trade — tinsmiths, glaziers, varnishers and painters; wood trade — joiners, turners; textile trade — hatters, “kapelusz” (felt-hat) makers, furriers, tailors, knitters, brush makers, trimmings-makers [?] and upholsterers; metal trade — coppersmiths, brass founders, locksmiths, engravers; food trade — bakers, confectioners, sausage makers, butchers; leather trade — stitchers (uppers), glove makers, shoemakers and bookbinders, photographers, etc.
I also do not wish to say that the Jewish craftsmen will be pushed aside because they are Jews — that may be naive on my part. But it is my firm conviction that if the Jewish craftsmen were properly prepared in the sense of organization, it would simply be impossible to push them aside.
It is true that the Chambers of Crafts will play a great role here in organizing the works and supplies, but the question of easing the Sunday rest has shown lately that the common institutions are not always able to defend the interests of their Jewish members. To this day the Jewish economic associations are still not truly economic ones, and here a broad organization is needed: the craftsmen’s production must be rebuilt from individual to mass production, financial means must be created, producers’ cooperatives, etc.
It is hard, responsible work that demands professional knowledge and will. And I allow myself to point out to the craftsmen’s organizations that they should pay attention to this question, since the law is still at the stage of preparation. It is to be hoped that no essential change concerning the craftsmen will be made. Therefore now is the time to set about systematic organizational work, in which the best professional forces in all fields must engage, since it demands such broadly ramified — and, for Jewish craftsmen in Poland — new work. Then it is to be hoped that Jewish craftsmen too, who fulfil all duties toward the state, will receive from the state in equivalent return what it is able to give them.
Dawid Koniecpoler.
For Whom Are the New Projects on School Holidays?

[Poland — education.]
A few weeks ago a notice appeared in the press about a decree of the Ministry of Education to change the school holidays, shortening the Passover holidays and lengthening the winter holidays.
As soon as the news appeared there was already a commotion [?] among parents and teachers. And although the new regulations are to be applied already this year, people nevertheless did not take it seriously.
These days the first voice on the matter has been heard in public. The well-known Wilno publicist Helena Romer-Ochenkowska wrote in “Kurier Wileński” a fairly long article under the heading “Theories and Experiments,” discussing there at length the question of holidays.
According to the new decree the summer holidays are to begin earlier than until now: instead of 28 June — on 15 June, and also to end earlier: instead of 1 September — on 15 August.
Romer holds that taking the 2 August weeks away from the children takes from them the possibility of gathering cheap and often free fruit in the country.
But since not every child has somewhere to gather fruit, and since the 2 June weeks also have enough sun — the question could still be discussed, especially since precisely in the month of June it is very hard for children to sit out the time in class.
Romer-Ochenkowska is, however, quite right when she speaks of the winter holidays. The decree says that the lengthening of the winter holidays should be used for sporting purposes; but the project does not reckon with the conditions of the majority of society. It is suited only to well-off children, who eat dinner every day and have a warm home, warm clothes and sports equipment. But what will the poor child look like, who lives a whole day on the little bit of cooked food he receives in the public school? Surely the central authority that devised the project did not concern itself with the climatic and material conditions of the Kresy [Eastern Borderlands]. Why, in our region there are 20 degrees of frost at the end of December. The children of the poor masses, who do not own even such a democratic piece of sports equipment as a little sled, not to speak of skates or skis, have no warm sweater and shoes and often live in cold, damp hovels — these children are simply condemned to influenza, colds and tuberculosis if in winter their school is taken away and they are sent to do sports.
Such questions penetrate deep into the local, material, climatic and cultural conditions of the population, and they must not be regulated uniformly for the whole country by the central organs.
All this Ochenkowska points out in her article, and she hopes that the Minister of Education will yet revise the decree.
D.
Don't Forget

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayishlach

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Vayishlach and the Haftarah.] The portion.
A) "I have sojourned with Laban" (32:5)
1.
"The blessings of my father, who blessed me: 'Be lord over thy brethren' — were not fulfilled in me." Rashi.
"Not fulfilled in me" — in my own eyes the blessing "be lord" has not been fulfilled, but in the eyes of strangers, of others — yes. The world already does take Jacob for a rich man... he must pay the highest taxes. After all, he is somehow rich!... Divrei David.
2.
"I have sojourned with Laban and kept the 613 commandments." Rashi.
Well, Esau will surely be delighted with that: a trifle, a fine boast for Esau: "and I kept the 613 commandments"...
But in fact he sent word to tell him: my father's blessings were not fulfilled in me; I did not grow rich in Laban's house; I am not overly well off. You don't believe it? — "and I kept the 613 commandments" — and if one keeps all 613 commandments, and on top of that together with a Laban, one cannot be too well off... That is how it is: either the World to Come or this world... Rashei Besamim.
B) "And four hundred men with him" (ibid., 7)
Esau takes four hundred men along from the outset. A mob — so that if riots break out and Jacob suffers, he will be able to claim: I am not to blame at all, only they, the mob; I could not restrain them, the pogrom broke out spontaneously.. Tiferet Yehonatan.
C) "Then the other camp which is left shall escape" (ibid., 9)
The Midrash says that the one camp was set apart from the other by one day's journey.
Why precisely such a distance?
On Rebecca's words "Why should I be deprived of you both in one day" it is expounded that prophecy spoke out of her, that Jacob and Esau would die on one day. And indeed so it was. So Jacob thought to himself: "If Esau come to the one camp and smite it" — if Esau comes and slaughters the first camp together with Jacob, he will himself have to die within the same twenty-four hours and will not manage to reach the second camp, which is exactly one day's journey away from him...
Rabbi Reb Heshel.
D) "And make thy seed as the sand of the sea" (ibid., 13)
Sometimes Jews are likened to the stars and sometimes to the sand on the ground, for such a people it is: either it climbs to the heavens, or it sinks into the depths of the earth... Midrash Rabbah.
E) "And there wrestled a man with him" (ibid., 28 [so printed; the verse is Genesis 32:25])
When Samael saw that "Jacob was left alone — for the sake of small jars," that he loved money, he said to himself: here is the place for "va-ye'avek" — to raise dust (avak), to blind his eyes with golden dust, so that he should see nothing before him..
Rabbi Shlomo Ephraim of Łęczyca.
F) "And he halted upon his thigh" (ibid., 32)
The Midrash says that Jacob was punished because he called Esau "my lord" and flattered him. And he was punished by being made lame because this symbolises the figurative image of flattery: the flatterer always limps, afraid to take a straight and firm step... Olelot Ephraim.
G) "Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew of the thigh" (ibid., 33)
In the little town of Wilkosz[?] there lived a famous maskil, Yosef Tarla. Once Rabbi Hersh Melekh of Dynów, a bitter opponent of the Haskalah, came there. While at prayer in the synagogue, Rabbi Hersh Melekh was studying Humash to himself, and when he came to the verse mentioned [printed: "rermantn"], Tarla remarked in jest:
— It's a miracle that the angel touched only the hollow of Jacob's thigh; had he touched him on the breast, we would not be allowed to eat breast either...
When Reb Hersh Melekh hears it, he grows angry and exclaims:
— I am sure he will convert.
So Tarla goes off to the Ropshitzer [R. Naftali of Ropczyce] and informs on Rabbi Hirsh Melekh for the harsh expression. Says the clever Ropshitzer:
— Truly a mitzvah to heed so upright a Jew as Reb Hersh Melekh..
—o—
Rabbi Hirsch Chajes came to the author of "Yeshuot Yaakov" for rabbinic ordination. The rabbi received him well, because he was a great genius, but his son, Reb Mordechai Ze'ev, bitterly hated the maskilim, and Reb Hirsch Chajes was, as is well known, a maskil. Reb Mordechai Ze'ev urges his father not to give the maskil prodigy ordination. Seeing, however, that he would get nowhere with his father, who was enchanted by the young prodigy, he says:
— Well, ordain him then, because if he doesn't become a rabbi among Jews, he will become a priest among the gentiles...
H) "Then receive my present at my hand" (33:10)
Esau actually had a fair claim: we divided things between us — to you the World to Come and to me this world. I shall enjoy nothing of your World to Come; so how come you, Jacob, have oxen and asses and other things of this world?
Jacob answered him: my property is no "this world". Who, who — a Jew has no enjoyment of his property. It is all for you, for Esau, after all... You are the master over my property — "and receive at my hand" (future tense): you will forever gnaw and gnaw at me... Arvei Nahal.
I) "Let them trade therein" (34:21)
Jews — say the antisemites — are a people devoted only to the coin; for trade they will sell their soul, God.
But see: Hamor persuaded his subjects that the sons of Jacob would trade with them, and at once they agreed even to convert, to be circumcised, to sell their idolatrous faith, and the mob-golem went along with everything, if only "they may trade therein," if only the Jews would do business with them... Hegyonot ha-RaMaH [printed: "Ḥegyonit"].
The Haftarah.
J) "For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee" (Hosea 12 [so printed; the verse is Obadiah 1:10])
"For violence against thy brother Jacob" — with what could Jacob rob, so to speak[?]? With a little trick, by tricking you out of the birthright. Therefore "shame shall cover thee" — be ashamed, then, that you let yourself be tricked out of the birthright! Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
Let Us Talk It Over a Little! On the Situation of the Jewish Sports Movement in Zagłębie

[Sport — Zagłębie; opinion.] In the recent issues of our paper we dwelt at length, in a series of articles, on the present state of the Jewish sports associations. Though without details, we pointed to the actual situation: that for all the recent achievements in the field of sport, the associations have nevertheless today [?] overstepped the bounds of their aims. The Jewish sports associations have strayed from the basic lines that were laid down for them more than 20 years ago by the pioneers of Jewish sport. After so many achievements in the field of work for the physical renaissance of the young generation, thanks to the lessons of its long-standing and — be it as it may — fruitful work, we ought already today to have been able to show [?] incomparable conquests in this field; instead we now stand — let us have the courage to say it openly — before a far worse state of affairs than at the beginning of the rise of the Jewish sports movement. Back then we at least possessed a strong idealism and a firm belief in our powers for the so useful ideals of physical education; we believed that our path was the right one and that no difficulties whatsoever could prevent us from realizing it.
What do we look like today?
Our sports associations have been turned into workshops for records, and thereby they serve a select few; whoever raises his feet 5 centimetres higher has become the „pan“ [master] of our clubs. The standing of an association is not measured by its mass reach. Instead of asking how many sportsmen are being „educated“ in it — how many young people straighten out their bones in this or that association — one asks how many goals it scored this year and how many championship titles it has already won. In our sports clubs today, instead of healthy, conscious and cultured people, there are being raised — parasites, who later remain a burden on society.
In the chase after records all means are sanctified; our associations are run to a great extent by people who have no calling for it.
If one were to collect and publish all the deceitful deeds committed by our „sport-makers“, a horrifying picture of the state of our sports clubs would emerge; and the worst of it is that all this is done with the words „for the good of Jewish sport“ on their lips.
We will only point out that we know of a case — by what means a Jewish club in Zagłębie wants to strengthen its football team with a player from a Warsaw Jewish sports association.
A leader of a certain sports club has for a long time been „running“ to the player's home; for a larger sum of money he is trying to obtain the consent of the player's family for him to play in the club's team. The footballer is promised „compensation“ for every match, and if his mother club, where he was brought up, will not release him to the team, they secure for themselves the „intervention“ of strong lads from the underworld... On this ground it has already come to scandals, and the matter is not yet over...
Such people carry out the office of educators of the growing generation — can one entrust them with the upbringing of our children? Or should we perhaps at least remain indifferent?
We shall now try to seek a way out of what we have set out [?] — our clubs must return to their aims. First of all, all undesirable elements must be removed from the leadership; the championship mania among our sportsmen must be uprooted.
Our sports associations must go along the paths that were marked out for them at the very beginning of their founding — the upbringing of our youth. Therefore, in our opinion, there is one way here — to keep as far away as possible from championship games. Such sections must exist as can still cultivate great masses of sportsmen.
In Wilno a sports club has now been founded (for the time being the first), which will cultivate all branches of sport but will not take part in championship contests; without any doubt other towns will also follow this example.
We are aware that at the beginning it is very hard; we leave the manner of structure and work of such associations to the discussion of the Jewish sports activists. We understand that everywhere there must be rivalry, for where there is rivalry — there is initiative. We will gladly give space for a discussion by the leaders of the Jewish sports movement; let them reflect openly before the broad public on the future fate of the youth. Let them, together with us, find the right path for the Jewish sports movement, or — justify the present system — and we will be very glad of it.
We know that the „sport-makers“ will shrug their shoulders and receive our arguments with a smile on their lips. But we shall not desist, for the ideals of physical education are close to us, and the fate of the growing generation — very dear.
H. B—n

100 Years of Matches and Other Things

[Feature — history of inventions; report from Leipzig.]
From our Leipzig correspondent Z. Haber
Today we do not even ask any more who invented the first matches; on the contrary, today we already have petrol lighters, because striking a match is too great a bother, which takes up too much time.
Nevertheless, this invention of matches caused, in its day, quite a great revolution.
In the archives of the Leipzig Fair we find that exactly a hundred years ago, in the year 1832, small sticks were brought to the Leipzig fair for the first time, which had heads of sulphur and which ignited when one rubbed them against a hard object. These matches were brought by the Englishman S. Tones [so printed], who had a patent issued so that the matches might not be imitated. Nevertheless, that very same year, at the second fair in Leipzig, a German merchant, Friedrich Kammerer, brought matches with phosphorus heads, exactly as we still have them today.
These matches were made by hand and cost a lot of money. In the archives of the Leipzig fair it is recorded that only a few pieces of these matches were sold. The population preferred to make fire with a piece of steel on a stone, because that cost no money... Only a few years later did people everywhere begin to use matches.
But other things too, without which one cannot live today and which seem to us to have existed since time immemorial, are only now celebrating their 100th anniversary. The telegraph, for example, is only now a hundred years old. In the year 1832 a telegram was sent from the Leipzig fair to Trier on the French border. That was the first telegram ever dispatched. This telegram passed through no fewer than 61 stations before it reached Trier. The whole world was abuzz at the time with the sensation.
After that several trials were made from Berlin, all of which succeeded. The military administration took the telegraph into its own hands, and only the military could send telegrams. If a private person wished to send a dispatch, he had to be acquainted with the military commandant, or one had to have a confirmation from the gmina [municipality] that he was worthy of sending a dispatch. Only in the year 1848 was everyone permitted to send dispatches.
Buses... There seems to be no single country and no single larger city that has not introduced buses, which connect the city streets with one another or with the surrounding places.
Very few people know, however, that in the year 1832 a bus was shown for the first time at the Leipzig fair; it was fitted with benches for fourteen people and could do 16 kilometres an hour. The bus had wide wheels, so that the streets should not be damaged, and it ran on steam.
A Viennese company wanted to buy this bus in order to introduce a regular service between Vienna and Munich. But as the company did not have enough money, the bus was bought by an Englishman, who had it run between London and Manchester.
But the railways too are not as old as we think. In Austria, for example, it was only a hundred years ago, in the year 1832, that the first railway lines were made between Linz and Budweis [České Budějovice], because the railway was needed to bring the salt from the Austrian "seas" [so printed] to Bohemia.
This railway did not look like today's railways, although as early as 1830 a railway already ran between Liverpool and Manchester. The Austrian railway ran on narrow rails and so slowly that nobody wanted to ride on it. Not only did a horse go faster, but even on foot one could get there sooner. Among the public the railway was called "the crooked duck"... And even the big railway that was built in 1835 between Nuremberg [printed "Kurnberg"] and Fürth also ran for years without passengers, because one got from one place to another faster on foot than by the railway. This railway was called "the crooked Caroline", meaning thereby to express how fast it goes...
And since we are already on this chapter, it is worth mentioning that a whole series of important inventions, which today rule the world and at which people everywhere laughed years ago.
But more about that in a separate article.
Misfortune Befell Me on Główna Street

[Sketch — at the editorial office; everyday life.]
Early in the morning the door of the editorial office flies open and in comes an elderly Jewish woman, emaciated, worn out, and in a voice full of tears she wails:
— Help, Jews, merciful sons of the merciful, save me, he has run away!
— What has happened? Who has run away? Calm down and speak more quietly.
The woman looks around on all sides and asks:
— Are there no strangers here? I am ashamed to tell it, after all; it is a disgrace before Jews —
So we think who knows what has happened, and ask several outsiders not to take it amiss and to step out for a while. Those people are not offended, thinking that perhaps the woman really has something to tell which she has reason to be ashamed of, and they leave the editorial office.
It turns out, however, that this is a story like all of today's stories — daily bread. But the old woman is naive and thinks that this has happened for the first time, to her, since the world has existed.
And the woman begins to tell her tale in tears, in the language of a tkhine [women's supplication], as on the High Holy Days:
— Dear people. Why should I not weep, why should I not lament, when such a misfortune could befall my child; help, save me, it is the end of the world.
— Well, tell us then, what is your name? — we grow calmer, so long as nothing has happened to her; we had thought that somebody wanted to harm her...
— I am, may it not happen to you, a widow, and I have a daughter. A decent, good child. She was a young girl, only 23 years old, and it was fated that she should meet a stranger, a young man; it was Chol ha-Moed Sukkot, and the misfortune befell me on Główna Street.
— What do you mean, the misfortune befell you on Główna Street? — we do not understand, because every time she breaks off and goes over to another subject.
— Why don't you understand? I mean the encounter: the meeting of the strange young man with my girl took place on Główna Street. He began going out with her, for so long, until I, the broken mother, consented to the match, and in a lucky hour, right after Sukkot, they set up a wedding canopy. I am a washerwoman; all my years I have washed laundry. I have broken hands and fingers, and today I am already old and can no longer work at my trade. With toil and torment I collected grosz by grosz, I saved from my own mouth. Here, look at me, see how I look. My face is already extinguished, my hands withered, and altogether I am already half dead. Yes, I have slaved hard and bitterly all my years, and the only consolation was that I would be privileged to marry off my daughter. What does a mother not do for a child? I rented her a flat, bought a bit of furniture, clothed him, gave him food until the wedding — what more could I have done?
None of it helped. Recently — it was Friday — my daughter had shopped for the Sabbath, wanted everything to be nice and good, but her husband, my son-in-law so to speak, got up in the morning and said he was going to the artisans' association, because a delegate of the artisans had come from Warsaw, and it was possible he would get a diploma. That was only a pretext. A whole day went by and he did not come. My daughter had already lit the candles and began waiting for her husband, but she sits and waits and he does not come. On the table the challahs are ready, wine for kiddush, but the one to make kiddush is not there. The candles are already going out and still there is no sign of him.
My daughter grows impatient, she runs to the bed and at once raises a cry: Mother, he has taken the 100 zł. from under the pillow!
Ah, then I already felt that the disaster was complete. He took her last hard-earned groszy and ran away. What does one do now? At least write it in the newspapers. He has a brother in Katowice; perhaps he has run off there.
Dear people, on the contrary, I ask you: is there justice in the world? How can one take a poor washerwoman and break her like that, and make her child so unhappy and leave her a living agunah [a wife chained to an absent husband]? Say it yourselves, has such a thing ever happened in the world? Is the world already so lawless that a man may abandon his own wife and take her last groszy as well? Tell me, have you ever heard of such a thing?
We explained to the woman that she is not the first and not the last, and that even greater crimes happen in the world. But the naive woman would not let herself be comforted, and went off with her lament-question: how can it be, how can a world exist without justice and without righteousness?
In truth, how right the plain, simple Jewish woman is.

To the Jewish Population of Zagłębie.

We hereby inform you that a special department for tourism and aliyah matters has been founded within our association, which has set itself the task of taking an interest in every single Jew who comes to Eretz Israel from Poland: to ease his way by every possible means through the difficulties every new oleh faces on getting off the ship, with transferring the baggage; to help him right at the first step he sets on the soil of Eretz Israel, from the most elementary trifles up to the settling-in of himself and his family; to help him by word and deed in all matters connected with his settling in every sphere of economic life in Eretz Israel. By founding this department we wanted to correct the various mistakes that made themselves felt in the days of the Fourth Aliyah. Had the aliyah of that time, in the year 1925, which consisted for the most part of Polish Jews, found here in Eretz Israel an organised Polish body, acquainted and versed in the Eretz-Israel possibilities of existence with all their conditions, and had it then taken an interest in the olim of that time, we would not have had the sad phenomenon of the "yordim" period, which brought with it undesired results. And now, as we stand on the threshold of the Fifth Aliyah, our association has resolved to avoid all the mistakes that were made at the time.
There are already in Eretz Israel various circles of Polish Jews who have taken good root there and are familiar with all the conditions one needs to know in settling into every sphere of the economy and industry, and who already have sufficient experience from their own practice. Among these circles there are also well-known public activists, known for their public work while still in Poland. We therefore turn to every Jew in Zagłębie who intends to make aliyah to Eretz Israel to get in touch with us, and we are always ready to help him within the limits of our possibilities in every respect. We also point out that at the port there is always a delegate of ours, who gives every kind of help the oleh needs. Every oleh or tourist can send his belongings straight from home directly to our address, and we will take off the baggage and settle everything at the customs office, and so every oleh will save superfluous, unnecessary expenses.
A very great and important task rests on all of us at the present moment: we must make every effort that the present aliyah be a blessing for the country and for the olim themselves. Our work is voluntary, and we hope that Polish Jewry will grant us its trust.
Association of Olim from Poland (Hitachdut Olei Polania), Tel Aviv.

The Winter Season in Trade Has Completely Failed

[Economy — crisis, transport and taxes.]
A standstill in all branches. — Enormous fall in rail freight and postal traffic. — Taxes must be reduced.
The winter season, which is always in full swing for the shops [?], has this year failed all along the line. Turnover is minimal, much smaller than last year, while warehouses everywhere are full of goods, even though almost all factories have produced much less than in previous years. This situation was bound to lead to all factories carrying out, on a larger or smaller scale, a reduction of workers. Because of the severe crisis, the unceasing growth of unemployment and the chronic shortage of cash, supply is considerably greater than demand; this causes prices to keep falling, but the cheapness of goods brings no benefit whatsoever to consumers. They do not buy even at the cheapest prices, because they have no money. The consequences of the minimal turnover are felt not only by private entrepreneurs but, to a quite considerable degree, also by state enterprises and state institutions. Freight transport on the railways has fallen colossally, as we see from the following figures: in the first half of 1929, 33 million tons of goods were carried on the Polish railways. In the first half of 1930 freight transport had already fallen to 26.4 million tons. In 1931, in the first 6 months, only 24.8 million tons were carried; [this year] freight transport amounted to barely 18 million tons, i.e. compared with last year, freight carried on the railways fell by 28 percent in the current year. Compared with 1929 the decline amounts to a full 45 percent. Transport of artificial fertilizer shrank from one million 57 thousand tons to 370 thousand tons. Coal and coke: in 1929, 15.5 million tons were carried; in 1932 only 9.4 million tons. Timber — in 1929 over four million tons, this year — 2.1 million tons. Grain, potatoes and beets, of which about a million tons were carried in 1929, have now fallen to 752 thousand tons. In more or less the same proportion transport fell for steel, iron, textile goods, "peynvel" [?], haberdashery, etc.
The same process can be observed in postal traffic. People write far fewer letters and postcards. In 1929, 675 million ordinary domestic letters were sent; in 1931 — 159 million. Postcards: 155 million were sent in 1929, in 1931 only 111 million. Samples: about nine and a half million were sent in 1929, in 1931 only 6.6 million. Ordinary foreign letters: 62.2 million were sent in 1929, 13.6 million postcards, over 10 million items of printed matter — in 1931 only 18 million letters, 7.4 million postcards and 7.6 million items of printed matter.
The same decline occurs in telegrams, telephones and the dispatch of valuables.
The figures given above provide a clear picture of the terrible decline of economic life, especially when one also takes into account that in the current year the situation is much worse than in 1931.
Industry, commerce, agriculture, the crafts, the stock exchange, etc., are going through an extraordinarily severe crisis. All are fighting with their last strength to hold on to their positions. But the ground keeps slipping away from under their feet. Turnover has shrunk, but taxes are not reduced; can this disproportion last long? The taxes will, after all, in the end completely ruin the commercial establishments (placówki) and the workshops.
At the beginning of the current year arrears in unpaid taxes amounted to a sum of one billion 300 million złoty. Now the sum is surely much larger, for from where, from what sources, is the impoverished population to take the money to pay the large current taxes and also the tax arrears? Everyone is already ruined, or stands on the threshold of ruin.
The decisive factors must absolutely reckon with the catastrophic situation if they do not want to bring the country to complete collapse and turn all taxpayers into common beggars. The current taxes must be reduced, and the tax arrears must be forgiven. Otherwise we shall keep sinking into the abyss of crisis and collapse.
Oskar Berman.
May It Get Better!

[Economy — taxes — trade licences.]
For the first time in all the years of Sanacja rule we are able to record concessions for commerce that have real significance.
The new circular of the Finance Ministry provides for a possible reduction of trade licences ("patents").
Thus, for example, if an enterprise of the second category had a turnover in 1931 of only 30 thousand złoty, it may buy a licence of the 3rd category.
Other enterprises too may go down from one licence category to a lower one, if they had a relatively small turnover.
Very small enterprises, on the other hand, which had a turnover of less than 2000 złoty a year, may be exempted from a licence altogether.
Although one cannot say that these concessions will simply rescue commercial existence from ruin — for no business has yet perished because of the differences between licences — they nevertheless undoubtedly bring a great easing of the difficulties of commerce.
We know, after all, with what torments the shopkeeper manages to buy his licence, and that for this he must turn for help to banks or to the members' organization, in order to stay on his feet. And how much harder it is to pay further superfluous hundreds, or tens of złoty, for a business that is not to blame!
As long as the economic level of the population had not yet reached the edge of the abyss, the Ministry did not reckon with the difficulties; every year the number of licences purchased decreased, and no serious steps were taken to halt the downhill course. This year, however, the impetuous decline was already too strong, and it had to be halted.
Moreover, until now small businesses kept no bookkeeping, and the government held the notion that the shopkeeper could not be trusted not to fool them, that he submits incorrect reports of his turnover anyway — even taxation here is not founded on trust! — and so the same measure was applied to licences as well. But now the reform is being considered under which all businesses, even the smallest, will have to keep books. The government has for the first time extended a hand to the merchant, to help him arrange his affairs with full accountability and exact punctuality, to give the state its share and to be able to live himself as well.
It goes without saying that the dead letter of the circular still has quite small significance if it is not brought to life with the dew of mutual trust and the sincere will on the part of those in power really to preserve the existence of commerce, which is writhing in death convulsions.
And here the Jewish aspect must step into the foreground.
Here in Poland Jews have formal equal rights. No decree and no concession is officially created specially on account of Jews. And there are surely also many Christian merchants who struggle with the licence question and will now seek comfort and relief in the new circular.
But for the Jews in Poland commerce is, after all, the backbone of the economy. And it is the Jews who have, after all, suffered most until now from the distrust arising from misunderstandings.
Our only wish now is that the new measure should apply to everyone equally.
For if one part of the population benefits from the concessions more than the other part, it will only serve to push that part still further out of its positions, and for it the concession will turn into a fresh decree!
Let us hope that this will not happen.
P. K.
The Jewish Heroine Judith

[Hanukkah — essay.]
Mikri.

Always, when one contemplates the miracle of Hanukkah, the "Hasmoneans" and the heroism of the Maccabees are invariably pushed to the foreground — they who bravely fought the enemy's incomparably stronger military, which had threatened to destroy the Jewish kingdom and the Jewish people, and in the end were completely victorious. Remarkable, however, is the fact that on this occasion the name of the Jewish woman "Judith" is almost never mentioned, she who through her heroism actually contributed in great measure to the victory of the Hasmoneans. This is perhaps explained by the fact that we find no hint whatsoever about the Jewish heroine "Judith" in our historical books; she is mentioned only in the Book of "Judith", which already belongs to the "Apocrypha" (sefarim hitsonim).

In this little book, "Judith", it is indeed told, with the familiar biblical simplicity and laconic brevity, how the beautiful widow "Judith daughter of Merari", a resident of the town of "Betul" [Bethulia] (in the province of Judea), undertook during the "Wars of the Hasmoneans" to protect her town from an attack by the Syrian army commander Holofernes, and thereby to avert the danger to the whole kingdom of Judea. In a truly diplomatic manner she succeeded in penetrating the enemy camp, where she was soon led to Holofernes. Astonished by her courage and enchanted by her extraordinary beauty, Holofernes gave a festive banquet in Judith's honour. In the night, while Holofernes was asleep, Judith killed him with his own sword, and with his severed head she returned to Betul. Having no commander any more, the army of Syria was thrown into confusion. The Jews took advantage of that moment: they went out to battle and won a victory.

That is the whole story as we find it in the "Book of Judith". In this short and simple tale the person of Judith, her individuality as a woman and heroine, is not emphasized, and is not even mentioned. Nor is the Greek tyrant Holofernes characterized any more than other warlike and tyrannical types with whom the Jewish people had to stand face to face — as, for example, a "Rabshakeh" or a "Nebuzaradan".

It is precisely on this circumstance that modern historical research dwells, seeking to delve into this remarkable historical event, to grasp the psychological state of the main characters, Judith and Holofernes, and so to supply the deficiencies which the author of the Book of "Judith" forgot, or did not find necessary, to fill.

The cruel Syrian army commander Holofernes is presented to us by the modern commentators as a mighty, a whole and a strong personality, who sets himself with unheard-of insolence "against Heaven" (klapei shmaya). And precisely because of this exaggerated, imagined sense of power and the self-persuaded consciousness of his invincibility, Holofernes in the end becomes the tragic figure who, by his downfall, demonstrates the sublimity of Divine Providence, in whose name and under whose shield the Jews waged the unequal war.

The messenger whom Providence makes use of is — Judith. But in order to possess the moral capacity and the physical strength to be a heroine, Judith must necessarily possess such virtues, such extraordinary qualities, as set her above the other Jewish women of that epoch.

And here modern Bible research indeed reveals to us a particularly characteristic picture of our heroine Judith, who is depicted as an extraordinary woman with a strong temperament, endowed besides with a great spirit and a firm will. Judith was indeed "officially" a widow, but, remarkably, her feeble husband, who died shortly after the wedding, had not managed to touch her. So the lonely Judith lives as a "virgin widow", yearning for a fitting man, whom she could not find among the petty Jewish young men around her. The only comfort in this sad situation of hers she finds in her strong trust in God and her great piety, in which she used to drown her worries and sad thoughts about her strange condition.

But then came "a time of trouble" (et tsara) upon the kingdom of Judea, and consequently also a danger to her native town of Betul. The tyrannical, insolent Syrian army commander Holofernes besieged her town with a great host — a town lying at the centre of the flaring war. Now Judith feels within herself an incomprehensible but strong, instinctive urge to undertake some extraordinary step, to carry out a heroic deed, in order to save her town and with it the whole land of Judea. Something draws her unconsciously into the enemy camp, but when she stands face to face with the cruel Holofernes, a "remonic" [so printed; presumably "demonic"] force awakens in her: the consciousness that she is still a young, beautiful, warm-blooded woman, with an unsatisfied feeling of love and tenderness. In vain she wrestles with herself, in vain is her prayer "not to be led into temptation and not to honour the one whom she despises". It does not help: Judith succumbs to the awakened feeling of love, but after she comes to her senses it becomes clear to her that she has betrayed her mission, that she has not withstood the temptation and has become unfaithful to her moral principles; and when she afterwards kills Holofernes, she no longer regards herself as an instrument of Divine Providence — rather, she thereby takes revenge for her weakness, which she now recognizes as a great sin.

It must be added that this peculiar interpretation of Judith's heroic deed, in connection with her extraordinary situation between "maiden and widow" and her unsatisfied erotic desire, is a product of poetic fantasy. This explanation, however, was made not for the sake of originality, but for other, deeper purposes. And through Judith's deed modern Bible criticism means to portray her heroism not merely as the result of the erotic feeling awakened toward a strong, powerful, albeit hostile, man; rather, it aims thereby to represent at the same time the eternal struggle of the two sexes — which is supposed to have been, from the outset, the main idea of the author of the "Book of Judith".
