Export and Import

A long time ago we drew attention to the abnormal phenomenon, which has by now even become a tradition, that the few handicraft articles exported from Poland abroad are shipped out by middlemen, and the craftsman not only does not enjoy the benefit that export brings, but is himself exploited to the utmost by the exporter. We cited at the time, as an example, the ready-made clothing (konfekcja) trade, which is exported on a large scale — and not by craftsmen.
If we are not mistaken, we also expressed the opinion that the question of export had, through various circumstances, become a "monopoly article" of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry, and that the Chambers of Crafts ought to take an interest in it, and not only take the export of handicraft articles under their protection and supervision, but also strive to find new sales markets for the crafts.
Our appeal remained a voice crying in the wilderness, and were it not for external factors, it is highly doubtful whether the Chambers of Crafts would have occupied themselves with the question more seriously.
Lately, however, a whole upheaval has taken place in the Chambers. Questionnaires are being filled in, material is being collected in connection with a possible export and import of handicraft articles. And this happened not out of a conviction that it is necessary, but because in the coming months Poland will have to conclude a series of trade agreements with various countries. The government, wanting practical material, turned to other institutions and also to the Council of the Chambers of Crafts to supply it with such material.
That, then, is the reason why such intensive work is going on in the Chambers.
The question, however, is so important that, regardless of the reason why it has now surfaced on the agenda, one must see to it that the material the government demands is supplied to it [as printed, "איר"[?]] in rich measure and in detailed form. Only conscious representatives of the various trades are capable of providing this, and we will try to explain more precisely how important the collection of material is, and especially for the crafts.
To strengthen export, or to introduce the export of an article that has not been exported until now, or to hinder the import of an article that is manufactured in the country, there are several means.
To make possible the export of an article, the government must see to it that the import duty in the country to which the article is to be exported is not too high; to hinder import, on the other hand, the government must introduce the so-called protective tariff, i.e. a high duty, so that it does not pay exporters from other countries to bring in the goods. There is yet another possibility: a manufactured product that is not made in Poland, raw material or a semi-finished product needed for further processing in Poland require, in turn, that the government make possible, through a low duty, the import of these articles into the country.
Every government must strive to exploit all possibilities in such cases, and instead of permitting another government to import an article it needs, it demands in return permission to import into that country, at a low duty, an article which it is able to export. Making use of all these factors means pursuing a rational tariff policy, and this is what all nations strive for.
When big industry feels a difficulty, be it in export or in import, it is able through its influence, by means of interventions, to obtain from the government what it demands. The crafts and small industry do not have the possibilities to carry out their postulates, and now perhaps the moment has come for the crafts, too, to have their say on the question — and this in view of a fact that occurs very rarely: whether through a calculation of the government or by chance, Poland will in the coming months renew most of its trade treaties, at least the most important of them. The material of which we spoke at the beginning of the article is thus needed for this purpose. While big industry can often carry out its postulates even during the period when the treaties are in force, the crafts and small industry, as said, cannot. Therefore the opportune moment must not be let slip, and if the craftsmen's representatives have sufficient material, this may perhaps make possible an export of handicraft articles. And it is surely superfluous to remark, it seems, that export is capable of improving the situation of the craftsmen and giving them new sources of livelihood. It is therefore very desirable that every trade think it over well and strive with all its strength to do something in this matter, in order to help.
B. Frajnd.
What Is Gemilut Chesed According to Our Time?

[Essay / Charity and gemilut chesed.] Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". By Prof. Moshe Schorr [Mojżesz Schorr, orientalist at Warsaw University and rabbi of the Great Synagogue on Tłomackie].
The ethics of Judaism is, in its deepest essence, a teaching about the happiness of the community (klal), in contrast to Hellenism, which considered all ethical problems solely from the standpoint of the highest well-being of the i n d i v i d u a l (yachid). All the problems — or, better said, the ethical laws of Judaism — revolve around the community and its well-being.
The entire biblical legislation aims not at the happiness and well-being of the individual, but has in mind the happiness and contentment of all together: the individual can, and is obliged to, find his highest happiness in the general happiness.
This s o c i a l element, which is the very deepest principle of our ethics, goes so far [printed "ווייס"] that its highest ideal, the ideal of holiness (kedusha), i.e. of the highest moral perfection, is addressed as a postulate not to the single person but to the whole people ("Ye shall be holy"). And the road to this ideal leads through the institutions for social welfare, which are stages toward the ever greater happiness of the whole people.
As a consequence of such a principled view toward a social-ethical — and not an individual-eudaemonistic — ideal, there emerges the feeling of moral responsibility of each one of us, especially for ensuring that happiness should constantly grow.
"Tsedaka", according to this view, is not an expression of the goodness of the individual, who, when he wishes, can give an alms, and when he wishes, can refuse it; rather it is a categorical duty arising from the feeling of justice toward one's neighbour [printed "גאנטסטן" for "נאנטסטן"] — as the very word t s e d a k a (justice) confirms beyond any doubt; and the alms is rather an alms that springs from duty, from which no one can exempt himself. (Compare: tithe [ma'aser], heave-offering [teruma], the corner of the field [pe'a], the forgotten sheaf [shikheha], gleanings [leket], etc.)
A further consequence of this view about the lasting happiness of the community is the teaching that tsedaka must not bear the character of a momentary, hand-to-mouth help, nor of individual help from hand to hand merely to satisfy the moral sentiment; rather this help must be imbued with the idea of a p u r p o s e f u l n e s s thought through in advance, and aimed at being lasting, so as to secure the existence of one's neighbour.
Clearly, and within the framework of a social imperative, this principle is formulated in the words of Moses:
"And if thy brother be waxen poor, and his hand fail with thee, then thou shalt relieve him [printed "והחוקה" for "והחזקת"]: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee" (Leviticus 25:36 [as printed; the verse is 25:35]).
That is the essence of our entire social legislation: "that thy brother may live with thee" (Leviticus 25:36).
With the same idea of lasting, p r o d u c t i v e help the entire legislation of the Talmud is imbued, which merely develops further and adapts [the printed phrase is garbled: "פאסט צו בעווייזן, צו צו"] to the conditions of the time the principles [printed "פריציפן"] of the Law of Moses. To prove this one passage suffices (Tractate Shabbat 43a [as printed; actually 63a]): "Greater is he who lends than he who gives charity, and he who puts [money] in the purse [i.e. invests in partnership with the poor man] is greatest of all" [printed "ומטין" for "ומטיל"].
This principle is formulated even more clearly elsewhere (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 41b): "Three things were said about charity [printed "בצרקה"]: he who gives charity brings a blessing upon himself; he who lends is better than he [printed "ממגו"]; he who gives for half the profit [i.e. a partnership] — he is above them all."
Such tsedaka is the true gemilut chasadim, the true compassion, which flows from the feelings of the individual but aims at the lasting happiness of the whole community, Klal Yisrael.
In this sense the i n t e r e s t - f r e e loan funds, whose goal is the lasting consolidation of the well-being of the broadest masses of our society through p r o d u c t i v e loans, deserve the name gemilut chasadim in the best sense of the word. The journal which has set itself the main goal of propagating t h i s  i d e a of social help is to be wished that it may develop in the best way, that it may go forth under the slogan "and thou shalt relieve him... that thy brother may live with thee", and it will have a great social merit.
The Last Little Leaf

The last little leaf of the calendar has already run out, so provide yourself with a new calendar for the year 1933. But do not forget to ask exclusively for the Zaglembie calendar "Di Vokh" ["The Week"].
The Eighth Candle

Is it really the eighth candle today? And I thought Hanukkah had already been dragging on for several weeks.
This year the pleasure of the Hanukkah candles has been taken from us. But tell me, I beg you, what pleasure of Hanukkah do we still have left?
Cards. Once, when one was allowed to play in honour of Hanukkah, it truly was a delight; but today, when people play poker winter and summer, by day and by night, the whole week and on Sabbath — who even remembers that today is Hanukkah?
Latkes. Once, when at Hanukkah they served the dish of fragrant, steaming potato pancakes, and the aroma tickled your nostrils and the taste caressed your palate and the fat ran down your lips and over your fingers — then you really felt the beloved holiday.
But today, when my menu includes broth with latkes once a week, and every Wednesday I am served on a little plate three small latkes with the broth — thin little latkes, dry, well baked, not over-greased — and I hold the latke on my fork and eat it slowly: a bite of latke and a spoonful of broth — what pleasure can I still get from the Hanukkah latkes?
Well, anyway, for us grown-ups Hanukkah was always a meagre holiday. What kind of holiday is it, when the shop is open and the bills of exchange have to be paid and your head is spinning? The main thing is that Hanukkah was always a children's holiday. So how do the little ones feel Hanukkah today?
First of all, the heder. When we were children, we studied in heder seven days a week, 50 weeks a year and 12 hours a day — we were always studying; what we actually learned is another question. So when Hanukkah came and we were free for eight whole evenings, it truly felt festive, no small thing: from Minha on you were your own master [?], go where you like, do what you like — nobody says a word to you!
But today, for our many sins, when they study 5 hours a day, 6 days a week and 30 weeks a year — true, it is arguable that they learn more than in the old days — and as for Minha prayers, nobody knows of them at all — so, what is different? What is the difference between a Hanukkah evening and the whole year?
Yes, dreidels. Tell me yourselves, by all means: can one compare the dreidel that the melamed's assistant made in heder, while the children watched how the lead bubbled and poured and took shape, and out came the little body with the little head and the little foot and the four mystical little letters, and the children's eyes sparkled and their mouths drooled [?] with wonder — with the dreidel the calendar-seller sells for 20 groszy: ready-made, machine-made, turned on a lathe and polished, like a porcelain doll? I would really like to know who buys that dreidel and who plays with it.
And what about Hanukkah gelt? The money matter is a bit complicated. In former years, when a child never saw a grosz from his mother, but every day took to heder a slice of bread with a round of farmer's cheese, or a piece [?] of herring, a two-grosz coin of Hanukkah gelt really meant a great deal. In recent years a schoolchild used to take a few ten-grosz coins of pocket money every day, and Hanukkah gelt lost all its charm for him. Now, however, that is over. Jews have no money. It is bad enough that there is none for school fees, and certainly none for pocket money — what consolation can one get from a few groszy of Hanukkah gelt?
Nothing more — except that things are now about to turn around. If we do not pay Hoover the instalment, and others do not pay either, perhaps a grosz will be left rolling around in our pockets and there will be something for the child too. But I can assure you that by this year's Zot Hanukkah it will not come to pass — let us hope by next year!...
What else is left of Hanukkah? Oh, a great deal, especially for the child. Hanukkah is, after all, the holiday of the Maccabees! Jewish heroism! National renaissance! Raise, children, the blue-and-white flags, line up in rows, take up the spirit of Judah the Maccabee and march forward like soldiers. Forward — mountains and valleys will be levelled before you, until you reach the border of the old-new national home.
But no. It does not go so smoothly. Besides the flag and the enthusiasm one must also have a certificate, and certificates are handed out on the tip of a fork; one has to fight for them, one has to wage stubborn battles. Almost as stubborn as those the first Maccabee once waged against the Greeks!...
And this Maccabean struggle does not begin with the first candle, nor does it end with the eighth. It goes on all year round. Armed camps stand against one another: here Hashomer, there Hehalutz and over there Betar. People sink their teeth and nails into the certificates, just as the Hasmoneans of old into the enemy's trophies. And when they are not fighting with their hands, they fight with pens, with resolutions, communiqués and manifestos and all sorts of other paper weapons, and the battles go on every day of the year. And everywhere, all over the world, wherever there are Jews, people stand in battle readiness, fully armed: the sword in one hand, the pen in the other — the only pity is that a third hand is missing to hold the trowel for building the national home — —
What is left of Hanukkah? But today it is, after all, already the eighth candle — so says the calendar.
Argus.

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Miketz
The Portion
—o—
a) "And it came to pass at the end of two full years" (Gen. 41:1)
"'Happy is the man who has made bashem [sic] his trust' — this is Joseph. 'And has not turned to the arrogant' — because he said to the chief butler 'remember me and mention me', two years were added to him." Midrash Rabbah.
"Who has made the Lord his trust" — usually a person wants this: if God wants him to put his trust in Him, let Him first give him riches and wealth, and in return he will be good and pious. God, however, wants the person to put his trust in Him: let him be good and pious, and then He will give him all good things. But "it is better to take refuge in the Lord than to trust in man." Surer, after all, is certainly God... and rather than God having to trust in man — "than to trust in man" — it is surely more fitting "to take refuge in the Lord" — that man should put his trust in God... Yalkut Tov.
• • •
"Put not your trust in princes, in the son of man in whom there is no help" —
Put not your trust in princes: do not rely on the rich, they help sparingly. "In the son of man who has nothing — there is help": help comes faster from those who have nothing, from the poor... A poor man helps out faster... Imrei Hen.
—o—
b) "Forasmuch as God has shown you all this" (ibid., 39)
There is an anecdote that in Prague two householders once came to a din Torah. Since their houses stood close to one another, it happened that musicians came and played between the two houses. One claimed: they played in my honor; the other claimed: they played in my honor. The rabbi has himself paid the ruling fee and pronounces his ruling:
— Not in your honor and not in your honor did they play, but in mine, so that I could earn a ruling fee...
That is what Pharaoh said: as I see it, the whole dream with the famine is only in your honor, so that you should become great... Yadav Emunah.
—o—
c) "There is none so discreet and wise as you" (ibid.)
That is indeed praise: first discreet (navon) and only then wise (hakham). For usually Jews are "a wise and understanding people, this great nation" — Jews are wise first and only then discerning; they play the clever ones before they have thought a matter through... Imrei Hen.
—o—
d) "I am Pharaoh" (ibid., 44)
It happens more than once that someone is made great, and afterwards he uses his power against the very one who made him great... That is why Pharaoh said to Joseph: "And without you no man shall lift up his hand" — that is how great I am making you — but "I am Pharaoh": remember that it was I who made you great... Kiflayim le-Tushiyah.
—o—
e) "And God Almighty give you mercy" (Gen. 43:14)
"He who said to His world 'Enough' — may He say to my troubles 'Enough'." Midrash.
What is the meaning of this?
The four [sic] patriarchs of the world lived — says the Midrash — five hundred years, corresponding to the five hundred years' journey of the world. So Jacob knew how long he had left to live. Had the world been bigger, he would have lived longer. And therefore "He who said to His world 'Enough' — may He say to my troubles 'Enough'" — since I have but little left to live, let me at least have something good in my life.. Edut bi-Yehosef.
—o—
f) "And they drank and were merry with him" (ibid., 34)
The Liser [?] Rav once came to Lemberg [Lwów], to the "Yeshuot Yaakov", on an agunah matter. He arrived at night. The rabbi was given a separate little room. For supper the rabbi had two liters of strong mead brought to him.
The next morning R' Mordechai Zeev, the son of the Lemberg rabbi, comes in to him and finds a large written responsum by the Liser Rav, which he had composed during the night after drinking up the two liters of mead. R' Mordechai Zeev looks into the responsum and sees that it is a wonder of wonders. He asks him:
— I know that you are a genius, but how does one write such a responsum after drinking so much mead?
The Liser Rav answers him:
— The Gemara says (Yoma 71a): "He who wishes to pour a libation of wine upon the altar should fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine." Why are the throats of Torah scholars compared to the altar? Because just as the altar does not let the wine into itself (see Yoma), so too the throat of a Torah scholar does not take in the wine — he does not feel it and it does not bother him...
—o—
g) "And as for you, go up [printed 'alei', for 'alu'] in peace to your father" (Gen. 44:17)
Joseph thought to himself: I know you, after all; I have indeed locked up your brother, but it is not in your nature to be troubled by your brother's grief... You will go home in peace, just as contentedly as you went away after throwing me into the pit... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
Hanukkah.
h) "Who performed miracles for our fathers in those days, at this season."
In our own time too the same miracles occur; in our own time too there are Antiochuses who want the same as those Antiochuses, and through miracles we too are saved from their hands... Hashvah le-Tovah.
—o—
i) Hanukkah gelt..
To R' Gershon Henekh of Radzyń [Radzyń Podlaski] came a dentist during Hanukkah to pull out an aching tooth. Before leaving, the dentist would not take any fee:
— Let it be Hanukkah gelt...
Says R' Gershon Henekh to him:
— For heaven's sake, just don't tell the householders of my town, because every one of them will want to pull a tooth out of me instead of giving Hanukkah gelt...
—o—
j) The secret of cards...
R' Itzikl Harif once saw his disciples sitting over a game of cards during Hanukkah. He said to them: I will tell you the secret of cards:
When God went to create the world, Falsehood (sheker) came and argued: why do You create me, God, so that I should deceive the world? Who will believe me anyway?
Likewise, when they went to create Satan (satan), he argued: why create me? Who will obey me and sin?
God answered: see, I have deliberately given you the letter Shin at the beginning of your names (Sh-atan; Sh-eker), because the letter Shin is an 'ot de-kshot', a letter of truth, a symbol of truth (see Zohar, Bereshit, folio 12), and with the little bit of truth you possess you will lead people astray and bring them to falsehood and to Satan.
Later people came to hate the truth so much that they took the letter of truth out of 'sheker' and 'satan', and what was left was: -ker, -tan, that is: karten [Yiddish for 'cards']...
That is the secret of cards...
Imrei Tzaddikim.
“Its Time Has Passed, Its Offering Is Void”

[Advertisement — the “Di Vokh” calendar.]
It is an old rule that every question must be considered in its time — all the more so when it concerns a topical matter, which later gets lost and afterwards no longer has its proper value and importance.
Tomorrow your calendar comes to an end, and although the Zagłębie calendar “Di Vokh” [“The Week”] is already popular enough among all strata of the population, we nevertheless wish to believe that there are many people who have not yet had it, for various reasons, and chiefly because not every buyer pays attention to the merchandise. Many people are so naive that whoever brings them a calendar is the one they buy from, and they do not consider what kind of publication it is.
We therefore turn chiefly to those who have never yet had our calendar: this time let them ask for this one specifically and examine it carefully, and they will then become convinced that no other calendar whatsoever can compare with the Zagłębie calendar “Di Vokh”, which, besides its various merits, has candle-lighting times specially for Zagłębie, with the approval of the Będzin rabbinate.
So do not forget to ask for “Di Vokh”, first quality.
A Hanukkah Miracle

[A Hasidic Hanukkah tale.]
An awesome tale: how Reb Berishl of Wolbórz saved a Jewish daughter from a sorcerer's hand.
In the little town of Pantshne [?] near Piotrków there lived a Jew, a great host of guests, who was renowned throughout the whole region for his righteousness and his piety. He was a Jew whose equal one would have to search for, and therefore his life, too, was not as simple and ordinary as another man's.
And it came to pass that Reb Zanvl had a daughter growing up, and he began to look for a match for her. So he travelled to Wolbórz, and Reb Shmuel Shloyme, an intimate of the old Rebbe of Wolbórz, made a match for him with a fine young man. The betrothal agreement [tna'im] was written right away in Wolbórz, and the wedding was set for Hanukkah.
When Reb Zanvl came home and wished his daughter “mazel tov”, she indeed answered quietly, “may it be in a lucky hour”, as befits a virtuous Jewish daughter. But from that day on one could see that something was wrong with the girl, and she went about as if in a world of chaos. Reb Zanvl did not know what to think or where this came from. But as was his way, he was absorbed in “business matters” and in his chief mitzvah, hospitality to guests: every day he had other arriving guests and wandering paupers to look after, and in all this he almost forgot that his daughter was somehow not quite herself.
One morning a coach drawn by two [?]-horses drove up to Reb Zanvl's house, and out of the coach stepped a special messenger from the squire of Dubershov [?], who had Zanvl told that he should come out to the squire at once: the squire had a deal to make with him, by which he stood to grow rich.
Reb Zanvl immediately drove over to Dubershov. The squire was very glad to see him and offered him a stretch of good forest, and while they were talking he wished him mazel tov and promised that when he was in town he would call on Reb Zanvl and bring a gift for his daughter the bride.
Reb Zanvl made the deal and indeed earned a handsome few hundred roubles, and the squire also kept his word: he came and brought a fine gift for his daughter. But as he handed the gift to the bride she turned pale, and with trembling hands she took the gift without uttering a word.
From that day on the bride became ever quieter and more withdrawn; she went about the house for whole days without uttering a word, and her parents did not know the reason. When they asked her what was the matter with her, she answered: nothing. And so time ran on, and the wedding date drew near.
Reb Zanvl prepared a wedding on a lavish scale. Special tables were set up for guests, and food was cooked [?] fit for a king. But when everything was ready and the klezmorim had already begun to play the “reception” tune, the bride suddenly waved her hand to the musicians as a sign that she had something to say. The musicians stopped and wanted to hear what the bride wished to say, but they all saw in horror that the bride was holding her mouth open, straining with all her strength to bring a word out of her mouth, but it would not come — she had been struck dumb, God spare us, and her power of speech had been taken from her entirely.
Well, there arose an uproar and wailing — such a calamity, on the wedding day! Reb Zanvl already wanted to run off to Wolbórz, but the in-law said to him: it's lost, Reb Zanvl, the wedding must be put off...
The weeping and screaming of the bride's mother were of no help: the wedding was postponed, the guests dispersed, the musicians went home, and Reb Zanvl left everything behind and the next morning set off for Wolbórz.
Arriving at the Wolbórz study house, he ran straight in to the beadle, Reb Dovidl, and told him what calamity had befallen him. Nothing else, Reb Zanvl told him, but that it must be witchcraft by the squire of Dubershov, who is known as a great sorcerer...
Having heard out Reb Zanvl's troubles, Reb Dovidl says: today, after all, we light the first candle; I don't know whether Reb Berishl will want to receive you, but what is lost is lost — I will go in and tell him.
When the beadle conveyed the sad news to Reb Berishl, the old man, of blessed memory, was seized by such faintness of heart that one could plainly see his very life was at stake. He ordered the beadle to let no one else into the shtibl, and he secluded himself a whole day and there stormed the heavens.
Toward evening, at Minha and Ma'ariv, Reb Berishl came into the study house to pray with the congregation, and at once he went back into his private room and again prayed and turned worlds upside down.
It was already long after Ma'ariv; people were waiting with the lighting of the Hanukkah candles, but the Rebbe Reb Berishl was still locked in his private room.
The tension among the crowd kept growing. Bold Hasidim could not restrain themselves, crept up to the door of the Rebbe Reb Berishl's private room and peeped in through the keyhole. And there a Hasid heard the Rebbe Reb Berishl crying out: “I shall not move from here” — I will not stir from this spot, I will not light any Hanukkah candle until You, Father in heaven, annul Your decree... The sentence on Reb Zanvl and his daughter is too harsh... I, Berishl of Wolbórz, cannot consent to such a ruinous verdict... “Is this the Torah, and is this its reward?”...
And suddenly the door of Reb Berishl's private room burst open with a crash, and the old man, of blessed memory, rushed in with a shout: Zanvl of Pantshne, light the Hanukkah candles...
The crowd was frightened and astounded. But when the Rebbe Reb Berishl answered “Amen” to Reb Zanvl's blessings, there lay in that Amen such a great spiritual arousal that the study house was literally lifted into the air...
“Ma'oz Tzur Yeshu'ati” [“Rock of Ages”], Reb Berishl himself sang, and afterwards he went up to Reb Zanvl and blessed him loudly before the whole congregation: by the merit of Hanukkah may you be helped, and when you marry off your daughter, for heaven's sake invite me to the wedding...
The next morning, when Reb Zanvl arrived from Wolbórz, a special messenger was waiting for him at the town barrier [rogatka] and brought him the good tidings that last night, at such-and-such an hour — precisely when the Rebbe Reb Berishl was singing “Ma'oz Tzur” — the mute girl had regained her speech. And she talks without stopping and is as cheerful as she had not been since her childhood years...
For joy Reb Zanvl even began to dance. Right after Hanukkah the wedding was celebrated, and Reb Berishl performed the marriage ceremony; and a few days later it suddenly became known that the squire of Dubershov, the sorcerer — may it not befall any Jew — had lost the power of speech...
Ben-Tsiyon Grinboym.
Tramway management's proposal to the magistrate to restrict bus traffic.

[Page banner: p. 7 — "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 53. "What's new in Zagłębie?" — Friday, 1 Tevet 5693 | piątek 30 grudnia 1932 (Friday, 30 December 1932). Section: Będzin.]
The tramway management in Katowice has approached the local magistrate (municipal council) with a proposal that the magistrate should not permit passenger buses to run through the streets where the trams operate.
The proposal is justified on the grounds that the buses have reduced the ridership of the trams.
The proposal was considered at a meeting of the committee for general affairs. The committee members Messrs. Rechnitz [?] and Gutensztajn spoke out against the proposal, pointing out [?] that the magistrate ought to see to it that traffic through the town expands rather than shrinks.
After the discussion it was resolved that the committee, together with the town engineer Mr. Winter, should work out a plan for how the matter is to be regulated.
A number of merchants and shop employees summoned to an inquiry at the police station.

A few weeks ago a well-functioning factory of counterfeit 10-złoty coins was discovered in Dąbrowa.
The arrested "manufacturers" then, during the inquiry, named the firms in Będzin from which they had bought the necessary materials.
Last Wednesday all the owners of drugstores (składy apteczne), paint shops, and the entire staff of the iron firm Jakub Gutman were summoned to the police station (komisariat), where a confrontation with the accused took place.
Examination celebration at the Będzin "Talmud Torah".

On Monday an examination celebration took place at the Będzin Talmud Torah. After the opening by the chairman, Mr. M. M. Janowski, the floor is given to Mr. Chaim Wellner, who dwells on the significance of Hanukkah for the Jewish people. Mr. Wellner dwells in particular on the education of the young generation in the present time in general, and of the local Talmud Torah in particular. Then, on behalf of the rabbinate, the rabbinic judges (morei hora'ah) R' Dan and R' Hanoch David bring greetings and hand over a written greeting from the Rabbi, may he live long and well, who because of his weak state of health was unable to take part in the celebration. Then comes the kindling of the lights, performed by a pupil, and the choir sings "Haneirot Halalu" and "Ma'oz Tzur".
Proceeding to the examination, two pupils delivered aggadah and pilpul sermons, which aroused enthusiasm among the assembled; the scholars present put questions and the pupils answer very much to the point and diligently. Then sweets are distributed among the pupils as Hanukkah gifts.
Mr. Dafner reads out a report on the two months' activity of the new management. From the report it can be seen that the Talmud Torah stands at a much higher level than hitherto; but much more effort is still required from the management, and assistance from the town, to bring the Talmud Torah up to the proper height, so that it may fulfil its proper tasks.
Mr. Wellner thanks, on behalf of the management, the principal, the melamdim (teachers) and those present, and especially the rabbinate, for their participation in the celebration; and in an elevated mood, inspired by the best impressions, the "examination celebration" is closed by the chairman, Mr. Janowski.
The celebration left a very good impression, and the participants went away in an elevated mood.

One loses the ryczałt if one changes the patent or the line of business.

We consider it necessary to draw the attention of all merchants who pay turnover tax as a ryczałt (fixed lump sum) to the fact that for any change one makes in the patent [trade licence] one can lose the ryczałt: for example, if one changes — adds a partner [to the registration]; if instead of the husband the patent is written in the name of the wife, or vice versa — one loses the ryczałt. Likewise one loses the ryczałt if one changes the lines of business, if one adds a new line of business, if one changes the line of business altogether, if one moves into new premises — and with all similar changes [the tax] will be assessed [individually].

Sosnowiec: From January 1st Electric Light Will Cost Less

[Sosnowiec — economy.]
The Małobądz electricity union [power company] has at last somewhat yielded to the demands of its subscribers in Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa, Czeladź and Niwka and decided to make the price of light and of the meter cheaper from January 1st.
Instead of 67 and a half groszy, which it has cost until now, from the New Year it will cost 56 and a quarter groszy. For the meter, until now 1,35 zł., from the New Year — 1,20 zł. Electric power for industrial purposes — instead of 25—30 gr.
Those who until now paid a lump sum (ryczałt) of 30 zł. will pay only 21 zł. 60 gr.
For these „favours“, however, the electricity union received from the Ministry of Trade the right to supply light to the above-mentioned towns for a period of 40 years, i.e. until the year 1972.

"Di Yidishe Bande" (On Their Guest Performances in Zagłębie) — with: Legal Answers; Sylwester Revue at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre

[Zagłębie — Theatre / Review.]
"Di Yidishe Bande" ("The Jewish Band")
(On their guest performances in Zagłębie)
[Cartoon: a horse-drawn wagon labelled "DI IDYSZE BANDE" with portraits of the performers; caption: "Oy vey, 'Dance, little Jews, dance!' / Just live, laugh and kvell — / The Jewish Band is on its way! — / 'The world is shaking'..."]
The "Yidishe Bande" takes leave of Zagłębie today.
For the thousands of visitors from Będzin and Sosnowiec, who were delighted by every song and dance and refreshed by the monologues and sketches, the "bandits" were like a remedy for today's troubles. The audience forgot its everyday worries and was carried away by the merry, sing-along[?] "Jewish Band".
The "Band" relies more on good acting than on content; the folksy primitiveness is often adapted a little too coarsely, sometimes too shrilly, and yet one sees that the "Band" is bold in performance; they present every number clearly, popularly and with a pronounced interpretation.
In their programmes, "Dance, little Jews, dance" and "The world is shaking", Jewish political and social life in Poland is reflected, as are general events in the world.
The "bandists" [sic], the performers of the programme, are well known to all of us. With her unique temperament and Hasidic fire the talented Chana Grosberg storms through "If the Rebbe wishes" and the "Little Passover-Eve Picture"; the audience won't let her leave the stage, which pleases her very much, as Chana Grosberg says: "First of all I want to act, act and act again, and if my strength allowed me I would perform all the numbers"...
The second "bandist" is the lovely, charming Róża Gawel, "the Jewish Ordonka" [after the singer Hanka Ordonówna]; she is a great gain[?] for a revue. She is splendid in her roles, especially in "The Zakopane Mountains".
Lora Folman surprises with her originality; she is artistic in her interpretation, sings heartily and in a folk manner. Yitskhok Perlov's lyrics suit her well.
The "bandits" too work wonders [lit. "work deeds"] and fulfil their tasks conscientiously. Zishe Kac and Dawid Lederman are no new faces here; the Jewish theatre public in Zagłębie has already had enough of them "to sing and to tell". In the half-topical sketch "A Groom for a Złoty" our dear Dawid Lederman works wonders as a matchmaker: he pairs off Zishe Kac with Chana Grosberg "for a złoty", and the audience rolls with laughter.
In the number "Badkhones" [jesting][?] the favourite Zishe Kac is masterly. The number is, first of all, very witty, and Kac accentuates it excellently. His monologue "A Haggadah of the Crisis" is also very successful.
A large share in the great success also goes to the likeable Menashe Openheim in his various roles, which he performs together with Róża Gawel.
The greatest yasher koyach is earned by the director and author Yitskhok Gaushik[?], who spares no effort and work so that "his kleynkunst theatre should become a true reflection of life".
His monologues, especially "The Madman", performed by the author himself, are successful.
The "Band" gives its last performances in Sosnowiec today, and if we are to believe them (bandits, after all), they will come back to us after returning from the Maccabiah in Zakopane.
Sh. L-tsh.
